understanding.title: What a regular expression is
understanding.p1: A regular expression is a small pattern language for describing shapes of text. Instead of asking whether a string equals something, you describe what it must look like — four digits, then a hyphen, then two more digits — and the engine reports every place that shape occurs.
understanding.p2: Most characters stand for themselves: the pattern cat matches the letters c, a, t. The power comes from the handful that do not. A dot means any character, a plus means one or more of whatever came before, square brackets enclose a set to choose from, and parentheses group a run so a quantifier or an alternation can act on the whole of it.
understanding.p3: Reading one is a matter of taking it token by token, which is exactly what the Explanation panel does. Every line names one construct and quotes the slice of the pattern it describes, nested so a quantifier sits under the token it repeats.

syntax.title: The building blocks
syntax.intro: Ten families cover almost everything you will write. The tokens below are ECMAScript syntax; where another flavour differs, the engine section says so.
syntax.tableCaption: Regular expression syntax, grouped by what each family does
syntax.anchorsMeans: Assert a position without consuming a character.
syntax.anchorsExample: ^cat matches cat only at the start.
syntax.classesMeans: Match one character out of a set, or out of everything but a set.
syntax.shorthandsMeans: Named sets: digit, word character, whitespace, and their negations.
syntax.shorthandsExample: \d\d matches two digits in a row.
syntax.quantifiersMeans: Repeat the previous token, greedily by default.
syntax.lazyMeans: The same repetitions, taking as little as they can.
syntax.lazyExample: <.+?> stops at the first closing bracket.
syntax.groupsMeans: Group a run, and capture it so it can be reused or reported.
syntax.alternationMeans: Try the left side, then the right.
syntax.lookaroundMeans: Assert that text does or does not appear either side, without consuming it.
syntax.lookaroundExample: \d+(?= kg) matches a number only before kg.
syntax.backreferencesMeans: Match the same text a capture group matched earlier.
syntax.escapesMeans: Write a literal metacharacter, a control character, or a code point.
syntax.escapesExample: \. matches a full stop, not any character.
syntax.note: When you want a metacharacter to be an ordinary character, put a backslash in front of it. That is why an email pattern reads \. in the middle: an unescaped dot would match any character at all, and the pattern would happily accept name@examplezcom.

flags.title: Every flag
flags.intro: Eight switches, opened from the letters at the right-hand end of the pattern field. Six are real ECMAScript flags the engine reads directly. Two are borrowed from PCRE, and this tool applies them by rewriting the pattern before it compiles.
flags.tableCaption: Every flag, what it changes, and when to reach for it
flags.globalDoes: Keeps searching after the first match instead of stopping there.
flags.globalWhen: You want every occurrence — which is nearly always, when testing.
flags.multilineDoes: Re-points ^ and $ at the start and end of each line rather than the whole string.
flags.multilineWhen: The input is a list, one entry per line.
flags.ignoreCaseWhen: The casing carries no meaning — a keyword, a domain name, a header.
flags.dotAllDoes: Lets the dot match line terminators, which it otherwise refuses.
flags.dotAllWhen: A pattern has to span lines, as when grabbing the body of an HTML element.
flags.extendedDoes: Ignores unescaped whitespace and treats # as the start of a comment.
flags.extendedWhen: A long pattern needs breathing room and notes; escape a space as \ to keep it.
flags.unicodeDoes: Treats the pattern as code points and enables \p{…} property escapes and \u{…}.
flags.unicodeWhen: The text is not plain ASCII — emoji, accents, or non-Latin scripts.
flags.ungreedyDoes: Inverts every quantifier: greedy ones become lazy, and an explicit ? makes them greedy again.
flags.ungreedyWhen: You are porting a PCRE pattern that relied on it; writing +? is clearer in new work.
flags.stickyDoes: Anchors each attempt at the position the previous match ended, so a gap stops the search.
flags.stickyWhen: Tokenising, where a run of matches must be contiguous.
flags.rewriteNote: Extended and ungreedy do not exist in JavaScript. Rather than pretend otherwise, this tool rewrites the pattern: under extended it strips the whitespace and comments the parser ruled inert, and under ungreedy it flips each quantifier in place. The pattern you typed is what gets highlighted and explained; the rewritten one is what the engine runs, and it is shown in full when a compile fails.
flags.defaultsNote: Global and multiline are on by default, which is what makes a list of test lines behave the way most people expect. Everything else is off.

modes.title: Match, substitution, and list
modes.intro: The three modes share one pattern and one test string; they differ in what they do with the matches.
modes.match: Match highlights each match in place and lists it in the Match information panel with its position and every capture group. A group that took no part in a match is reported as such, which is not the same as a group that matched the empty string — a distinction that decides what $1 inserts.
modes.substitute: Substitution rebuilds the whole test string with each match replaced. It follows String.prototype.replace exactly, so what you see in the result box is what that call would return in your own code.
modes.list: List gives one line per match, each expanded through the same replacement tokens. Leave the box empty and you get the matches themselves — useful for pulling a column out of a log.
modes.tableCaption: Replacement tokens and what each one inserts
modes.token_group: Capture group 1; use $2, $3, and so on for the rest.
modes.token_before: Everything in the test string before the match.
modes.token_after: Everything in the test string after the match.
modes.zeroNote: One difference worth knowing if you arrived from regex101: there the whole match is written $0. JavaScript reads $0 literally, and this tool shows what JavaScript does rather than a friendlier fiction, so the whole match is $&. A group number beyond what the pattern declares is likewise left as written — $12 against a pattern with one group inserts group 1 followed by the character 2.

delimiters.title: Why there is a delimiter picker
delimiters.p1: The delimiter never reaches the engine. It decides how the pattern is written down when it leaves this page — as /…/ in JavaScript, or ~…~ in a PHP codebase that prefers it — and therefore which character has to be escaped inside the literal.
delimiters.p2: That escaping is the practical part. A pattern matching a path is full of slashes, and inside a slash-delimited literal every one of them needs a backslash. Switch the delimiter to a tilde and they can stay as they are, which is why PCRE offers the choice at all.
delimiters.p3: Pasting works the other way round. Drop a complete literal into the pattern field and the delimiter, the body, and the flags are all read off it — so a pattern copied out of source code arrives intact, with its escaping undone. A bare pattern is left exactly as pasted; only a well-formed literal is unwrapped.
delimiters.p4: Sharing goes out the same way. Share copies a link carrying the pattern, the flags, the delimiter, the mode, the replacement, and the test string, so a colleague opens exactly what you are looking at. Only what differs from the defaults is written, which keeps an ordinary link short; a test string too large to fit is left out and the tool says so rather than sending a link that quietly lost half its meaning.

engine.title: Which engine runs your pattern
engine.p1: Matching runs on the JavaScript engine already in your browser. There is no other option: a browser cannot execute PCRE, Python's re, or Go's RE2, and a tool claiming to would be reporting one engine's answers under another's name.
engine.p2: Nearly everything is shared. Anchors, classes, shorthands, quantifiers, groups, alternation, backreferences, and all four lookarounds behave the same in JavaScript as in PCRE or Python. What JavaScript does not have is atomic groups, possessive quantifiers, recursion, subroutine calls, and inline flag switches of the (?i) form. Rather than let those fail with a message about an invalid group, this tool names the construct and points at its position before compiling.
engine.p3: Two smaller differences are worth remembering when a pattern is going somewhere else. Go's RE2 and Rust's regex crate have no lookaround or backreferences at all, by design — they trade those for a guarantee against the backtracking described below. And \A, \z, and \Z are PCRE anchors; in JavaScript they are ordinary escaped letters, so \Afoo quietly matches the text Afoo. The Explanation panel says so in as many words.

performance.title: Catastrophic backtracking, and the limits here
performance.p1: A backtracking engine — JavaScript's, PCRE's, Python's — tries alternatives until one fits. Usually that is quick. But nest one unbounded quantifier inside another, as in (a+)+b, and the number of ways to divide the input between them grows exponentially. Against a string of thirty a characters with no b, the engine will still be working long after you have closed the tab.
performance.p2: This tool warns about that shape as you type. The warning is a heuristic, not a proof: it fires on a quantified group that contains another quantifier, which is the pattern behind most real incidents, and it will occasionally flag something that is perfectly safe.
performance.p3: The real protection is architectural. Matching runs in a web worker rather than on the page, because a running regular expression cannot be interrupted from inside — no timeout, no cancellation, nothing. What the page can do is stop waiting: after two seconds it terminates the worker outright and starts a fresh one on your next keystroke. The tab stays responsive whatever the pattern does.
performance.p4: Three ceilings sit underneath that: a pattern of 1,000 characters, a test string of 50,000, and 1,000 matches. When the match cap is reached the panel says so rather than quietly showing a short list. There is also a time budget inside the match loop itself, which stops a global pattern grinding through a long input — though only between matches, never inside one, which is precisely why the worker exists.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Which regex flavour does this use?
faq.a1: ECMAScript — the engine in your browser. It is the only one that can run client-side. In practice the difference rarely bites: anchors, classes, quantifiers, groups, alternation, backreferences, and lookaround all behave identically to PCRE and Python. Where JavaScript genuinely lacks something, such as an atomic group or a possessive quantifier, the tool names the construct rather than letting the engine complain about an invalid group.
faq.q2: Why does the whole match not respond to $0?
faq.a2: Because JavaScript reads $0 as two ordinary characters. regex101 defines it as the whole match, but the substitution preview here is meant to show what String.prototype.replace would actually return, so it follows JavaScript's tokens exactly. Write $& for the whole match.
faq.q3: What does the Steps counter show?
faq.a3: There isn't one. regex101's step count comes from its own engine; JavaScript's RegExp reports nothing at all about the backtracking it did, so any number here would be invented. Groups takes that slot instead, and the timing is a real measurement of how long the match loop took.
faq.q4: Can a bad pattern freeze the page?
faq.a4: No. Matching runs in a web worker, and the page terminates it after two seconds — a running regular expression cannot be interrupted any other way. You will see a message saying the pattern was stopped, the highlighting and explanation stay as they were, and the next keystroke starts a fresh worker.
faq.q5: Is anything sent to a server?
faq.a5: No. The pattern, the test string, and the replacement never leave your browser. Nothing is uploaded, stored, or logged, and the whole tool works offline once the page has loaded.
faq.q6: Why does my pattern match one fewer thing than I expected?
faq.a6: Two usual causes. Without the global flag the engine reports only the first match, so check the flags at the end of the field. And an unescaped dot matches any character rather than a full stop — the classic reason an email pattern accepts an address it should have refused.

understanding.title: What placeholder text is for
understanding.p1: Placeholder text is copy that fills a layout without ever being read. It has the shape of language — word lengths, sentence rhythm, paragraph mass — so a design behaves the way it will behave in production, while carrying no meaning anyone could stop and argue about.
understanding.p2: The classic version is lorem ipsum, and it is older than any software that renders it. A printer in the 1500s scrambled a passage from Cicero's De Finibus Bonorum et Malorum, written in 45 BC, into type specimens. Letraset put it on dry-transfer sheets in the 1960s, desktop publishing shipped it in the 1980s, and it has been the default ever since.
understanding.p3: That history is why the words look Latin but parse as nothing. It is a feature: a stakeholder who cannot read the copy looks at the layout instead, and nobody ships "Lorem ipsum dolor" to production believing it was the real headline.

why.title: Why not just use real copy
why.p1: Real copy gets read. Put a finished paragraph in a mockup and the review turns into a discussion of the wording, while the column width, the line height and the widow on line four all go unexamined.
why.p2: Real copy in one language also hides how a layout fails in another. English words are short and evenly sized; German compounds overflow a fixed-width button, Bengali ascenders push line boxes taller than Latin ever does, and a single emoji occupies width no Latin glyph accounts for. Generating from those scripts on purpose surfaces the problem while it is still cheap to fix.
why.p3: And exact counts are the real reason to reach for a generator rather than copying a paragraph from somewhere. A field capped at 140 characters, a card clamped to three lines, a summary column budgeted at 50 words — each of those is a specific number, and guessing at it wastes the test.

sources.title: The twelve sources
sources.intro: Every source draws from a different pool, so the output stresses a different part of a layout. Latin and Occidental sit close to the rhythm of English; German brings length and diacritics; Bangla brings a script with taller line boxes and no letter case; pangrams, alphabet runs and emoji abandon prose entirely.
sources.tableCaption: Text sources available in the generator
sources.publicDomain: All twelve are public domain. The Latin and its translation predate copyright by centuries, Goethe died in 1832 and Kafka's Metamorphosis was published in 1915, and the remaining sources are either sample texts in long-standing public use or generated from characters. Nothing here needs attribution, and nothing here is stored or transmitted.

options.title: Every control, and what it changes
options.intro: Six controls, and two of them constrain the others. Rather than listing every pairing, the generator applies one rule per interaction and disables the control it makes meaningless, with a hint saying why.
options.tableCaption: Generator options and when to use each
options.sourceDoes: Chooses which passage, phrase list or character pool the output is drawn from.
options.sourceWhen: You are testing a font, a script, or a language you actually ship.
options.unitDoes: Decides what the amount counts: words, characters, sentences or paragraphs.
options.unitWhen: The limit you are checking is expressed in one of those four units.
options.amountDoes: How many of the chosen unit to emit. The result lands on this number exactly, not near it.
options.amountWhen: Always — it is the number the whole tool is built around.
options.paragraphsDoes: Spreads the amount across this many paragraphs, dividing evenly and giving any remainder to the first.
options.paragraphsWhen: You need the text broken into blocks rather than delivered as one run.
options.openerDoes: Leads the very first sentence with the line the source is known for, and only that sentence.
options.openerWhen: The placeholder should be obviously recognisable as placeholder.
options.htmlDoes: Emits one escaped paragraph element per block instead of plain text.
options.htmlWhen: You are pasting into markup rather than into a design tool.
options.splitNote: Measuring in paragraphs already sets the paragraph count, so the split control goes quiet rather than silently doing nothing. Asking for fewer units than paragraphs — three words across ten paragraphs — produces three paragraphs rather than seven empty ones.
options.openerNote: Pangrams, alphabet runs and emoji have no opening line, so the opener switch is disabled for them and says so. Where an opener does apply it is never broken by an inserted comma, because a recognisable line with punctuation dropped into the middle of it reads as a bug.
options.defaultsNote: The defaults are lorem ipsum, 100 words spread across 3 paragraphs, the classic opening on, and plain text. Switching to HTML re-renders the passage you already have rather than generating a new one, so you never lose text you were about to copy.

howItWorks.title: How the text is composed
howItWorks.p1: A prose source composes each sentence from its word pool: six to sixteen words drawn at random, a comma placed inside longer sentences about two times in five, a capital on the first letter and a full stop at the end. Bangla is handled on its own terms — it closes with a danda and is never capitalised, because the script has no letter case.
howItWorks.p2: Counts are exact rather than approximate. Asking for words fills a paragraph with whole sentences until one more would overshoot, then trims that closing sentence to the remaining words and re-punctuates it. Asking for characters cuts precisely on the number, clipped final word and all — which is the whole point when what you are testing is a field that truncates at 140.
howItWorks.p3: Characters are counted as characters, not as UTF-16 code units. One emoji is one character, and a cut never lands between the two halves of a surrogate pair, so the output is always well-formed text no matter where the limit falls.
howItWorks.p4: Everything runs on your machine. The first batch is composed on the server so the page is never blank on arrival, every batch after that is composed in the browser, and no text is uploaded, logged or stored at any point.

useCases.title: When you will want it
useCases.p1: Filling a mockup, a component library or a staging CMS, where the layout has to be reviewed before the copy exists. Paragraph mode with three to five paragraphs covers most of it.
useCases.p2: Testing limits. Character mode gives you a string of precisely the length a field, a meta description or a preview clamp is budgeted for, and word mode does the same for a summary column.
useCases.p3: Checking internationalisation and typography. Generate German for length, Bangla for line height and taller ascenders, emoji for astral characters, and an alphabet run when you want to see raw glyph coverage with no language in the way.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Is lorem ipsum real Latin?
faq.a1: Not quite. The individual words are Latin, taken from Cicero's De Finibus, but they were scrambled and clipped centuries ago and the sentences no longer parse. Pick the Cicero source if you want the passage unscrambled, or its English translation if you want to read what it actually says.
faq.q2: Why not fill the layout with asdf or a repeated word?
faq.a2: Because it does not behave like language. Repeated characters wrap, hyphenate and justify differently from real word lengths, so the line breaks you see are not the line breaks you will ship. Placeholder text is worth generating precisely because it is meaningless while still being shaped like prose.
faq.q3: Can I get an exact character count?
faq.a3: Yes. Measure by characters and the output is that length exactly, including a final word cut mid-way if that is where the number falls. That is deliberate: the reason to ask for 140 characters is usually to see what a field does at 140.
faq.q4: Is anything uploaded?
faq.a4: No. The generator is ordinary client-side code with no network calls. The first result is rendered on the server so the page arrives with text already in it, and neither that result nor anything you generate afterwards is stored, logged or sent anywhere.
faq.q5: Can I use the generated text commercially?
faq.a5: Yes. Every source is public domain, and generated placeholder text carries no rights of its own. Use it in client work, in products, in published templates — no attribution needed.
faq.q6: Why are emoji and pangrams in a lorem ipsum tool?
faq.a6: Because they catch layout bugs that prose hides. A pangram exercises every letter, which surfaces a missing glyph or an awkward pair in a webfont; emoji are astral characters that stress line height, alignment and any code that counts characters by UTF-16 unit.

hexCasing.hint: Affects the HEX row and the generated scale only.

palette.tailwindNote: Read straight out of the Tailwind CSS {version} stylesheet.
palette.cssNote: All {count} colour keywords defined by CSS Color Module Level 4.

errors.unrecognised: That is not a colour this tool recognises.

understanding.title: One colour, six ways of writing it down
understanding.p1: A colour on a screen is three numbers: how much red, green and blue each pixel emits. Every notation on this page describes that same triple — HEX packs it into six digits, RGB spells it out, HSL and HSV rearrange it into something a person can reason about, CMYK restates it as ink, and OKLCH places it on a perceptual axis. Converting between them changes the spelling, not the colour.
understanding.p2: Which one you reach for depends on what you are about to do. HEX is the shortest thing to paste into a design file. HSL is the one to nudge when you want the same hue a little lighter. OKLCH is the one to build a scale in, because equal steps in it look like equal steps. CMYK is the one your print shop asks for.
understanding.p3: The tool keeps a single colour in memory and renders it six ways at once, so switching notation costs nothing and nothing drifts between them. Everything is computed in the page — no colour you paste is ever sent anywhere.

models.title: The six notations
models.intro: What each model measures, and the job it is actually good at.
models.tableCaption: Colour models, their channels, and what each is best suited to
models.hexBestFor: Pasting anywhere. The shortest unambiguous form, and the one every design tool accepts.
models.rgbBestFor: Talking to code that manipulates pixels directly — canvas, image processing, shaders.
models.hslBestFor: Hand-tuning. Hold the hue and move lightness to get a tint or a shade of the same colour.
models.hsvBestFor: Colour pickers. Saturation and brightness stay independent, which is why the square above uses it.
models.cmykBestFor: Print handoff. A rough separation into cyan, magenta, yellow and key black.
models.oklchBestFor: Building scales and palettes. Equal steps in lightness look equal, which HSL cannot promise.
models.gamutNote: OKLCH can describe colours no ordinary screen can show. When a value falls outside sRGB, the tool walks its chroma down until it fits rather than clipping the channels — clipping shifts the hue, which is exactly what makes a hand-built scale look wrong at its saturated end.
models.cmykNote: The CMYK figures here are the device-independent conversion every design tool shows, not a colour-managed separation. A real print profile needs an ICC transform and the paper stock it will be printed on; treat these numbers as a starting point to hand to a printer, not as the final plate values.

controls.title: Every control on the page
controls.intro: Nine controls, and what each one is for.
controls.tableCaption: Controls, what each does, and when to reach for it
controls.inputDoes: Reads HEX, RGB, HSL, HSV, CMYK, OKLCH or a CSS keyword and tells you which one it saw.
controls.inputWhen: You already have a value and want it in another notation.
controls.squareDoes: Sets saturation left to right and brightness bottom to top, at the current hue.
controls.squareWhen: You are looking for a colour rather than converting one.
controls.hueDoes: Sweeps the full 360° of hue without touching saturation or brightness.
controls.hueWhen: You have the right tone and want a different colour family.
controls.alphaDoes: Sets alpha from fully clear to fully opaque, carried into every notation that has room for it.
controls.alphaWhen: You need a translucent overlay, scrim, or tint.
controls.notationDoes: Switches the RGB, HSL, HSV and CMYK rows between the modern space-separated form and the legacy comma form.
controls.notationWhen: Your codebase has a house style, or you are supporting a browser that predates the modern syntax.
controls.hexCasingDoes: Writes hex digits in lower or upper case.
controls.hexCasingWhen: Your linter or design system insists on one of them.
controls.randomDoes: Jumps to a random colour drawn away from the washed-out greys a uniform draw would land on.
controls.randomWhen: You want a starting point rather than a specific colour.
controls.eyedropperDoes: Opens the browser's eyedropper and reads a pixel from anywhere on your screen.
controls.eyedropperWhen: The colour you want is on screen but not in a file you can read.
controls.downloadDoes: Downloads a stylesheet holding the colour, the other five notations as a comment, and the whole generated scale as custom properties.
controls.downloadWhen: You are ready to drop the scale into a theme.
controls.alphaNote: CMYK is the one row that cannot carry opacity — there is no alpha channel in the model. When the colour is translucent, that row says so rather than silently pretending the colour is solid.
controls.notationNote: The notation switch deliberately leaves OKLCH alone. CSS has never defined a comma form for it, so writing one would produce a declaration no browser accepts.
controls.clampNote: Out-of-range channels are clamped rather than rejected, which is what a browser does with rgb(300 0 0). Pasting what a stylesheet actually contains should show you what the browser actually renders.
controls.defaultsNote: The defaults are modern notation and lower-case hex, matching what CSS Color 4 and most linters prefer. Both settings change the spelling only; neither one touches the colour itself, and neither is carried into the eyedropper or the palette browser.

contrast.title: Contrast, and what the grades mean
contrast.p1: WCAG measures legibility as a ratio between the relative luminance of two colours, running from 1:1 for identical colours to 21:1 for black on white. Body text needs 4.5:1 to reach AA and 7:1 to reach AAA. Large text — roughly 24px, or 19px bold — only needs 3:1. Icons, borders and focus rings need 3:1 under Success Criterion 1.4.11.
contrast.p2: The panel checks your colour as a background against the two text colours every design starts from. It grades on the exact ratio and only rounds afterwards: a pairing at 4.497:1 displays as 4.50 but is still a failure, and showing it as a pass would be worse than showing nothing.
contrast.p3: Opacity is left out of the calculation on purpose. A translucent colour's real contrast depends on whatever sits behind it, which this page cannot know. If you are building a scrim, flatten it against its actual backdrop first and check that colour instead.

scales.title: How the generated scale is built
scales.p1: The ladder borrows its proportions from Tailwind's own palette rather than inventing them. Each rung takes a reference family's lightness outright, and scales your colour's chroma by that rung's share of the family's 500 — so the pale end stays pale without turning muddy, and the dark end keeps its identity.
scales.p2: Every step is computed in OKLCH. That matters: an HSL lightness ramp bunches the mid tones together and washes out both ends, because HSL lightness is not perceptual. Stepping through OKLCH gives you rungs that actually look evenly spaced.
scales.p3: The outlined rung is whichever step sits nearest your colour on the lightness axis, so you can see where what you picked would land in a Tailwind-shaped theme. Export writes the whole ladder out as custom properties, ready to paste into a :root or @theme block.

palettes.title: Where the palettes come from
palettes.p1: The Tailwind swatches are read straight out of the stylesheet shipped with Tailwind CSS {version} in this project, not transcribed from documentation. They are the exact OKLCH values your build compiles, which is why the closest-match badge can be trusted against a real theme.
palettes.p2: The CSS keywords are the full set defined by CSS Color Module Level 4 — the ones you can write as tomato or rebeccapurple in a stylesheet. Several are aliases of each other: aqua and cyan are the same colour, as are grey and gray, magenta and fuchsia.
palettes.p3: Closest-match distance is measured in OKLab rather than RGB. RGB distance calls a pair of dark blues further apart than a pair of light greens that plainly differ, which produces obviously wrong answers; OKLab tracks what the eye actually reports.

useCases.title: What people use it for
useCases.p1: Translating a handoff. A designer sends HSL, the stylesheet wants OKLCH, and the icon export wants HEX. Paste once and copy whichever row the next tool needs.
useCases.p2: Checking a brand colour before committing to it. Drop the hex in, look at the contrast panel, and find out immediately whether body text will be legible on it or whether it can only carry headings.
useCases.p3: Building a theme from a single colour. Pick the brand hue, take the generated 50–950 ladder, and export it as custom properties instead of hand-tuning eleven values.
useCases.close: Nothing you paste leaves the page. There is no upload, no request, and no log — the whole conversion is a few hundred lines of arithmetic running in your own browser.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Why does the same colour give a different HSL and HSV?
faq.a1: They measure different things. HSL's lightness runs from black through the pure hue to white, so a pure red sits at 50%. HSV's value runs from black to the pure hue, so the same red sits at 100%. Neither is wrong; HSV is what colour pickers use because saturation and brightness stay independent of each other.
faq.q2: Are the CMYK numbers safe to send to a printer?
faq.a2: As a starting point, yes. As final plate values, no. This is the device-independent conversion every design tool shows, with no ICC profile, no paper stock, and no ink limit behind it. Give them to your printer as an indication of intent and let their profile do the real separation.
faq.q3: What is OKLCH, and why does the scale use it?
faq.a3: OKLCH describes a colour as lightness, chroma and hue on a perceptually uniform axis, which means a ten-point step looks like a ten-point step wherever you take it. HSL does not have that property, so an HSL ramp produces a scale whose middle is crowded and whose ends are washed out. Every modern browser supports oklch() in CSS.
faq.q4: Why does the closest Tailwind match sometimes name a colour I do not recognise?
faq.a4: The palette is read from the Tailwind version installed in this project, which includes every family that version ships. Several families also round to the same 8-bit value at their palest and darkest ends, so which of them wins a tie is arbitrary — the hex beside the name is what matters.
faq.q5: Can I share a link that opens on a specific colour?
faq.a5: Yes. Add ?color= to the URL with any value the field accepts, remembering to encode the hash as %23 — /tools/color?color=%23c46895 works, as does /tools/color?color=tomato. You can pin the notation and hex case the same way with ?notation=legacy and ?hexCase=upper.
faq.q6: Why is the eyedropper button missing?
faq.a6: It only appears where the browser provides the EyeDropper API, which today means Chrome, Edge and other Chromium-based browsers on the desktop. Everywhere else the button is not rendered at all, rather than shown and then failing when pressed.

meta.title: Cron Expression Parser — Explain a Crontab and Preview Its Next Runs
meta.description: Paste a cron expression and read it back in plain English, column by column, with the next run times in any IANA time zone. Handles 5-field crontab, 6-field with seconds, 7-field Quartz with a year, the @daily family, and the L, W and # calendar syntax. Runs entirely in your browser.

hero.title: Cron Expression Parser
hero.subtitle: Paste a schedule and find out what it actually does — read as a sentence, broken down column by column, and turned into the next run times in whichever time zone the job runs in.

workbench.title: Cron expression
workbench.description: Five fields, six with seconds, or seven with a year. Macros such as @daily are expanded to the columns they stand for.
workbench.readAsReboot: Read as a boot-time schedule, with no clock columns
workbench.dayUnionNote: Both day columns are set, so this fires when either one matches — not when both do.
workbench.weekdayBaseHint: Unix counts Sunday as 0 and accepts 7 for it too. Quartz counts Sunday as 1. Names such as MON mean the same under both.
workbench.runCountHint: Between {min, number} and {max, number} upcoming runs.
workbench.runsDescription: Counted forward from now, on the wall clock of the zone you picked.
workbench.runsZoneNote: Times are the wall clock in {zone}.
workbench.neverRuns: This schedule never runs. Check the day and month columns — 30 February and similar combinations can never be satisfied.
workbench.scheduleExhausted: No further runs were found within the next hundred years.

errors.fieldCount: A cron expression needs 5 fields, 6 with a leading seconds column, or 7 with a trailing year
errors.unknownMacro: {token} is not one of the cron macros — try @yearly, @monthly, @weekly, @daily, @hourly or @reboot
errors.emptyTerm: The {field} column has an empty entry — check for a stray or doubled comma
errors.invalidTerm: {token} is not something the {field} column can hold
errors.outOfRange: {token} is outside the range the {field} column allows
errors.reversedRange: {token} runs backwards — cron ranges do not wrap, so write the days out as a list instead
errors.invalidStep: {token} has a step cron cannot use — a step must be a whole number of at least 1

toast.copyFailedEmpty: Nothing to copy yet

understanding.title: What a cron expression actually says
understanding.p1: A cron expression is a filter over the clock, not a countdown. Every minute the scheduler wakes up, looks at the current time, and asks each column whether it matches. When they all agree, the job runs. Nothing anywhere records when the job last ran or when it is due next — which is why an expression alone can never tell you it has drifted.
understanding.p2: That framing explains the two things people find surprising. A schedule has no start date, so changing the file changes the very next run. And a schedule has no duration, so a job that takes eleven minutes on a five-minute schedule will happily start again before the last copy has finished.
understanding.p3: This tool reads the expression the way the scheduler does, then says the result out loud and lists the instants it produces. Everything happens in your browser: the expression is never sent anywhere, which matters more than usual because schedules tend to sit in the same files as credentials.

fields.title: The columns
fields.intro: Fields are separated by whitespace and read left to right. The five-field form is what crontab has used since the 1970s; the seconds column in front and the year column behind are later additions that Quartz, Spring and node-cron accept.
fields.tableCaption: Cron columns, the values each accepts, and the special characters it allows
fields.counts: Which columns you get depends on how many you write. Five fields start at the minute. Six put seconds in front. Seven put seconds in front and a year behind. Anything else is rejected rather than guessed at, because a six-field line read as five would silently move every run by a whole column.
fields.secondNotes: Only present in the six- and seven-field forms. A five-field line fires on the zeroth second.
fields.minuteNotes: The first column of a classic crontab line.
fields.hourNotes: Always a 24-hour clock. There is no AM or PM anywhere in cron.
fields.dayOfMonthNotes: Days that a month does not have are simply never matched — 31 in February costs you nothing, it just does not fire.
fields.monthNotes: Accepts JAN through DEC, case-insensitively, as well as 1 through 12.
fields.dayOfWeekNotes: Accepts SUN through SAT. The numbering depends on the dialect, which is what the Weekday numbering control is for.
fields.yearNotes: Quartz only, and rarely useful outside a one-off migration job.

syntax.title: Syntax, one character at a time
syntax.intro: Each column is a comma-separated list of terms, and each term is one of the shapes below. The last six are Quartz extensions: plain crontab does not know them, so a line using them will not load into a Unix crontab.
syntax.tableCaption: Cron term syntax, what each means, and which columns accept it
syntax.noWrap: Two things are worth remembering. A range never wraps: FRI-MON is rejected rather than read as the weekend, so write FRI,SAT,SUN,MON instead. And a step counts from the bottom of its column, not from now — */20 in the minute column fires at :00, :20 and :40 whatever time you save the file.
syntax.starMeans: Every value the column can hold.
syntax.listMeans: Each listed value, merged and deduplicated.
syntax.rangeMeans: Every value from the first to the last, inclusive.
syntax.rangeWhere: Every column. Names may be used where the column accepts them.
syntax.stepMeans: Every nth value, counting from the bottom of the column.
syntax.rangeStepMeans: Every nth value inside a range — 0, 10, 20 and 30 here.
syntax.openStepMeans: Every nth value from a starting point to the top of the column — 5, 20, 35 and 50 here.
syntax.openStepWhere: Every column. A Quartz spelling that most crontabs also accept.
syntax.unspecifiedMeans: No value of its own; leaves the decision to the other day column.
syntax.unspecifiedWhere: Day of month and day of week only.
syntax.lastDayMeans: The last day of the month, whether that is the 28th or the 31st.
syntax.lastDayOffsetMeans: That many days before the last day of the month.
syntax.lastWeekdayMeans: The last Monday-to-Friday day of the month.
syntax.nearestWeekdayMeans: The weekday nearest that date, without crossing into another month.
syntax.lastNamedWeekdayMeans: The last Friday of the month. Any weekday number or name works.
syntax.nthWeekdayMeans: The third Friday of the month. The ordinal runs from 1 to 5.

macros.title: The @ macros
macros.intro: Vixie cron accepts eight shorthands in place of five fields. They are expanded before anything else, so the breakdown above shows the columns they stand for rather than the macro itself.
macros.tableCaption: Cron macros and the five-field expressions they expand to
macros.yearlyNotes: @annually is a second spelling of the same thing.
macros.monthlyNotes: Midnight on the first of every month.
macros.weeklyNotes: Midnight on Sunday, whichever numbering the dialect uses.
macros.dailyNotes: @midnight is a second spelling of the same thing.
macros.rebootNotes: Not a clock schedule at all. It fires once, when the daemon starts, so it has no next run to show — and it does not fire again if you merely reload the crontab.

options.title: The controls
options.intro: Three settings change what the run list means. None of them change how the expression is read except the second, which changes what a bare weekday digit stands for.
options.tableCaption: Cron tool controls, what each does, and when to reach for it
options.timeZoneDoes: Works out the run times against that zone's wall clock, including its daylight saving rules.
options.timeZoneWhen: Always — set it to whatever the machine running the job is set to, which is very often UTC.
options.weekdayBaseDoes: Decides whether a bare digit in the day-of-week column counts Sunday as 0 or as 1.
options.weekdayBaseWhen: The expression came from Quartz, Spring or Jenkins and uses digits rather than names.
options.runCountDoes: How many upcoming run times to list, from 1 to 25.
options.runCountWhen: You need to see a whole week of a daily job, or just confirm the next one.
options.zoneNote: The zone is a property of the machine, not of the expression. A crontab line carries no zone at all; it fires on whatever the host's clock says. Kubernetes CronJob and Quartz can each be told a zone explicitly, and this control is how you model that.
options.baseNote: Weekday numbering only matters for digits. SUN, MON and the rest name the same day under both dialects, which is the strongest argument for always writing names — a schedule that reads the same everywhere cannot be misread when it moves between systems.

traps.title: Five ways a schedule surprises people
traps.dayUnion: When both day columns are restricted, cron fires when either matches, not when both do. 0 0 1 * MON runs on the first of the month and on every Monday — four or five times as often as most people expect. If only one of the two columns is a star, the columns are intersected as usual, which is why the rule is so easy to miss.
traps.stepFromZero: A step counts from the bottom of its column, not from the moment you saved the file. */7 in the hour column fires at 00:00, 07:00, 14:00 and 21:00, then jumps back to 00:00 — the gap across midnight is three hours, not seven. Steps that do not divide evenly into their column always have a short interval at the wrap.
traps.dst: In a zone that observes daylight saving, an hour goes missing every spring. A job at 02:30 does not run at all on that day, because 02:30 never happens. This tool counts those and tells you underneath the run list rather than quietly listing 03:30 instead.
traps.zoneless: In the autumn the same hour happens twice. Most schedulers fire once, on the first pass, which is what the run list shows — but implementations genuinely differ here, and a job that must run exactly once should not be scheduled inside the repeated hour at all.
traps.overlap: Cron never waits for the previous run to finish. A five-minute schedule around a job that sometimes takes seven minutes will eventually run two copies at once. Guard it with a lock file, flock, or whatever your runner offers — the schedule cannot do it for you.

useCases.title: When to reach for this
useCases.p1: Reviewing a pull request that touches a crontab, a Kubernetes CronJob, or a Quartz trigger. Reading the sentence and the next five runs takes a few seconds and catches the off-by-one-column mistakes that a diff makes almost invisible.
useCases.p2: Working out why a job ran at the wrong time. Set the zone to the server's, and the run list will usually show the answer straight away — a UTC box firing a report at what the reporter thought was local midnight is the single most common cause.
useCases.p3: Writing a new schedule from scratch. Start from an example, adjust one column at a time, and watch the sentence and the run times change as you type.
useCases.offline: Everything runs in your browser. The expression is never uploaded, which matters because schedules usually live beside secrets, hostnames, and internal paths.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Why does my schedule with both a day of month and a weekday run so often?
faq.a1: Because cron unions the two day columns rather than intersecting them. When neither column is a star, a day matches if it satisfies either one. To restrict on both at once, pick one column and leave the other as a star — or, in Quartz, as a question mark.
faq.q2: What time zone does a cron expression use?
faq.a2: None of its own. A classic crontab entry fires on the host's clock, so the answer depends entirely on how the machine is configured — very often UTC on a server and local time on a laptop. Kubernetes CronJob has a timeZone field and Quartz takes a TimeZone on the trigger; the Time zone control here is how you model whichever applies.
faq.q3: Is 0 Sunday or is 1 Sunday?
faq.a3: Both, depending on the dialect. Unix crontab counts Sunday as 0 and also accepts 7 for it. Quartz counts Sunday as 1 through Saturday as 7. Switch the Weekday numbering control to match where the expression came from, or write SUN and MON instead — names mean the same day everywhere.
faq.q4: What are L, W and # for?
faq.a4: They are Quartz extensions for schedules a plain range cannot express. L is the last day of the month, LW the last weekday of it, 15W the weekday nearest the 15th, 5L the last Friday, and FRI#3 the third Friday. Plain Unix crontab does not understand any of them, so a line that uses one will not load into a system crontab.
faq.q5: Why is my job not running on 31 February?
faq.a5: Because there is no such date. Cron matches days that exist, so a day-of-month value a month does not have simply never fires. This tool tells you when a combination can never be satisfied instead of showing an empty list with no explanation.
faq.q6: How many fields should I write?
faq.a6: Five for anything going into a Unix crontab. Six if your runner takes a seconds column — node-cron, Spring and Quartz all do. Seven only for Quartz, where the last field is a year. If you are unsure, five is right far more often than not.
faq.q7: Is my expression sent to a server?
faq.a7: No. The parser, the explanation and the run times are all computed in your browser. Nothing about the expression leaves the page, and the tool works with the network switched off.

understanding.title: What a Unix timestamp actually is
understanding.p1: A Unix timestamp is a count of seconds since 1 January 1970 at 00:00:00 UTC — an instant on a single, unbroken number line. It names no place and no calendar. That is the whole point: two machines on opposite sides of the planet can agree on the number without agreeing on anything else.
understanding.p2: Everything readable comes later. "29 July 2026, 6:00 pm" is that number after a time zone and a calendar have been applied to it. Change the zone and the wall clock changes; the timestamp does not. This is why storing a timestamp is safe and storing a local time is not.
understanding.p3: The count ignores leap seconds. A Unix day is exactly 86 400 seconds even on the rare days that were 86 401 seconds long, so the number is a count of nominal seconds rather than of elapsed physical ones. For everything short of satellite navigation, that is the right trade.

formats.title: Formats this tool reads
formats.intro: Paste any of these and the shape is detected for you. Every example below names the same instant, 2026-07-29T12:00:00Z, so you can see how the same moment is spelled in each.
formats.tableCaption: Input formats, an example of each, and what to know about them
formats.epochSecondsNotes: Ten digits today. The default reading for any number below 100 000 000 000.
formats.epochMillisNotes: Thirteen digits. What JavaScript's Date.now() and most log formats emit.
formats.epochNanosNotes: Nineteen digits — past what a JavaScript number can hold, so this tool keeps them as exact integers.
formats.isoNotes: The Z means UTC. Fractional seconds to nanosecond depth are kept.
formats.isoOffsetNotes: An explicit offset always wins over the input zone setting.
formats.isoWeekNotes: Week dates such as 2026-W31-3 and ordinal dates such as 2026-210 both work.
formats.rfcNotes: Also reads what Date.prototype.toString() prints, trailing zone name and all.
formats.dateTextNotes: Month names in any order, 12-hour clocks, and ordinals such as 29th.
formats.uuidNotes: These versions embed their creation time. Versions 3, 4, 5 and 8 hold none.
formats.objectIdNotes: The leading four bytes are the creation time in seconds.
formats.filetimeNotes: Both count 100-nanosecond intervals, from 1601 and from year 1. Pick the unit — their digit counts collide with nanoseconds.
formats.excelNotes: Days since 30 December 1899, phantom leap day included. Pick the unit; a bare number cannot be told apart from an epoch.
formats.ambiguity: Two shapes are deliberately refused rather than guessed at. A date such as 07/08/2026 could be 7 August or 8 July, and picking one silently is how a report ends up five weeks out; write it as 2026-07-08 instead. A zone abbreviation such as IST means three different offsets depending on the country, so an abbreviation outside the small set RFC 2822 defines is treated as though no zone were given at all.
formats.detection: A bare eight-digit number such as 20260729 is read as an epoch, not as a compact ISO date, because that is what such a number nearly always is in a log file. Write 20260729T000000Z if you meant the date.

zones.title: Time zones, offsets and daylight saving
zones.p1: A time zone is not an offset. "Asia/Dhaka" is a zone: a named region with a history of rules. "+06:00" is the offset those rules produce at one particular instant. Storing the offset loses the rules, which is why every card here shows the zone and works the offset out for the moment you are looking at.
zones.p2: Daylight saving is why that distinction matters. New York is −05:00 in January and −04:00 in July, so an event stored as "−05:00" and replayed in summer is an hour wrong. Each card here marks whether the zone is on daylight time at that instant.
zones.p3: Two moments each year are genuinely awkward. When clocks spring forward, an hour of wall-clock time never happens; a date written inside that hour is placed just after the jump. When clocks fall back, an hour happens twice; a date written inside it is read as the first of the two. Both choices match what other date libraries do, but if the exact hour matters, write the offset out.
zones.p4: The zone list here is the full IANA database, shipped as a fixed list rather than read from your browser. Browsers and servers ship slightly different versions of that database, and a picker whose options depended on which one you were on would break the moment a page rendered on a server and then came alive in a browser. If your browser's data is missing a zone you pinned, the card is left out and the tool says so.

options.title: The controls
options.intro: Four settings, and only the first two change how your input is read.
options.tableCaption: Every control, what it does, and when to reach for it
options.unitDoes: Fixes the scale a plain number is read at, instead of choosing one from its magnitude.
options.unitWhen: The value is a FILETIME, .NET ticks or an Excel serial — or the automatic reading is wrong because the number is unusually small or large.
options.inputZoneDoes: Supplies a zone for input that carries none of its own, such as 2026-07-29T12:00:00 or a date you typed.
options.inputZoneWhen: The log you are reading writes local times without an offset. It is ignored entirely when the input names its own.
options.pinnedZonesDoes: Adds up to four more cities to the board, alongside your own zone and UTC.
options.pinnedZonesWhen: You are scheduling across teams, or checking what a deploy timestamp means to somebody else.
options.clockDoes: Ticks the current Unix time, and drives the relative and day-count lines further down.
options.clockWhen: You want the epoch for right now. Pause it if a moving number is distracting.
options.zoneNote: The input zone and the pinned zones do different jobs and never interact. One decides how ambiguous input is read; the other decides how the answer is displayed. Changing which cities are on the board can never change the underlying instant.
options.defaultsNote: The defaults read numbers by magnitude and treat zone-less input as UTC. UTC rather than your own zone on purpose: a bare timestamp in a log file is almost always UTC, and a default that changed with whoever opened the link would make a shared URL mean two different things.

precision.title: Seconds, milliseconds, and the digits in between
precision.p1: The same instant is written four ways depending on how much precision the system that produced it kept. Seconds is the classic Unix form; milliseconds is what most languages hand you today; microseconds turns up in databases; nanoseconds in tracing and in Go.
precision.p2: Telling them apart is a matter of magnitude. A ten-digit number is seconds until roughly the year 5138; the same digit count in milliseconds would put you in 1973. Because those ranges do not overlap, reading the size of the number is reliable — which is what the automatic setting does.
precision.p3: Nanosecond timestamps are nineteen digits, which is more than a JavaScript number can hold exactly: 1785326400123456789 becomes 1785326400123456800 the moment it is treated as a number. Every scale here is computed with exact integers instead, so the digits you paste in are the digits you get back.
precision.year2038: A signed 32-bit second counter overflows on 19 January 2038, which is the Year 2038 problem. Nothing here is affected — the counts are arbitrary-precision — but a system that still stores time in a 32-bit integer is, and pasting a date past 2038 into this tool is a quick way to see what value it ought to be holding.

useCases.title: When you need this
useCases.p1: Reading a log. A line says 1785326400 and you need to know whether the incident was during business hours in Dhaka or overnight in New York. Paste it, pin both cities, and read both answers at once.
useCases.p2: Writing a fixture. You need a timestamp for a test that expires next Tuesday, or the exact millisecond value for a date somebody described in prose. Type the date, copy the scale you need.
useCases.p3: Debugging an id. A UUID v7 or a MongoDB ObjectId carries the moment it was created, so pasting the id tells you when the row was written without opening the database.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Why does my timestamp show a different time here than in my database?
faq.a1: Almost always a time zone difference rather than a wrong number. Databases usually display in the server's zone or in UTC, while the first card here shows yours. Compare the UTC card with what your database reports — if those agree, the timestamp is fine and only the display differs.
faq.q2: Should I store seconds or milliseconds?
faq.a2: Store whatever the systems around you already use, and write it down. Milliseconds is the more common default now and matches what JavaScript, Java and most JSON APIs produce. The real failure is not the choice but the mixture: a field holding seconds in some rows and milliseconds in others is off by a factor of a thousand, which reads as the year 1970 or the year 56000.
faq.q3: What time zone is used when my input has no offset?
faq.a3: The input zone setting, which defaults to UTC. A date such as 2026-07-29T12:00:00 is genuinely incomplete, so something has to supply the missing piece. This tool never uses your computer's own zone for that, because then the same link would mean different instants for different people.
faq.q4: Can I convert a date to a timestamp, rather than the other way round?
faq.a4: Yes — it is the same field. Type or paste a date in any of the formats above and the epoch values appear underneath, ready to copy. There is no separate mode to switch into.
faq.q5: Why does it refuse to read 07/08/2026?
faq.a5: Because that is 7 August in most of the world and 8 July in the United States, and there is no way to tell from the string which was meant. A tool that picks one quietly will eventually be wrong by weeks in a way nobody notices. Write it as 2026-07-08 or as 8 July 2026 and it will be read exactly.
faq.q6: Does any of this reach a server?
faq.a6: No. The parsing, the zone arithmetic and the formatting all run in your browser, using the time zone database that already ships with it. The page works with your network disconnected.
faq.q7: What is the earliest and latest date this handles?
faq.a7: Roughly 20 April 271821 BC to 13 September 275760 AD, which is the range a JavaScript date can hold. Anything outside it is reported as out of range rather than quietly wrapping around. Dates before the Gregorian reform are given in the proleptic Gregorian calendar — the modern rules, projected backwards.

understanding.title: What an AI image detector actually does
understanding.p1: No detector opens a file and knows which program made it. What this one does is look at the picture the way a suspicious reader would, and weigh the marks generated imagery tends to leave: skin and metal smoother than any lens records, light arriving from two directions at once, hands and text and jewellery that dissolve under attention, reflections that disagree with what is being reflected.
understanding.p2: The upload goes to a Cloudflare Worker, which passes it to Llama 4 Scout — a vision-language model running on Cloudflare's network. Back comes a yes or no, a word for how strongly the model holds it, and a sentence naming what it saw. ToolForge normalises that answer before showing it: a reply it cannot place becomes “Inconclusive”, rather than a guess that looks decisive.
understanding.p3: Nothing else about the file is measured. The name, size, type and pixel dimensions beside the preview are read in your browser and are context, not evidence. There is no metadata forensics here and no C2PA provenance check; those answer a different question and deserve their own tool.

reading.title: Reading the result
reading.intro: The label is the model's call. The confidence beside it is how strongly the model holds that call — not the probability that the call is right.
reading.tableCaption: What each detection label means and what to do about it
reading.ai-generatedMeans: The picture carries the marks the model associates with image generators.
reading.ai-generatedDo: Treat it as a reason to look harder, not as a finding. Ask where the picture came from before acting on it.
reading.authenticMeans: The picture has the irregularity, grain and optical behaviour the model associates with a camera.
reading.authenticDo: Reasonable reassurance, and no more. A generated image that has been cropped, compressed or photographed off a screen often reads exactly like this.
reading.unknownMeans: The model's answer could not be placed, so nothing is being claimed.
reading.unknownDo: Analyse again. If it repeats, the picture is probably too small, too abstract, or too heavily processed to judge.
reading.bandsNote: Confidence arrives as a word rather than a number — low, moderate or high — so the meter counts three steps instead of showing a percentage. Turning “high” into “87%” would dress a rough judgement up as a measurement. A high-confidence “AI-generated” means the model is confident about what it saw. It never means a camera was not involved.

facts.title: What the file panel tells you
facts.intro: Everything beside the preview is read in your browser and never sent anywhere. None of it decides the verdict; all of it is context for reading one.
facts.tableCaption: Each fact about the uploaded file, what it is, and what to watch for
facts.nameMeans: The name as your device reported it, unchanged.
facts.nameWatchFor: Generator output is often a long hash, or carries the prompt in it. A hint at most — anyone can rename a file.
facts.sizeMeans: Bytes on disk, which is also what the 10 MB ceiling is measured against.
facts.sizeWatchFor: A very small file gives the model little to look at, and heavy compression erases exactly the texture it reads.
facts.typeMeans: The MIME type the browser reported, lower-cased.
facts.typeWatchFor: Blank means the browser could not identify the file. The upload is refused rather than guessed at.
facts.dimensionsMeans: Pixel width and height, read by decoding the image locally.
facts.dimensionsWatchFor: Exact squares such as 512×512 or 1024×1024 are common generator defaults, though a cropped stock photo lands there too.
facts.note: None of this proves anything on its own. A screenshot has no camera grain either, and a photographer exporting a square crop has done nothing suspicious.

controls.title: Every control on this page
controls.intro: The tool is deliberately small: one drop zone, one button, and the things you do with a result.
controls.tableCaption: Each control, what it does, and when to reach for it
controls.uploadDoes: Holds the picture to check. Click the panel or drop a file onto it; the preview, size and dimensions appear as soon as the browser has decoded it. Choosing a different file discards the current result.
controls.uploadWhen: Always — one JPEG, PNG, WebP, GIF or BMP, up to 10 MB.
controls.analyseDoes: Uploads the picture for detection. Stays disabled until the file passes the format and size rules and the bot check has passed.
controls.analyseWhen: Once the status line under the panel says it is ready.
controls.clearDoes: Drops the picture, its preview and the current result.
controls.copyDoes: Puts the label, the confidence, the reasoning and the file's name and size on the clipboard as plain text.
controls.copyWhen: When the finding is going into an email or a ticket.
controls.downloadDoes: Saves a JSON file holding the verdict, the confidence, the reasoning, the file's details and a timestamp. The picture itself is not embedded — the reviewer already has it.
controls.downloadWhen: When the check has to be filed alongside the image.
controls.challengeDoes: A Cloudflare Turnstile widget above the buttons. It normally clears itself and settles on a success tick; now and then it asks for a click. Every analysis has to carry the single-use token it issues.
controls.challengeWhen: Only when it asks for a click — otherwise it runs on its own and renews after each analysis.
controls.formatNote: The five accepted formats and the 10 MB ceiling are the worker's own limits, checked in the browser first so a hopeless upload never costs a model call, and again on the server so nothing gets past. SVG, AVIF and HEIC are refused because the model cannot read them — convert to PNG or JPEG first. An animated GIF is accepted, but the model reasons about a still image, so treat a verdict on one as weaker evidence.
controls.challengeNote: A token can only be spent once, so the Analyse button greys out for a moment after each check while a fresh one is issued. If the bot check reports an error, reload the page — the widget cannot recover on its own. There is a limit of five uploads a minute per connection behind it as well.

limits.title: What this cannot tell you
limits.p1: Every AI image detector, this one included, produces false positives. Studio product shots, heavily retouched portraits, CGI from films and games, smooth vector-like illustration, and anything an algorithm has upscaled all carry the marks a statistical judge reads as synthetic.
limits.p2: The reverse holds just as firmly. A generated image that has been cropped, filtered, compressed for a messaging app, or photographed off a screen will usually come back as a real photograph. Detection measures surface texture, and surface texture is the easiest thing to destroy.
limits.p3: So a result here is something to talk about, never something to act on alone. Nobody should have a submission rejected, a claim denied, or their honesty questioned because a model returned a word. Ask where the picture came from; the answer is worth more than any score.

privacy.title: What leaves your browser
privacy.p1: Most tools on ToolForge run entirely on your device. This one cannot: detection needs a vision model, and the model runs on Cloudflare's network. The file you choose is uploaded to a ToolForge Worker, which passes it to Llama 4 Scout and returns the verdict.
privacy.p2: The preview, the file name, the size, the type and the pixel dimensions are read in your browser and are never transmitted. Neither is a file you choose but never analyse — nothing is uploaded until you press Analyse.
privacy.p3: Do not upload anything confidential: unreleased work, photographs of people who have not agreed to it, identity documents, or material under an agreement you would rather not test. When a picture is sensitive, the honest answer is not to check it here.

useCases.title: Where a detector earns its place
useCases.p1: Triage. A moderator with a queue of submissions can use verdicts to decide which handful to examine properly — as long as the examination, and not the verdict, is what decides anything.
useCases.p2: Commissioning. Editors and art directors buying illustration use it as a conversation starter. “How was this made?” is a fair question, and a flagged image is a fair reason to ask it.
useCases.p3: Reading the news. A striking photograph that arrives without a source is worth a check before it is passed on — less to prove anything than to slow down for a moment.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: How accurate is this AI image detector?
faq.a1: Accurate enough to be useful for triage, and not accurate enough to decide anything on its own. Detectors call retouched photographs, CGI and clean studio work machine-made, and they miss generated pictures that have been cropped or compressed. Treat the label as a reason to look closer.
faq.q2: Which formats and sizes can I upload?
faq.a2: JPEG, PNG, WebP, GIF and BMP, up to 10 MB each, one at a time. SVG, AVIF and HEIC are refused because the model cannot read them — convert to PNG or JPEG first. Both rules are checked in your browser and again on the server.
faq.q3: Is my image stored anywhere?
faq.a3: The file is uploaded to a Cloudflare Worker and passed to the model that judges it. ToolForge does not write it to a database or keep a copy; Cloudflare's own handling is governed by their terms. Because the file does leave your browser, do not upload anything confidential.
faq.q4: What is the bot check for?
faq.a4: Each analysis costs a vision-model call, and the daily allowance is shared by everyone using the page. The Cloudflare Turnstile widget above the buttons makes every request prove it came from a browser, which stops a script spending the whole day's budget in an hour. It usually clears itself without asking you for anything. There is a limit of five uploads a minute per connection behind it as well.
faq.q5: Which model does the detection?
faq.a5: Llama 4 Scout 17B Instruct, a vision-language model running on Cloudflare Workers AI. It is asked to examine the picture and commit to a yes or no with a confidence word, which is why the result carries reasoning you can read and disagree with.
faq.q6: Does it check metadata or C2PA content credentials?
faq.a6: No. This tool judges pixels only. EXIF fields and C2PA provenance manifests answer a genuinely different question — who says they made this, rather than what does it look like — and both are trivially stripped, so a missing manifest proves nothing either. That belongs in a dedicated provenance tool.

understanding.title: What an AI text detector actually does
understanding.p1: No detector reads a document and knows who typed it. What this one does is weigh the statistical fingerprints machine-written prose tends to leave: unusually even sentence lengths, a narrow vocabulary, transitions that arrive on schedule, and a fluency that never stumbles. A language model is asked to judge those patterns and to say how strongly it holds its answer.
understanding.p2: The passage goes to a Cloudflare Worker, which forwards it to Llama 3.1 running on Cloudflare's network. Back comes a label, a figure between 0 and 100, and a sentence of reasoning. ToolForge normalises that answer before showing it — a label it cannot place becomes “Inconclusive” with zero confidence, rather than a guess that looks decisive.
understanding.p3: Alongside the verdict sit five signals measured in your browser, which never leave it. They are not a second opinion; they are the raw material a careful reader uses to sanity-check the first one.

reading.title: Reading the result
reading.intro: The label is the model's call. The number beside it is how strongly the model holds that call — not the probability that the call is right.
reading.tableCaption: What each detection label means and what to do about it
reading.ai-generatedMeans: The prose carries the patterns the model associates with machine generation.
reading.ai-generatedDo: Treat it as a reason to read closely, not as a finding. Ask the author how the text was drafted before acting on it.
reading.human-writtenMeans: The prose has the irregularity and voice the model associates with a person.
reading.human-writtenDo: Reasonable reassurance, and no more. Careful editing makes generated text read exactly like this.
reading.mixedMeans: Some of it reads as machine-written and some does not — typical of a draft that was generated and then reworked.
reading.mixedDo: Check whether AI assistance was allowed at all; that is usually the real question.
reading.unknownMeans: The model's answer could not be placed, so nothing is being claimed.
reading.unknownDo: Analyse again. If it repeats, the passage is probably too short or too unusual to judge.
reading.bandsNote: Confidence is bucketed for display: below 50 reads as low, 50 to 79 as moderate, and 80 or above as high. A high-confidence “AI-generated” means the model is confident about a pattern. It never means a person did not write the text.

signals.title: The five signals measured in your browser
signals.intro: These are computed locally from whatever is in the box, updating shortly after you stop typing. None of them is sent anywhere.
signals.tableCaption: Each local text signal, what it measures, and what to watch for
signals.charactersMeasures: Length of the trimmed passage — the same count the detector's limits are enforced on.
signals.charactersWatchFor: Under 50 there is nothing to judge; over 10,000 the passage has to be trimmed.
signals.wordsMeasures: Runs of letters or digits, counting a hyphenated compound or a contraction once. Unicode-aware, so Bangla counts like English.
signals.wordsWatchFor: A very short sample makes every other signal unstable.
signals.sentencesMeasures: Breaks at full stops, question and exclamation marks, ellipses, and the Bengali daṛi. A fragment with no terminator counts as one.
signals.sentencesWatchFor: A wall of text with no punctuation collapses into a single sentence and skews the average.
signals.averageSentenceWordsMeasures: Words divided by sentences, to one decimal place.
signals.averageSentenceWordsWatchFor: Human prose varies. A passage that sits on one number for pages is worth a second look.
signals.uniqueWordRatioMeasures: Distinct words as a share of all words, ignoring capitalisation.
signals.uniqueWordRatioWatchFor: A low ratio across a long passage suggests recycled phrasing, which generated filler is prone to.
signals.note: None of these proves anything alone. A technical specification legitimately has even sentences and a narrow vocabulary, and so does a careful writer working to a house style.

controls.title: Every control on this page
controls.intro: The tool is deliberately small: one box, one button, and the things you do with a result.
controls.tableCaption: Each control, what it does, and when to reach for it
controls.inputDoes: Holds the text to check. The signals recount shortly after you stop typing, and the box itself is never truncated. It locks while an analysis is in flight, so the verdict always describes the passage that was actually sent.
controls.analyseDoes: Sends the trimmed passage for detection. Stays disabled until the length is in range and the bot check has passed.
controls.analyseWhen: Once the status line under the box says it is ready.
controls.clearDoes: Empties the box and discards the current result.
controls.copyDoes: Puts the label, the confidence, the reasoning, and the word and sentence counts on the clipboard as plain text.
controls.copyWhen: When the finding is going into an email or a ticket.
controls.downloadDoes: Saves a JSON file holding the verdict, the local signals, the passage, and a timestamp.
controls.downloadWhen: When the check has to be filed alongside the submission.
controls.challengeDoes: A Cloudflare Turnstile widget above the buttons. It normally clears itself and settles on a success tick; now and then it asks for a click. Every analysis has to carry the single-use token it issues.
controls.challengeWhen: Only when it asks for a click — otherwise it runs on its own and renews after each analysis.
controls.lengthNote: The 50-character floor and the 10,000-character ceiling are enforced in the browser and again on the server, and both are measured on the trimmed passage. Padding a short sample with blank lines will not carry it over the floor.
controls.challengeNote: A token can only be spent once, so the Analyse button greys out for a moment after each check while a fresh one is issued. If the bot check reports an error, reload the page — the widget cannot recover on its own. Separately, passages containing vulgar or slurring language are refused outright: the offending words are named in masked form under the box, the button stays disabled until they are gone, and the same check runs again on the server so nothing gets past it. Matching is whole-word and sees through spacing, punctuation and letter-swapping, so “Scunthorpe” and “classic” are safe while “f-u-c-k” is not.

limits.title: What this cannot tell you
limits.p1: Every AI text detector, this one included, produces false positives. Writers working in a second language, anyone writing in a plain institutional register, and anyone editing to a rigid style guide all produce prose that reads as machine-like to a statistical judge.
limits.p2: The reverse holds just as firmly. A generated draft that has been reworded, reordered, and given a few asides will usually come back as human-written. Detection measures surface patterns, and surface patterns are the easiest thing to change.
limits.p3: So a result here is something to talk about, never something to act on alone. Nobody should fail a course, lose a commission, or have work rejected because a model returned a number. Ask the author how the text was written; the answer is worth more than any score.

privacy.title: What leaves your browser
privacy.p1: Every other tool on ToolForge runs entirely on your device. This one cannot: detection needs a model, and the model runs on Cloudflare's network. The passage you paste is sent to a ToolForge Worker, which forwards it to Llama 3.1 and returns the verdict.
privacy.p2: The five local signals — characters, words, sentences, the sentence average, and the unique-word ratio — are computed in your browser and are never transmitted. Neither is anything you type but never analyse.
privacy.p3: Do not paste anything confidential: unreleased work, personal data, or material under an agreement you would rather not test. When a passage is sensitive, the honest answer is not to check it here.

useCases.title: Where a detector earns its place
useCases.p1: Triage. A tutor with ninety submissions and an afternoon can use scores to decide which five to read closely — as long as the reading, and not the score, is what decides anything.
useCases.p2: Commissioning. Editors buying freelance copy use it as a conversation starter. “How was this drafted?” is a fair question, and a flagged passage is a fair reason to ask it.
useCases.p3: Self-checking. Writers who use a model for early drafts run the finished piece through to see how much of the machine's cadence survived the rewrite.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: How accurate is this AI text detector?
faq.a1: Accurate enough to be useful for triage, and not accurate enough to decide anything on its own. Detectors label human writing as machine-written regularly — plain institutional prose and writing by people working in a second language are the usual casualties — and they miss generated text that has been edited. Treat the label as a reason to look closer.
faq.q2: Why does it need at least 50 characters?
faq.a2: The signals detection relies on — sentence rhythm, vocabulary spread, how fluency varies — need enough text to be measurable at all. Below a sentence or two, any answer would be noise dressed up as a number, so the tool declines rather than guessing.
faq.q3: Is my text stored anywhere?
faq.a3: The passage is sent to a Cloudflare Worker and on to the model that judges it. ToolForge does not write it to a database or keep a copy; Cloudflare's own handling is governed by their terms. Because the request does leave your browser, do not paste confidential material.
faq.q4: What is the bot check for?
faq.a4: Each analysis costs a model call, and the daily allowance is shared by everyone using the page. The Cloudflare Turnstile widget above the buttons makes every request prove it came from a browser, which stops a script spending the whole day's budget in an hour. It usually clears itself without asking you for anything, and shows a tick when it has. There is a per-connection rate limit behind it as well.
faq.q5: Which model does the detection?
faq.a5: Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, running on Cloudflare Workers AI. The exact identifier is shown beside every result and recorded in the downloadable report, so a filed check says what judged it.
faq.q6: Can I check text in Bangla or another language?
faq.a6: Yes, and the local signals handle non-Latin scripts correctly — Bengali combining marks and the daṛi are counted properly rather than fragmenting words. The model's judgement is strongest in English, though, so treat a verdict on other languages as weaker evidence still.
