howItWorks.title: How the removal actually works
howItWorks.p1: Nothing here erases a watermark. What happens is repainting: you mark the pixels you want gone, and a diffusion model invents plausible pixels to stand in their place, using what surrounds the mark as its guide. What you get back is a good guess at what the picture would have looked like — not a recovery of what was underneath.
howItWorks.p2: The model works on a 512-pixel square, which is small. Rather than shrink your whole picture down to fit — which would cost the entire image its detail — this tool crops a square around what you painted, at that area's own resolution, and sends only that. A logo in the corner of a 4000-pixel photograph is therefore repainted at close to its original scale.
howItWorks.p3: The crop and a black-and-white mask of your strokes go to a Cloudflare Worker, which passes both to Stable Diffusion 1.5 Inpainting on Cloudflare Workers AI. The square comes back repainted, still 512 pixels square.
howItWorks.p4: Your browser then puts it back: the repainted square is scaled to the crop's original size and composited onto the picture through your strokes, with a soft edge so the join does not show. Every pixel you did not paint over is the pixel you started with, at the size you started with, and the download is a PNG at the original dimensions.

painting.title: Painting a mask that works
painting.intro: The mask is the whole job. The model repaints exactly what you mark and nothing else, so a stroke that misses part of a letter leaves that part of the letter behind.
painting.tableCaption: How to mask each kind of watermark, and what to expect back
painting.cornerLogoDo: Cover the mark and a little past its edge. Anti-aliased edges fade out further than they look, though the mask sent upstream is already grown slightly to catch them.
painting.cornerLogoExpect: The best case by far. Corners are usually sky, wall, grass or blur, and a model continues any of those without trouble.
painting.tiledTextName: Text tiled across the whole frame
painting.tiledTextDo: Paint over all of it, in as many strokes as it takes. Expect the crop to grow to the picture's shorter side, since the square has to cover everything you marked.
painting.tiledTextExpect: The weakest case. Masking the whole frame leaves the model almost nothing unmasked to match against, and the crop is now the whole picture, so detail is lost.
painting.overSubjectName: A mark over a face or fine detail
painting.overSubjectDo: Mask tightly, one stroke at a time, and run it again if the first attempt is wrong.
painting.overSubjectExpect: Diffusion models reproduce faces, hands and text badly. Over a busy or meaningful subject, expect something plausible from a distance and wrong up close.
painting.largeObjectName: A whole object you want gone
painting.largeObjectDo: Cover the object and its shadow. Missing the shadow is the single most common reason a removal looks wrong.
painting.largeObjectExpect: Often convincing against a simple background, and often a smear against a complicated one.
painting.tightNote: Two habits help more than anything else. Mask tightly: every pixel you paint is a pixel the model gets to invent, so a generous stroke across a detailed area gives away detail you wanted to keep. And run it more than once — diffusion is not deterministic, so the same mask on the same picture gives a different repaint each time, and it is normal for the third attempt to be the one worth keeping.
painting.keyboardNote: The brush slider is measured in screen pixels, so it covers the same visible area whatever the preview is scaled to, while the strokes themselves are stored in the picture's own pixels. Without a pointer, focus the canvas and move the crosshair with the arrow keys — hold Shift to cross the picture faster — then press Enter or Space to dab at that spot. Undo removes one whole stroke; Clear mask removes all of them.

controls.paintWhen: After choosing a file, and before the Remove button will do anything.

controls.clearMaskDoes: Removes every stroke and leaves the picture in place.

The status line under the drop zone always names whichever one is missing, so a disabled button is never unexplained.
controls.challengeNote: A token can be spent only once, so the Remove button greys out for a moment after each attempt while a fresh one is issued. If the bot check reports an error, reload the page — the widget cannot recover on its own.

quality.title: What a good result looks like, and what it costs
quality.p1: The repaint is generated, so it will not match the original at the pixel level. Over sky, water, foliage, carpet, a plain wall or any soft blur, that is invisible. Over brickwork, printed text, a regular pattern or a face it is obvious, because those are what a diffusion model reproduces worst.
quality.p2: The patch also comes back through the model's own encoder, so its grain and sharpness differ slightly from the pixels beside it. The composite fades the edge to hide the join, and confining the change to the mask means the rest of the photograph keeps its original grain rather than being re-encoded along with it.
quality.p3: Because the crop is square and taken at native resolution, small marks come back sharp and large ones come back softer: a mask covering most of a picture forces a crop as large as the picture, which the model then sees at 512 pixels. When a result looks soft, the fix is usually a tighter mask rather than another attempt.

rights.title: What this tool is for
rights.p1: This is a general image editor: it repaints a region of a picture you supply, and the watermark case is simply the most common reason to want that. It is meant for your own photographs and for images you hold the rights to — clearing a preview watermark from a frame you have licensed, taking your own overlay off an export whose source file is long gone, removing a date stamp burnt into a holiday photo, deleting a bin or a passer-by from a shot you took, or clearing the visible mark a generator left on an image you made with it.
rights.p2: It is not a way around someone else's licence. Removing a watermark grants you no rights to the work underneath, and a watermark is often there precisely because those rights have not been granted. Taking a credit, signature or provenance mark off an image and passing it on as your own is straightforward infringement, and removing rights-management information is separately unlawful in many places. Doing it through a model changes none of that.
rights.p3: The judgement is therefore yours, and it cannot be made here: the tool cannot see who owns the picture in front of it. A workable test is whether you would be comfortable telling the person who made the image what you are about to do to it. Anything whose point is to leave someone misled about where an image came from is not a use this tool is for.

limits.title: What this cannot do
limits.p1: It cannot recover what a watermark covered. There is no original underneath to find — those pixels were overwritten before the file ever reached you, and what comes back is invention, however convincing it looks.
limits.p2: It cannot remove an invisible watermark. Statistical marks spread across a whole image, SynthID and similar provenance signals among them, are not what this touches; masking a region says nothing about them. It also cannot repaint an animation, which is why GIF is not accepted at all.
limits.p3: And it cannot do very much of it. The worker accepts five uploads a minute in total across everyone using the page, not five per person, so a busy moment arrives as a rate-limit message. Repainting runs twenty diffusion steps on a shared queue, so a single attempt can take the better part of a minute.
limits.formatNote: JPEG, PNG and WebP, up to 10 MB, one at a time. GIF and BMP are refused because a single still repaint of an animation is not a useful answer, and SVG, AVIF and HEIC because the pipeline cannot decode them — convert to PNG or JPEG first. Both rules are checked in your browser and again on the server. The download is always a PNG whatever went in, because the composite has to be lossless to avoid re-compressing the pixels it did not change.

privacy.title: What leaves your browser
privacy.p1: Most tools on ToolForge run entirely on your device. This one cannot: inpainting needs an image model, and the model runs on Cloudflare's network.
privacy.p2: Only the square you marked is uploaded — cropped in your browser, scaled to 512 pixels, and sent alongside a black-and-white mask of your strokes. The rest of the picture never leaves the page, and nothing at all leaves it until you press Remove. The compositing that produces the final image happens in your browser too, so the full-resolution result exists only on your own device.
privacy.p3: Do not upload anything confidential. Even a crop can carry a face, a document or an address. When the marked area is sensitive, the honest answer is not to run it here.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Does this really remove the watermark?
faq.a1: It replaces it. The marked pixels are repainted by a diffusion model using their surroundings as a guide, so the mark is gone and what stands in its place is invented. Over a plain or soft background that is indistinguishable from a clean photograph; over text, brickwork or a face it usually is not.
faq.q2: Will my picture lose quality?
faq.a2: Only inside the mask. The download is a PNG at your original pixel dimensions, and every pixel you did not paint over is the one you started with — the repainted square is composited into the mask alone, rather than the whole image being re-encoded.
faq.q3: Which formats and sizes can I upload?
faq.a3: JPEG, PNG and WebP, up to 10 MB each, one at a time. GIF and BMP are refused because the model would return a single still; SVG, AVIF and HEIC because the pipeline cannot decode them. Convert to PNG or JPEG first.
faq.q4: Why does it say the rate limit was hit when I have only run it once?
faq.a4: The limit lives on the worker and counts per calling address. Because the page calls the worker from ToolForge's own server rather than from your browser — the API key has to stay secret — everyone using the page shares a single bucket of five uploads a minute. It is not counting you; it is counting everybody. Waiting a minute is the only fix from this side.
faq.q5: Can it remove an invisible or SynthID watermark?
faq.a5: No. This masks and repaints a region you can see. Invisible watermarks are statistical patterns spread across an entire image, and nothing here detects, reads or removes them.
faq.q6: Is it legal to remove a watermark?
faq.a6: That depends entirely on whose image it is, and this tool cannot tell. On your own work, or on an image licensed in a way that permits it, this is ordinary editing. On someone else's work it usually is not: the watermark does not hold the rights, but removing it does not grant them either, and stripping rights-management information is separately unlawful in many jurisdictions. When you are unsure, ask whoever made the image.

understanding.title: What makes a password strong
understanding.p1: A password is strong when it is hard to guess, and nothing else. Not when it has a capital letter, not when it has a symbol, not when it satisfies a form's validation rules. Those rules were written to nudge people away from dragon and 123456, and what they mostly produced was Dragon1!.
understanding.p2: What actually resists guessing is unpredictability, and a person cannot supply it. Human-chosen passwords cluster in the same few shapes: a word, a capital at the front, a digit and an exclamation mark at the end. An attacker's dictionary knows that shape, so a nine-character password built that way falls in seconds while a nine-character password drawn at random does not.
understanding.p3: So the useful question is never how a password looks. It is how many equally likely passwords the thing that made it could have produced instead. This tool draws every character and every word uniformly from the browser's cryptographic generator, then tells you exactly how large that set was.

entropy.title: Entropy, and what the number means
entropy.p1: Entropy is that set size, written as a power of two. A password with 40 bits of entropy is one of 2⁴⁰ — about a trillion — equally likely results. Each extra bit doubles the work, so 41 bits is twice as hard as 40, and 60 bits is a million times harder.
entropy.p2: Bits come from the number of choices multiplied by how many times you make one. A random character out of 94 is log₂(94) ≈ 6.55 bits, so twenty of them is about 131. A word out of the 1024-word list is exactly 10 bits, so six words is exactly 60. A digit is log₂(10) ≈ 3.32 bits, which is why a six-digit PIN comes to 19.9 no matter how carefully it was drawn.
entropy.p3: The figure describes the generator, not the string that came out of it. That distinction is where most strength meters go wrong: they inspect the characters, find mixed case and a symbol, and award points. But Password1! and a random k7#Qm2vL look similar to a checker and are astronomically far apart in practice, because one came from a list of common shapes and the other from a uniform draw.
entropy.p4: It also means the number moves when you change a setting, not when you press regenerate. Two passwords made with the same options are exactly as strong as each other, however different they look.
entropy.tableCaption: Strength bands and the entropy each one opens at

bands.very-weak: Falls in seconds. Fine for nothing.
bands.weak: Falls in minutes to weeks. Not enough for an account.
bands.fair: Months to a few hundred thousand years. Adequate, not comfortable.
bands.strong: Out of reach of a single rig today.
bands.very-strong: Out of reach of any attacker worth modelling.

entropy.guaranteeNote: One wrinkle, and it goes the honest way. A random password is guaranteed to contain at least one character from every class you switched on, which removes every result that misses a class — so the real keyspace is slightly smaller than the pool size raised to the length. This tool counts the difference by inclusion–exclusion rather than ignoring it. At twenty characters it costs well under a bit; at four characters it is worth knowing about.

attackers.title: How long it takes to crack
attackers.p1: There is no such thing as the time to crack a password. The same secret falls in an afternoon or outlasts the sun depending entirely on who is guessing and what they are guessing against, and a tool that shows one number without saying which is hiding the interesting part.
attackers.p2: So the attacker is a control here rather than a hidden constant. Pick the scenario that matches what you are protecting: a password on a live login form is up against something very different from the same password sitting in a database that leaked.
attackers.tableCaption: Attacker scenarios and the guess rate each one assumes

when.throttled: Guessing at a login form that rate-limits. Nothing has leaked.
when.bcrypt: A breach where passwords were hashed with bcrypt at cost 12, attacked offline on a multi-GPU rig.
when.sha256: A breach where a fast hash was used. The default, because it is the common case.
when.md5: A breach using MD5 or NTLM — still depressingly common. The worst case worth planning for.

attackers.roundingNote: The rates are rounded to a power of ten on purpose. They are the order of magnitude of published hashcat-class benchmarks for a multi-GPU rig, not measurements taken here, and each GPU generation moves them. A figure like 164,100,000,000 would imply a precision this estimate does not have. If you need current numbers, run hashcat -b on the hardware you are actually worried about.
attackers.magnitudeNote: The result is written out rather than abbreviated: 410 quintillion years, not 4.1E20 and not 410,000,000T. Both of those are the same figure, and neither is a quantity anyone can picture. Past a decillion — 10³³ — the names stop helping too, so the estimate switches to 10ⁿ notation, and once it has outrun the age of the universe it says by how many times rather than leaving you to divide.
attackers.averageNote: The time shown is the average, not the worst case. A search through a uniformly random secret finds it after half the candidates, so the figure is half the keyspace divided by the rate. Exhausting the whole space takes twice as long — reporting that instead would be the more flattering error.
attackers.knowledgeNote: The estimate assumes the attacker knows exactly which settings produced the password and searches only that keyspace. That is deliberately pessimistic: not knowing makes their job harder, never easier, so the figure stays a lower bound on the work. It is also why guessing a human-chosen password is so much faster than these numbers suggest — the set a person really draws from is far smaller than they think.

modes.title: The three types
modes.intro: Three ways to make a secret, for three different jobs. The type also decides which of the controls below do anything.
modes.tableCaption: Password types, their ranges and what each is for

when.random: Anything a password manager will remember for you. This is the default, and it should stay the default.
when.memorable: A secret you have to type from memory or read aloud — a device login, a disk passphrase, a Wi-Fi key.
when.pin: A phone, a card or a lock that limits attempts. Never an account.

modes.wordlistNote: The passphrase list holds exactly {words, number} words, and that number is the point: one word is exactly ten bits, so the arithmetic needs no rounding and six words is exactly sixty. Every word is three to eight lowercase letters and common enough to retype after reading it once — a passphrase you cannot remember is a passphrase you will replace with something worse.
modes.pinNote: A PIN has no options beyond its length, and that is not an oversight. Every rule you might add — no repeats, no runs, no birthdays — removes candidates and makes it weaker, not stronger. A six-digit PIN is one of a million, which an offline attacker clears instantly. It is safe only behind a device that locks after a handful of tries.

options.title: Every control, and what it changes
options.intro: Nine controls. Three of them belong to a random password, three to a passphrase, and the rest apply throughout — so a control that cannot do anything in the current type is disabled and says why, rather than sitting there being ignored.
options.tableCaption: Generator options and when each one helps
options.modeDoes: Switches between random characters, a wordlist passphrase and a numeric PIN. Each counts its length differently.
options.modeWhen: Start here — it decides which of the controls below are live.
options.lengthDoes: Characters, words or digits, depending on the type. The one lever that always increases strength.
options.lengthWhen: Before reaching for anything else. Length beats complexity at every size.
options.classesDoes: Which of the four alphabets a random password draws from. At least one character of every class you switch on is guaranteed to appear.
options.classesWhen: Turn symbols off when a system rejects them — then add length back to make up for the smaller pool.
options.excludeSimilarDoes: Drops the glyphs that read as each other in most fonts.
options.excludeSimilarWhen: Someone will read the password off a screen and type it somewhere else.
options.excludeAmbiguousDoes: Drops brackets, quotes, slashes and punctuation that shells, CSV columns and JSON strings mangle.
options.excludeAmbiguousWhen: The password is going into a config file, a connection string or a command line.
options.separatorDoes: What goes between the words of a passphrase.
options.separatorWhen: Hyphen unless something downstream objects. It adds no entropy either way.
options.capitalizeDoes: Upper-cases the first letter of every word in a passphrase.
options.capitalizeWhen: A form demands a capital. It adds nothing to the strength.
options.includeNumberDoes: Appends one digit to one randomly chosen word.
options.includeNumberWhen: A form demands a number. Worth about six extra bits at six words.
options.attackDoes: Chooses the guess rate the crack-time estimate assumes.
options.attackWhen: Match it to the threat you actually care about. It never changes the password itself.
options.modeGatingNote: The gating follows one rule rather than a list of pairs: character classes and both exclusions need a character pool to trim, and only a random password has one. A passphrase is drawn from a wordlist and a PIN from the ten digits, so in those types the whole panel goes quiet. The three passphrase controls are the mirror of that.
options.similarSetNote: Excluding look-alikes drops {characters} — the classic seven plus the pipe, which is indistinguishable from a lowercase L in several common terminal faces.
options.ambiguousSetNote: Excluding awkward symbols drops {characters}. Both exclusions cost entropy by shrinking the pool: all four classes together give 94 characters, and both exclusions leave 67. The meter accounts for it, so raise the length if the band drops.
options.capitalizeNote: Capitalising every word adds exactly zero bits, and the entropy figure says so. A rule the attacker can apply themselves is not a secret — it turns one candidate into one different candidate, and the set does not grow. The separator is the same kind of nothing. The digit is different: both the word it lands on and its value are drawn at random, so it really is worth log₂(words × 10) bits.
options.separatorNote: What the separator does change is what the password contains. A hyphen is a symbol, so river-candle-motor satisfies a form demanding a symbol without any of the character controls being involved. The composition row under the generator counts it, because the finished string genuinely does contain it.
options.defaultsNote: The defaults are a twenty-character random password using all four classes with no exclusions, scored against leaked SHA-256 hashes. That comes to about 131 bits, which none of the attackers in the table gets close to. Switch to a passphrase and the default is six words — sixty bits — because that is the shortest passphrase that is not honestly weak.

privacy.title: Where the password goes
privacy.p1: Nowhere. Every password on this page is composed in your browser: there is no request to generate one, no request after one is made, and no server that has ever seen one.
privacy.p2: That is why the box is briefly empty when the page loads. Every other generator on this site renders its first result on the server and sends it down with the HTML, and this one deliberately does not. A generated secret in an HTTP response body is a secret that can end up in an access log, in a proxy that terminates TLS, or in whatever buffered the response on the way. The page ships a placeholder, and the first password appears a moment later, made locally.
privacy.p3: The link carries your settings and never the result. A URL like ?mode=memorable&length=8 is safe to share or bookmark; a password in a query string would land in browser history, in the referrer header of the next page you visit, and in every log between here and there.
privacy.p4: There is no download button either, and that is on purpose. Every other tool here offers one. Writing a secret into your downloads folder as a plain-text file, where it sits until you remember to delete it, is not a feature.
privacy.p5: The one exposure worth knowing about is the clipboard. Copying puts the password somewhere any application on your machine can read it, and it stays there until something replaces it. Paste it into your password manager, then copy something harmless.

practices.title: What to do with it
practices.p1: Use a password manager, and let it hold a long random password for every account. That is the whole recommendation, and it makes most of the rest academic: a password you never type can be thirty characters of noise, and the only one you have to remember is the one that unlocks the manager.
practices.p2: Make that one a passphrase. Six words from this list is sixty bits and you can memorise it in a couple of minutes; the same effort spent on random characters gets you about nine of them, which is worse. Length is the lever that always works — one more character on a random password is worth more than every complexity rule ever written.
practices.p3: Reuse is the failure that actually happens. Strength does not help if the same twenty-character password is also on a site that stored it badly: the attacker does not crack it, they read it and try it everywhere else. Unique per account is worth more than strong.
practices.p4: Turn on two-factor authentication wherever it is offered, and stop rotating passwords on a schedule. Forced expiry moves people from a strong password they chose once to a weak one they increment every quarter. Change a password when you have reason to think it leaked, not because ninety days elapsed.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Is it safe to generate a password on a website?
faq.a1: On this one the password is never transmitted: it is composed in your browser by the platform's cryptographic generator and stays there. You do still have to trust that the page you loaded is the page we published, which is the trust any web tool asks for. If you would rather not extend it, a local password manager's generator does the same job — the arithmetic on this page is here so you can check that whatever you use is telling you the truth.
faq.q2: Where does the randomness come from?
faq.a2: crypto.getRandomValues, the browser's cryptographically secure generator, seeded by the operating system. Math.random is never used anywhere in this tool: it is fast and predictable, and a predictable password generator is not one. Selections use rejection sampling rather than a modulo, so no character in the pool is very slightly more likely than another.
faq.q3: How accurate is the crack-time figure?
faq.a3: The keyspace is exact — counted rather than estimated, including the cost of guaranteeing one character per class. The guess rate is rounded to a power of ten, because it depends on the attacker's hardware and on the hash the target chose, and both change. So read the result as an order of magnitude against the scenario you picked. The distance between the four scenarios tells you far more than the digits inside any one of them.
faq.q4: Why is a six-digit PIN called very weak?
faq.a4: Because there are only a million of them, and a machine allowed to try them offline finishes before you let go of the mouse. That is not a flaw in the PIN, it is what a PIN is. It works because the phone or card behind it locks after a few wrong tries, not because the number is hard to guess — so never use one where an attacker can guess as fast as they like.
faq.q5: Is a passphrase really as strong as random characters?
faq.a5: It can be, but it takes more of it. Six words from the 1024-word list is sixty bits; ten random characters across all four classes is about sixty-six. The trade is memorability against length, and a passphrase you can hold in your head beats a stronger one you write on a sticky note. For anything a manager remembers for you, use random characters.
faq.q6: Why does capitalising the words not make it stronger?
faq.a6: Because it is a rule, and an attacker searching this keyspace applies the same rule for free. Upper-casing the first letter of every word turns one candidate into exactly one different candidate — the set does not grow. Any transformation you could describe in a sentence costs them nothing. Only choices made at random count, which is why the digit option adds bits and the capitalisation option does not.
faq.q7: Can I reuse a strong password across sites?
faq.a7: No. Strength protects against guessing, and reuse is not a guessing problem: when a site is breached and had stored passwords badly, the attacker gets yours directly and tries it on your email. A unique password per account is the highest-value habit here, and it is only practical with a manager.

understanding.title: What a QR code actually holds
understanding.p1: A QR code is a grid of black and white squares, called modules, that encodes bytes. Nothing more. The three large squares in the corners tell a scanner where the code is and which way up it sits; the rest is data, error-correction codewords, and a handful of fields describing how to read them.
understanding.p2: The grid comes in {versions, number} sizes, called versions. Version 1 is 21 modules across and version {versions, number} is 177. This tool picks the smallest version your content fits into, so a short link stays a coarse, forgiving code rather than a dense one.
understanding.p3: Because the payload is only bytes, the meaning of a code is a convention between whoever wrote it and whoever reads it. A phone offers to join a network when it sees a string beginning WIFI:, and to save a contact when it sees BEGIN:VCARD. That is why picking the right type matters more than it looks.

types.title: The seven types, and what a phone does with each
types.p1: Each type writes a different string into the same kind of code. The behaviour column is what a modern iOS or Android camera app offers when it sees one.
types.p2: Whatever the type, the payload is capped at {limit, number} characters here. Longer content technically fits in the largest codes, but the result is so dense that phone cameras and consumer printers both start to struggle — at that point a link to the content beats the content itself.

url.behaviour: Opens the address, usually after showing it first.

text.behaviour: Shows the text. Nothing is opened or dialled.

wifi.behaviour: Offers to join the network, password included.

contact.behaviour: Offers to save a new contact.

sms.behaviour: Opens the messaging app with the number and text filled in.

email.behaviour: Opens a draft with the address, subject and body filled in.

errorCorrection.title: Error correction, and why it is not free
errorCorrection.p1: Every QR code carries Reed–Solomon parity alongside its data, so a scanner can rebuild modules that are scratched, smudged, or hidden. The level decides how much of the code can be lost and still decode.
errorCorrection.p2: The parity is not magic — it is extra codewords, and they take space. Moving from L to H roughly halves how much content fits in a given version, which pushes the code to a larger version and makes every module smaller at the same printed size. A denser code on cheap paper can scan worse than a sparser one with less parity.
errorCorrection.p3: Level M is the default here because it survives ordinary handling without inflating the grid. Reach for H when something is going to sit on top of the code — which is exactly why setting a logo forces H and takes the choice away.

rows.L: The code lives on a screen, or on print you control and can reprint.
rows.M: Ordinary printing: posters, packaging, business cards. The default.
rows.Q: Industrial or outdoor labels that will collect dirt and scuffs.
rows.H: Anything with a logo over it, or a surface that will be handled hard.

design.title: Every option, and when to change it
design.p1: Styling a QR code is a trade against the one thing it has to do. These are the controls, what each one changes, and the case that justifies it.
design.p2: Contrast is the setting people get wrong most often. A scanner has no context to fall back on: it thresholds the image and reads squares. This tool warns below about {ratio, number}:1, well above the 4.5:1 that body text needs, because a camera in a badly lit room is working with far less than your monitor showed you. Dark on light also beats light on dark — some older scanners will not attempt an inverted code at all.
design.p3: Logo size ranges from {min, number}% to {max, number}% of the code width. Even at the top of that range and level H, the covered modules plus a scratch can be more than the parity can rebuild, so print one and scan it before committing to a run.
design.p4: The quiet zone runs from {min, number} to {max, number} modules. The specification says four, and that is the default. Dropping it is a design decision to make deliberately: the blank border is how a scanner finds the code’s edge against a busy background.

dynamic.title: Dynamic codes: changing a printed code
dynamic.p1: A static QR code is permanent. The bytes are in the ink, and the only way to change where it goes is to reprint it. A dynamic code solves that by encoding a short link on this site, which redirects to wherever you point it — so the paper stays valid while the destination moves.
dynamic.p2: Creating one gives you two links. The printed link is short — {length, number} characters after the domain, drawn from an alphabet with no vowels and no look-alike glyphs, so it survives being read aloud or typed by hand.
dynamic.p3: The other is the edit link, and it is a credential rather than a URL. It carries a {length, number}-character token, it is shown once, and it is stored here only as a SHA-256 digest — so a copy of the database does not let anyone re-point your codes. The browser that created the code also keeps a copy in its recent-codes list, which is how most people find it again; clear that list, or use another device, and the token is gone for good.
dynamic.p4: Every scan is counted, along with the time of the most recent one. That is the whole of it: no location, no device, no visitor identifier, and nothing that could distinguish one scanner from another.
dynamic.p5: There are real trade-offs to weigh before choosing dynamic over static:
dynamic.point1: A dynamic code stops working if this site does. A static code works forever and needs nothing from anyone.
dynamic.point2: Scanners see a link to this domain, not to yours. Where that matters for trust, print the destination beside the code.
dynamic.point3: A short link can point anywhere its owner later chooses, which is why creating one is behind a challenge, why the destination must be http or https, and why a chain of short links pointing at each other is refused.

reading.title: Reading codes back
reading.p1: The reader decodes with your camera or from a picture you pick. Camera frames are drawn to a canvas in this tab, decoded, and discarded — no frame is uploaded, recorded, or kept, and the scanner stops the moment it finds a code.
reading.p2: What comes back is split into labelled fields, so a Wi-Fi password appears on its own row rather than buried in a WIFI:T:WPA;S:… string. The raw payload is always available underneath, because sometimes that is exactly what you needed to see.
reading.p3: Links found in a scanned code are never opened automatically, and never made clickable unless they are http or https. A QR code hides its destination by design, which is what makes it good for posters and equally good for phishing — read the address before you follow it.

privacy.title: What leaves your browser
privacy.p1: Generating never does. The encoder, the Reed–Solomon parity, the styling and the PNG rasteriser all run in this tab. Your Wi-Fi password, your contact details and your links are turned into a code on your own machine, and no request is made while you type.
privacy.p2: Reading never does either. Both the camera and the upload path decode locally, and your logo is embedded straight into the SVG as data rather than being uploaded anywhere.
privacy.p3: Dynamic codes are the one exception, and they are opt-in. Choosing one sends the destination to this server, which stores it against a short slug so that scans can be redirected and counted. Everything else on this page stays where you typed it.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Do QR codes expire?
faq.a1: Static ones never do. The data is in the pattern itself, so a code printed today will still scan in twenty years if the ink survives. A dynamic code depends on the redirect behind it and stops working if that goes away.
faq.q2: Why did my code stop scanning after I changed the colours?
faq.a2: Almost always contrast. Scanners threshold the image into light and dark before they read anything, so two mid-tone colours become one. Keep the foreground dark, the background light, and pay attention to the warning under the colour fields.
faq.q3: Can I put my logo in the middle?
faq.a3: Yes, and doing so forces error correction to level H, which is what lets a scanner rebuild the modules the logo covers. Keep the logo modest and print a test — parity spent on your logo is parity that is no longer available for a scratch.
faq.q4: Is a Wi-Fi QR code safe to put on the wall?
faq.a4: It contains the password in plain text, so treat it exactly like writing the password on the wall. That is fine for a guest network and a bad idea for the one your file server is on.
faq.q5: PNG or SVG?
faq.a5: SVG for anything that will be printed or resized — it is vector, so it stays sharp at any size. PNG for places that will not take an SVG, such as some social platforms and older design tools.
faq.q6: What happens if I lose the edit link?
faq.a6: The code keeps working and keeps redirecting to wherever it last pointed, but nobody can change it again. The token is stored only as a hash, so this service cannot look it up or recover it. The recent-codes list in the browser you created it from keeps a copy, which is the practical answer for most people — save it elsewhere too if the code is going on something you cannot reprint.
faq.q7: Does this tool track the codes I make?
faq.a7: Static codes are never sent anywhere, so there is nothing to track. Dynamic codes store the destination, a count of scans and the time of the last one. No location, device, or visitor identity is recorded with them.

understanding.title: What a short link actually is
understanding.p1: A short link is not a copy of your address — it is a pointer to it. This tool stores your destination against a {length, number}-character code and hands you an address ending in that code. Whoever follows it is sent on with an HTTP 302, so their browser asks this service where to go every single time.
understanding.p2: That is what makes the destination changeable. A permanent redirect would be cached by every browser that followed it once, and re-pointing the link later would reach only people who had never used it. Every hop here is temporary, uncached, and marked so search engines neither index the link nor pass this site's ranking on to yours.
understanding.p3: Destinations may be up to {limit, number} characters and must be http or https. A short link that could carry any scheme would be a way to host an attack behind a name people trust, so nothing else is accepted.

options.title: Every option on the form
options.p1: One field is required and the rest are switches. Each one is off until you turn it on, and a panel that is off sends nothing.

target.name: Destination
target.what: Where visitors end up. Required, and re-checked every time the link is followed.
target.when: Always. A bare host gets https:// added.

alias.name: Custom name
alias.what: You choose the end of the link instead of having one drawn.
alias.when: The link goes on a poster, a slide, or anywhere someone reads it aloud.

password.name: Password
password.what: Visitors land on a gate and type a password before the redirect happens.
password.when: The destination is not secret, but you would rather it were not stumbled upon.

startsAt.name: Starts
startsAt.what: The link answers with a “not live yet” page until this instant.
startsAt.when: The link is printed before the thing it points at exists.

expiresAt.name: Expires
expiresAt.what: The link stops working at this instant and says so.
expiresAt.when: An offer, an event, or anything with a last day.

options.aliasRules: A custom name is {min, number} to {max, number} characters of lowercase letters, numbers and single hyphens, and cannot start or end with one. Capitals and spaces are folded for you — “Summer Sale” becomes “summer-sale”. Names that could be mistaken for something this site owns, or that a phishing link would want, are refused. If somebody already has the name you asked for, you are told so rather than quietly given a different one.
options.passwordRules: A link password is at least {min, number} characters and is stored as a salted PBKDF2 digest, never as text. It cannot be recovered — only replaced or removed from the edit page. Treat it as a curtain rather than a lock: it keeps a link from being casually opened, and nothing more.
options.scheduleRules: Both ends of the window are read in the time zone of the browser you fill the form in, and stored as an exact instant — so a link set to expire at 5pm in Dhaka expires at that moment everywhere. The start is inclusive and the expiry is exclusive. An expiry that has already passed is refused rather than saved, so “saved” never quietly means “still broken”.

editing.title: Changing where a link goes
editing.p1: Every link is created with a second address: its edit link. Open it and you can change the destination, add or remove the password, and move either end of the window. The short link itself is never editable, because everything already shared would break.
editing.p2: The edit link carries a {length, number}-character token, which is the only credential involved. It is stored as a SHA-256 digest, so a copy of the database does not hand anybody the ability to re-point your links. It is also shown exactly once, and cannot be recovered afterwards.
editing.p3: There are no accounts, so the token is the whole of the security model. Anyone holding it can re-point your link; nobody without it can.
editing.point1: Changing the destination takes effect immediately, everywhere the link has been shared or printed.
editing.point2: Removing a password takes effect on the next visit — anyone already through the gate has already been sent on.
editing.point3: A link cannot point at another short link on this site, on the way in or on the way out. A chain of redirects is how a destination gets hidden.

history.title: The list this browser keeps
history.p1: Every link you create is saved to this browser's local storage, up to {limit, number} of them, newest first. Nothing about that list leaves your machine — it is not an account, and this service cannot see it.
history.p2: Each entry keeps the edit link along with the short one. That is deliberate: an edit link shown once and never saved is a feature nobody can use. It also means the list is a credential store, so it comes with a button that empties it, and it is worth using that button on a shared machine.
history.p3: Clearing your browser's site data clears the list too, and the links themselves keep working — the list is a convenience, not the record. If a link matters, save its edit address somewhere you trust.

safety.title: What this service refuses to do
safety.p1: A public link shortener is an abuse surface before it is a feature. Anything that lets a stranger create a redirect on a domain other people trust is, without care, a phishing host that happens to shorten URLs.
safety.p2: So creation sits behind a challenge, destinations are limited to http and https, and a short link may never point at another short link on this host. Every hop is sent with no referrer, is never cached, and carries a header telling search engines not to index it or pass any ranking to the destination.
safety.p3: None of that makes a short link trustworthy on its own — no shortener's does. If you are following one you did not create, the only thing it tells you is that somebody wanted you to click it.
safety.point1: Names like “login”, “verify” and “secure” are reserved, because a link reading like one is a lure wearing this site's name.
safety.point2: The destination behind a password gate is never sent to the browser until the password checks out.
safety.point3: A link's visit count is the only thing recorded. There is no per-visitor log, no fingerprint, and nothing handed to the destination.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Can I change where a short link points after sharing it?
faq.a1: Yes — that is the point of the edit link you get when the link is created. Open it, change the destination, and every copy of the short link already out there follows the new one immediately. The short link itself never changes.
faq.q2: What happens if I lose the edit link?
faq.a2: The link keeps working, but you cannot change it. Edit links are shown once and stored only as a digest, so nobody — including this service — can recover one. The recent-links list in your browser keeps a copy, which is the practical answer for most people.
faq.q3: Do short links expire on their own?
faq.a3: Only if you ask for it. Leave the schedule switch off and a link works until you change it. Turn it on and you can set when it starts working, when it stops, or both.
faq.q4: How safe is the password on a link?
faq.a4: It is stored as a salted PBKDF2 digest and the destination is never sent to the browser until the password is right. But there is no attempt limit beyond the cost of the hash, so treat it as a way to stop a link being casually opened rather than as protection for something genuinely sensitive.
faq.q5: Can I pick my own short name?
faq.a5: Yes. Turn on “Custom name” and type one — lowercase letters, numbers and single hyphens, three characters or more. If it is already taken, or reserved, you are told which so you can pick another rather than being handed something you did not ask for.
faq.q6: Is the list of my links stored on your server?
faq.a6: No. It lives in your browser's local storage and never leaves your machine. Open the tool in a different browser, or clear your site data, and the list is empty — though the links themselves keep working.
faq.q7: Do you track who clicks my links?
faq.a7: Only a count, and the time of the most recent visit. No per-visitor record is kept, the destination is sent no referrer, and nothing about the visitor reaches this service beyond the request itself.

understanding.title: What a slug actually is
understanding.p1: A slug is the human-readable part of a URL that names one page: the how-to-build-a-website in example.com/blog/how-to-build-a-website. It is not the title and it is not an id. It is a short, stable label that a reader and a crawler can both make sense of at a glance.
understanding.p2: RFC 3986 sorts URL characters into groups. Letters, digits and four marks — hyphen, full stop, underscore and tilde — are unreserved: they travel through a URL untouched. Everything else either means something to the parser or has to be percent-encoded, which is how a space becomes %20 and a readable address turns into a wall of digits. A slug is what is left once you keep only the safe part.
understanding.p3: Which makes a slug generator mostly a set of decisions rather than an algorithm: what separates the words, whether the accents survive, how long is too long. Each of those is a control on this page, and the sections below say what each one costs.

separators.title: Choosing a separator
separators.intro: The separator is the only character that appears between words, so it is the one choice that shows up in every slug you make. All four below are unreserved, so none of them is ever escaped and none of them can break a link.
separators.tableCaption: The four separator characters a URL leaves untouched
separators.dashDoes: The web's default. Search engines have read it as a word boundary for as long as they have parsed URLs.
separators.dashWhen: Almost always — articles, docs, product pages, anything someone might read aloud.
separators.underscoreDoes: Just as safe, but historically read as part of a word rather than a break between two.
separators.underscoreWhen: File names, database identifiers, and anywhere the slug has to match a symbol in code.
separators.dotDoes: Legal in a path segment, and also how file extensions are written.
separators.dotWhen: Rarely — it can make the last word look like a file type.
separators.tildeDoes: Unreserved and uncommon, which is exactly what makes it unambiguous.
separators.tildeWhen: Internal or generated links, where you want the shape to stand out from editorial ones.
separators.custom: Choosing Custom hands the field over: type up to three characters and the words are joined with exactly what you typed, so a double dash or an underscore between dashes is yours to make. An empty field is a real answer too — it runs the words together, which is what onelongword needs.
separators.refused: The field accepts only those four marks. Type a space, an ampersand or a slash and the tool names the character and stops, rather than handing back a slug that a URL would immediately percent-encode into something nobody can read.

options.title: Every option, and what it costs
options.intro: Seven controls, and no hidden behaviour behind any of them. The defaults produce the shape most publishing tools expect, so the fastest way to use this page is to type a heading and copy the result.
options.tableCaption: Every option the slug generator exposes
options.separatorDoes: The character placed between words, chosen from four presets or typed by hand.
options.separatorWhen: Set it once and forget it. The dash suits nearly every public page.
options.lowercaseDoes: Sends the whole slug to lower case, using the invariant rules rather than your device's locale.
options.lowercaseWhen: Leave it on. A URL path is case-sensitive, so /About and /about are two pages to a crawler.
options.asciiDoes: Folds accents to plain letters, spells out letters such as ß and æ, then drops whatever has no ASCII form.
options.asciiWhen: On, unless the slug has to keep letters from a script that ASCII cannot represent.
options.stopWordsDoes: Removes about thirty function words — a, the, of, with — once the heading has been split.
options.stopWordsWhen: Long headings that would otherwise make a slug nobody reads to the end.
options.numbersDoes: Strips every digit, and with it any word that was only digits.
options.numbersWhen: Titles carrying a year or a count you would rather not freeze into the URL.
options.maxLengthDoes: Caps the slug, cutting on a word boundary instead of mid-word. Zero removes the cap.
options.maxLengthWhen: A house style fixes a limit; 60 to 80 characters is a common one.
options.perLineDoes: Treats each input line as its own heading and answers with one slug per line, blanks included.
options.perLineWhen: Converting a list of titles, a sitemap or a spreadsheet column in one pass.
options.orderNote: The order the steps run in is fixed, and it shows up in the output. The text is normalised and folded first, then split into words, then digits go, then the case changes, then stop words are dropped, and only then are the words joined and cut to length. That is why dropping numbers can remove a whole word — 2026 has nothing left once its digits go — while html5 simply becomes html.
options.lengthNote: The ceiling counts the separators it emits, not only the letters, and in bulk mode it is spent per line rather than across the batch. A single word longer than the whole budget is cut rather than dropped: half a word still points at the right page, and nothing at all does not.
options.defaultsNote: The defaults are a dash, lowercase, ASCII only, no filters and no ceiling. If a combination leaves nothing behind, the tool says so instead of handing back an empty slug that looks like it worked.

scripts.title: Accents, and everything ASCII cannot hold
scripts.p1: ASCII only does two jobs. First it decomposes the text, so é becomes a plain e with a separate accent mark that is then discarded — the same trick handles ü, ñ, å and the rest of the accented Latin range. Then it spells out the letters that have no accent to remove, because they were never accented letters: ß is not an s with a mark, so it becomes ss, while æ becomes ae, ø becomes o and þ becomes th.
scripts.p2: What it does not do is romanise. Bangla, Chinese, Cyrillic, Greek, Arabic and Hebrew have no single agreed spelling in Latin letters — the answer depends on the language, and often on the country. Rather than guess on your behalf, the tool drops what it cannot fold, and tells you plainly when nothing survived.
scripts.p3: Switch ASCII only off and those letters stay. Every modern browser and host accepts them: the link is percent-encoded on the wire and shown as the original letters in the address bar. It is a real choice, not a fallback — a Bangla heading gets a Bangla slug, and combining vowel marks stay attached to their consonants instead of being treated as word breaks.

useCases.title: Where slugs show up
useCases.p1: Slugs turn up wherever a machine needs a name a person also has to read: article and documentation routes, product and category pages, anchor ids inside a long page, branch names, files in a repository, and the keys in a translation catalogue.
useCases.p2: Two habits are worth more than any option here. Keep a slug stable once it is published — changing it breaks every link that pointed at the old one, so the fix is a redirect rather than an edit. And keep it short enough to survive being pasted into an email, a chat message or a printed page.
useCases.p3: If what you actually need is a link whose destination can change later, that is a different job: the URL Shortener makes a short address you can re-point after it has been shared.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Should I use a dash or an underscore?
faq.a1: A dash, unless you have a specific reason not to. Search engines have long read a hyphen as a word boundary and an underscore as part of a word, so learn-css reads as two words where learn_css can read as one. The difference is smaller than it once was, but the safer choice costs nothing.
faq.q2: Why does Next.js become next-js rather than nextjs?
faq.a2: Because the tool follows one rule: anything that is not a letter or a digit ends a word. The full stop in Next.js is a boundary like any other, so the two halves are joined by your separator. If you want nextjs, take the dot out of the heading first, or edit the result — this is a deliberate call rather than a guess about which dots are meaningful.
faq.q3: Can I use any character I like as a separator?
faq.a3: Only the four that RFC 3986 leaves unreserved: hyphen, underscore, full stop and tilde. Anything else — a space, a slash, an ampersand, a percent sign — either means something to a URL parser or is percent-encoded on the way out, which turns a readable slug into an unreadable one. Type one of those and the tool names the character and refuses, rather than quietly rewriting your choice.
faq.q4: What happens to a Bangla or Chinese heading?
faq.a4: With ASCII only switched on those letters have no ASCII form to fold to, so they are dropped — and if that leaves nothing at all, the tool says so instead of handing back an empty slug. Switch ASCII only off and the letters are kept exactly as typed, which every modern browser and host will accept.
faq.q5: How long should a slug be?
faq.a5: Short enough to read at a glance, long enough to say what the page is. Three to six words, or roughly 40 to 70 characters, covers most pages. The ceiling here cuts on a word boundary, so a capped slug still ends on a whole word.
faq.q6: Does any of this leave my browser?
faq.a6: No. Every character is transformed by JavaScript running in this tab. Nothing is uploaded, the page keeps no record of what you typed, and the tool works with the network disconnected.

howItWorks.title: What a diff actually computes
howItWorks.p1: Comparing two texts is not a matter of walking both from the top and reporting the first place they stop matching. Insert one line at the start of a file and every line after it moves down by one; a naive comparison would call the whole file rewritten. What a diff looks for instead is the longest sequence of lines the two texts still share, in order. Everything in that sequence is unchanged, and everything else is an insertion or a deletion.
howItWorks.p2: That is the whole model: two operations, insert and delete. A rewritten line is a deletion and an insertion that happen to land in the same place, which is why this tool pairs them back up before drawing anything — a deletion sitting next to an insertion is shown as one changed row with both halves on it, and the leftovers stay a plain addition or removal.
howItWorks.p3: Once a pair is on the same row, the same comparison runs again inside it, over words or characters instead of lines. That is what makes only the changed part of a line light up rather than the whole thing, and it is the difference between reading a diff and hunting through one.
howItWorks.p4: Nothing here reaches the network. The comparison runs in your browser, on text that never leaves it — which is why a contract draft or a production config is as safe to paste here as a code snippet.

options.title: Every control, and when to reach for it
options.intro: Five controls, and each one changes a different thing. Two change what counts as a difference, one changes how closely a difference is examined, and two change how the result is laid out.
options.tableCaption: The Diff Checker's controls and what each one does
options.viewDoes: Puts the two texts in facing columns, or in one column with removals and additions marked.
options.viewWhen: You are reading on a phone, or you want something that reads like a patch.
options.precisionDoes: Sets what a changed line is compared by inside itself: nothing, whole words, or single characters.
options.precisionWhen: A line changed by one character and you want to see which, or the highlighting is too noisy and you want it off.
options.ignoreCaseDoes: Compares lines and words with case folded away.
options.ignoreCaseWhen: One side has been through a formatter, or you are comparing values from case-insensitive systems.
options.ignoreWhitespaceDoes: Folds every run of spaces and tabs into one and trims both ends before comparing.
options.ignoreWhitespaceWhen: Indentation changed, or one side was re-wrapped, and you only care about the content.
options.hideUnchangedDoes: Keeps a few lines either side of every change and folds the rest into a marker saying how many are hidden.
options.hideUnchangedWhen: Two long files differ in three places and you do not want to scroll past the rest.
options.p1: The two ignore options are the ones worth being careful with, because they make differences disappear. A line that matches only after case or whitespace was folded away is still marked, quietly, on the row itself and counted in the line under the boxes — so "no differences" never means "no differences, as long as you do not look too closely".
options.p2: They apply inside a line as well as between lines. With case ignored, a word that differs only in case is not highlighted either; anything else would be a comparison that disagrees with itself depending on how far you zoom in.
options.p3: Precision is the one control that cannot change the verdict. Line, word or character, the same lines are added, removed and rewritten — all it changes is how much of a rewritten line is tinted.

views.title: Split or unified
views.p1: The split view puts the two texts in facing columns with their own line numbers, which is the layout to reach for when you want to read both versions. A changed line sits on one row with the old text on the left and the new text on the right, so your eye can move across rather than up and down.
views.p2: The unified view puts everything in one column: removals first, then additions, each marked with the leading minus or plus that every patch file uses. It is narrower, which is why it is the better choice on a phone, and it is the same shape as the patch the export button hands you.
views.p3: Both views fold unchanged runs the same way when you ask them to, and both let you step between changes with the arrows rather than scrolling for them.

patch.title: Exporting a unified patch
patch.p1: Copy or download gives you a unified diff — the format git apply and patch read, with a header naming each side, one hunk per region that changed, and three lines of context around each. It is built from the same comparison on screen, so what lands on disk cannot disagree with what you were looking at.
patch.p2: One detail is worth knowing, because it trips people up in every diff tool. A text ending in a newline is shown here with a final blank line, because that blank line is really there. A patch describes the same thing differently: it counts one fewer line and marks any side whose last line has no ending with “\ No newline at end of file”. The export converts between the two, which is why the patch can have one line fewer than the screen does.
patch.p3: Lines that matched only because an ignore option was on are context in the patch, not changes — the patch describes what has to happen to the text, and folding case or whitespace away is a way of reading it, not an edit to make.

limits.title: How big a comparison can get
limits.p1: Lining up two texts costs work in proportion to the size of both multiplied together, so there are limits: 200,000 characters and 5,000 lines a side, and a ceiling on the comparison itself. Identical runs at the start and end are matched off before any of that is measured, which is why two long files that differ in a few places sit well inside the limits while two entirely different ones of the same size may not.
limits.p2: When a limit is hit the tool says which one rather than hanging or silently truncating. The answer is usually to compare the part you care about: a section, a function, a single object out of a config.

useCases.title: What people compare here
useCases.p1: Two responses from an API before and after a deployment. A config file against the one that actually shipped. Two exports of the same table. A contract draft against the version that came back from the other side. A block of generated code against the block it replaced.
useCases.p2: It is also the fastest way to answer "are these two things the same?" for anything long enough that reading both is not an option — two keys, two long identifiers, two minified bundles. Turn precision up to character and the answer is a single tinted run.
useCases.p3: For anything where the two sides are versions of a file you keep, a real version control system will always tell you more. This is for the two things in front of you right now, neither of which is in a repository.

faq.title: Questions people ask
faq.q1: Does anything I paste leave my browser?
faq.a1: No. The comparison, the highlighting and the patch are all computed in your browser, and the page has nothing to send them to. Uploading a file reads it locally too. You can put the page in a tab, disconnect, and it will keep working.
faq.q2: What does diff precision actually change?
faq.a2: Only what happens inside a line that already changed. At line precision the whole line is tinted. At word precision the comparison runs again over the words in it, so only the words that differ light up. At character precision it runs over single characters, which is what you want for a one-character difference and too noisy for a rewritten sentence. The set of changed lines is the same in all three.
faq.q3: I moved a block of lines and it says they were deleted and added. Why?
faq.a3: Because that is what a diff is: a list of insertions and deletions that turn one text into the other. A moved block is a deletion in one place and an insertion in another, and no ordering of those two operations describes it as a move. Some tools guess at moves afterwards; this one shows you the edit script, which is what a patch has to carry anyway.
faq.q4: Why is a line shown as unchanged when the two sides clearly differ?
faq.a4: An ignore option is on. Ignoring case or whitespace makes lines that differ only that way count as the same line — the row is marked and the count under the boxes says how many, so you can tell at a glance whether the match is real or the option's doing.
faq.q5: Will the patch apply cleanly with git?
faq.a5: Yes, provided the file you apply it to is the text you put in the left box. It is a standard unified diff with three lines of context, including the no-newline marker where a side needs one. Give it real filenames by renaming the download, or paste it wherever you would paste any patch.
faq.q6: Can I compare two files instead of pasting?
faq.a6: Yes — each side has an upload button that reads a text file into that box. It is read in your browser like everything else, so nothing is transferred, and the same size limits apply once the text is in.

howItWorks.title: How this compressor works
howItWorks.p1: Every file you drop is decoded to raw pixels, optionally scaled down, and handed to a WebAssembly build of a real production encoder — MozJPEG, libwebp, libaom or OxiPNG. These are the same codecs Squoosh ships, and they are meaningfully better than the one built into your browser: `canvas.toBlob` gives you the browser's default JPEG writer with a single quality knob and no way to ask for anything else.
howItWorks.p2: The difference is not marketing. MozJPEG runs trellis quantisation, which searches for the set of coefficients with the best size-to-distortion trade at your chosen quality instead of taking the first one the quantiser produces. libwebp is set to its slowest analysis mode with sharp YUV conversion, which removes the coloured fringing on saturated edges that people usually mistake for WebP looking worse than JPEG. Both are off by default in a browser because both cost encoding time, and here you are the one waiting.
howItWorks.p3: Downscaling goes through a Lanczos3 filter in linear light rather than through the canvas. Drawing an image smaller with `drawImage` gives you whatever your GPU driver does, which on a large reduction is a box filter and visible aliasing. Doing the arithmetic in linear light also stops the picture darkening as it shrinks, which is the artefact you see when a bright checkerboard turns grey instead of staying bright.
howItWorks.p4: All of that runs in this tab. There is no upload, no queue on somebody else's server, and no limit imposed by a plan — the ceiling is your own machine's memory, which is why the file count and megapixel caps exist.

formats.title: Choosing a format
formats.intro: The format decides more than the quality slider does. A photograph in PNG will always be larger than the same photograph in WebP, whatever the quality is set to, because PNG has no way to throw away what the eye will not miss.
formats.tableCaption: Output formats and when each is the right answer
formats.autoDoes: Keeps each file in the format it arrived in, so a JPG comes back a JPG.
formats.autoWhen: Something downstream expects the extension it already has.
formats.smallestDoes: Encodes each file with every codec that suits it and keeps the shortest result.
formats.smallestWhen: Size is what matters and you can wait — this is three or four encodes per file.
formats.webpDoes: Lossy or transparent, roughly 25–35% smaller than JPEG at a matched quality.
formats.webpWhen: You want one format that is smaller than JPEG and read everywhere current.
formats.avifDoes: Usually the smallest of the four on photographs, at several times the encoding cost.
formats.avifWhen: The file is served to browsers you control, and bytes matter more than encode time.
formats.jpegDoes: MozJPEG with trellis quantisation and a progressive scan order.
formats.jpegWhen: The file has to open in anything, including software from before 2010.
formats.pngDoes: Rewrites the file losslessly with OxiPNG — same pixels, fewer bytes.
formats.pngWhen: The image is a logo, a diagram or a screenshot of text, where a lossy artefact is obvious.
formats.alphaNote: JPEG has no alpha channel. Send it a transparent image and this tool composites the picture onto white first and says so on the row, rather than letting the encoder keep whatever colour happened to sit under the transparency — usually black.
formats.smallestNote: Under Smallest of all four, JPEG only competes for an image that is fully opaque, and PNG only competes against a source that was already lossless. Both exclusions save an encode that could not have won.

controls.title: Every control
controls.intro: Three settings decide the output, and they are applied in the order listed: the picture is scaled first, then encoded at the quality you chose, in the format you chose.
controls.tableCaption: What each control does and when to move it
controls.qualityDoes: Sets the encoder's quality parameter from 10 to 100. Ignored by PNG, which is lossless here.
controls.qualityWhen: The default is visibly soft on your image, or is leaving more bytes than you need.
controls.formatDoes: Picks the encoder, or asks for all of them and keeps the smallest result.
controls.formatWhen: See the table above — this is the setting with the largest effect on size.
controls.resizeDoes: Scales the picture so its longer side is at most the value you pick, keeping the aspect ratio.
controls.resizeWhen: A 12-megapixel photograph is going into a page that will display it 800 pixels wide.
controls.compressDoes: Runs every file that has no result yet, one at a time, and reports progress as it goes. Files already compressed are left alone.
controls.compressWhen: You have dropped files in — nothing is encoded until you press it.
controls.redoDoes: Re-encodes that one row under the settings showing now, replacing its result.
controls.redoWhen: A finished row has dimmed and you want it done again at the new quality.
controls.downloadDoes: Saves one result under the original name with -min and the new extension.
controls.downloadWhen: You only wanted the one file.
controls.downloadAllDoes: Packs every finished result into one archive, numbering any names that would collide.
controls.downloadAllWhen: There is more than one result and you would rather not click through them.
controls.removeDoes: Drops a single file from the queue along with its result.
controls.removeWhen: One file in a batch was picked by mistake.
controls.clearDoes: Empties the queue and releases every preview.
controls.clearWhen: You are done, or want to start from nothing.
controls.orderNote: Because scaling happens before encoding, a size cap and a lower quality compound: halving the longest edge quarters the pixel count before the encoder ever sees it, which is why the cap usually saves more than the slider does.
controls.staleNote: Changing a setting never rewrites a result you already have. The finished rows dim, the status line says so, and Compress still only runs the files that have none — so adding a second image at a different quality leaves the first one exactly as it was. Redoing one is the Compress again button on that row.

quality.title: Picking a quality
quality.p1: Quality numbers are not comparable between codecs. MozJPEG at 75 and libwebp at 75 do not target the same distortion, and AVIF's scale is different again — libaom's own default is 50, which on most photographs looks like JPEG at somewhere in the seventies. Compare the output, never the number.
quality.p2: For photographs, 70 to 80 is the range where the saving is large and the artefacts are hard to find without flicking between the two at full size. Below about 60 the flat areas of sky and skin start to band, and the edges around text pick up a halo. Above 90 the file grows quickly for a difference almost nobody sees.
quality.p3: Images with hard edges — screenshots, diagrams, anything with text in it — behave differently. A lossy codec spends its bits on the edge and leaves ringing beside it, which is far more visible than the same artefact in foliage. Those are the images to keep as PNG, or to push to 90 and up if they must be lossy.

metadata.title: What happens to metadata
metadata.p1: A re-encode starts from decoded pixels, so nothing that was attached to the original file survives: EXIF, GPS coordinates, camera and lens details, capture time, copyright fields, and any embedded colour profile are all gone from the result. That is a privacy improvement most of the time and a loss if you were relying on it — export the metadata first if you need it.
metadata.p2: One tag is applied rather than dropped. A phone usually records a rotated photograph the right way up in the pixels and writes an orientation tag saying which way to turn it. Discarding the tag without acting on it is why so many compressed photographs come back sideways, so the decode step applies the rotation to the pixels before anything else happens.
metadata.p3: The missing colour profile matters for images that were not sRGB to begin with. A photograph exported in Display P3 or Adobe RGB is decoded to those numbers and written back without the profile that explains them, so a wide-gamut original can come back looking flat. Convert to sRGB before compressing if the source was not sRGB already.

limits.title: Limits, and why they exist
limits.p1: Up to 40 files can be queued at once, each up to 25 MB, and each up to 40 megapixels once decoded. The last of those is the one that catches people out: a 2 MB PNG can hold a hundred megapixels, and decoded pixels cost four bytes each regardless of how small the file was.
limits.p2: Files are compressed one after another rather than all at once. A parallel run would be faster on paper and would also hold every decoded image in memory simultaneously, which is how a tab crashes halfway through a batch. Sequential work also means the progress count is honest.
limits.p3: AVIF is slow. A large photograph can take several seconds per file, and Smallest of all four runs AVIF alongside the others. That is the trade for the smallest output; if you want a quick answer for a large batch, choose WebP outright.

privacy.title: Where your images go
privacy.p1: Nowhere. The codecs are WebAssembly modules running inside this page, so the decode, the resize and the encode all happen on your own machine. There is no request carrying your file, which is why the tool keeps working after the page has loaded and the network has gone.
privacy.p2: Nothing is stored either. The queue lives in the page for as long as the tab is open, and the preview thumbnails are object URLs released when you remove a file or leave. Reloading the page loses everything, on purpose.
privacy.p3: This matters more for images than for text. A photograph carries where it was taken and often which device took it, and an ordinary online compressor has both the moment you upload. Here the only copy of your file is the one you already had.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Is this better than compressing with an online service?
faq.a1: For output quality it is comparable — the encoders are the same ones most services run, at settings tuned past their defaults. For privacy it is not close: nothing is uploaded, so there is no copy on a server to be retained, indexed or leaked, and there is no per-day limit to hit.
faq.q2: Why did my file get bigger?
faq.a2: Because it was already compressed well. Re-encoding an image that was written at a high quality by a good encoder cannot find much left to remove, and the second encode adds its own overhead. When that happens the row shows a negative saving rather than hiding it, so you can keep the original.
faq.q3: Does compressing twice lose more quality?
faq.a3: Yes, for any lossy format. Each encode discards detail the previous one kept, and the losses accumulate — a JPEG re-saved five times looks visibly worse than the same image encoded once at the lowest of those five qualities. Always compress from the original, not from an earlier result.
faq.q4: Why is AVIF so much slower than the rest?
faq.a4: It is doing far more work. libaom searches many more ways of predicting each block than a JPEG or WebP encoder does, and that search is what buys the smaller file. Running it in WebAssembly costs a further factor on top. It is worth it for images you will serve many times, and rarely worth it for a one-off.
faq.q5: Can I compress an animated GIF?
faq.a5: Not as an animation. A GIF is decoded to its first frame and written back as a still image, so the animation is lost. Nothing here writes an animated format.
faq.q6: What happens to a transparent PNG if I choose JPEG?
faq.a6: It is composited onto white before encoding and the row tells you so. JPEG has no alpha channel, and the alternative — handing transparent pixels straight to the encoder — produces the black boxes you sometimes see where a logo used to be.
