howItWorks.title: How the conversion works
howItWorks.p1: Every file you drop is decoded to raw pixels in this tab, scaled if you asked for that, and handed to a real encoder compiled to WebAssembly — MozJPEG for JPG, libwebp for WebP, libaom for AVIF and OxiPNG for PNG. These are the same encoders Squoosh runs, and they are why the output is not simply what canvas.toBlob would have written.
howItWorks.p2: Nothing is uploaded. There is no server in this flow at all: the codecs are downloaded once, on demand, and everything after that happens on your machine. A picture you convert here never leaves the browser tab it was dropped into.
howItWorks.p3: Codecs load only when they are used. If you never pick AVIF, libaom is never fetched — so the first conversion into a format you have not used yet takes a moment longer while its encoder arrives.
howItWorks.p4: Files are worked through one at a time rather than all at once. A decoded picture costs four bytes per pixel whatever the file size, so converting twenty at the same time is how a tab runs out of memory halfway through. One at a time is also the only way the progress count can be honest.

targets.title: Which format to convert to
targets.intro: Four of the six targets name a single encoder. The other two build an icon file, which is a container rather than a format — PNG all the way down, arranged so a browser or an operating system can pick the size it wants.
targets.tableCaption: Conversion targets and what each one is for
targets.pngDoes: A lossless PNG, run through OxiPNG. Transparency is kept.
targets.pngWhen: The picture is a screenshot, a diagram or a logo, or anything that must not lose a pixel.
targets.jpegDoes: A progressive JPEG from MozJPEG, with trellis quantisation. No alpha channel.
targets.jpegWhen: It is a photograph and it has to open literally anywhere.
targets.webpDoes: A WebP from libwebp at its slowest analysis setting, with sharp YUV and alpha.
targets.webpWhen: You want a photograph noticeably smaller than JPG without giving up transparency.
targets.avifDoes: An AVIF from libaom, with chroma delta Q and sharp YUV.
targets.avifWhen: Size matters more than encode time and you do not need to support every browser ever shipped.
targets.icoDoes: One .ico file holding a PNG for each square size you selected.
targets.icoWhen: You need a favicon.ico and nothing else — a legacy path, a desktop shortcut, a Windows application icon.
targets.faviconDoes: A ZIP holding favicon.ico, four PNG sizes, a site.webmanifest and the HTML to link them.
targets.faviconWhen: You are setting up a site's icons from scratch and want the whole set rather than one file.
targets.note1: There is no wrong answer between WebP and AVIF; there is only a trade. AVIF is usually smaller at the same visual quality, and it takes appreciably longer to encode — on a large photograph, seconds rather than a moment. WebP encodes fast and is read by everything still receiving security updates.
targets.note2: Converting a format into itself is allowed and is not a no-op: it re-encodes the picture at the quality you set, which is how you shrink a WebP that was written at quality 95. It also means the output keeps the input's filename, which is correct — it is the same picture.

controls.title: Every control on this page
controls.intro: Controls that cannot affect the target you picked are disabled rather than left live and quietly ignored, and the hint underneath each one says why it went grey.
controls.tableCaption: The converter's controls and what each one does
controls.targetDoes: Chooses the encoder or the icon container everything in the queue is written with.
controls.targetWhen: Always — it is the one setting that decides what the other four mean.
controls.qualityDoes: Sets the encoder's quality, 10 to 100. Live for JPG, WebP and AVIF only.
controls.qualityWhen: The output is bigger than you want, or a gradient has visible banding in it.
controls.resizeDoes: Caps the longest side in pixels, scaling down with Lanczos3 in linear light. Never enlarges.
controls.resizeWhen: The source is a camera original and the destination is a web page.
controls.backgroundDoes: Decides what sits behind transparency: keep it, or composite onto white or black.
controls.backgroundWhen: The picture has transparency and the target either cannot carry it or should not show it.
controls.sizesDoes: Chooses which squares go inside the .ico. Live for the ICO target only.
controls.sizesWhen: You need a size beyond the usual three — a 256 for a desktop shortcut, say.
controls.convertDoes: Runs every file that has no result yet, one at a time. Files already converted are left alone.
controls.convertWhen: You have dropped files in — nothing is encoded until you press it.
controls.redoDoes: Converts that one row again under the settings showing now, replacing its result.
controls.redoWhen: A finished row has dimmed and you want it in the target you have just picked.
controls.downloadDoes: Saves that one row's output. A row that produced several files is packed into a ZIP first.
controls.downloadWhen: You only wanted one file out of the batch.
controls.downloadAllDoes: Packs every finished row into one ZIP, with a folder per row that produced more than one file.
controls.downloadAllWhen: You converted a batch and want it in one go.
controls.removeDoes: Drops that file from the queue and releases its preview.
controls.removeWhen: You dropped in something you did not mean to.
controls.clearWhen: You are starting on a different set of pictures.
controls.orderNote: The order of operations is fixed and worth knowing: the picture is scaled first, then flattened onto the background if that applies, then encoded. Scaling before flattening is what keeps the edges of a soft-edged logo clean, because the resizer works on premultiplied alpha in linear light and there is still an alpha channel to work on at that point.
controls.staleNote: Changing a setting never redoes a result you already have. Finished rows dim, and Convert still only runs the files that have none — so adding a second picture with a different target leaves the first one exactly as it was. Redoing one is the Convert again button on that row. A setting the current target ignores does not dim anything either — nudging the quality slider while PNG is selected cannot change a byte, so it does not pretend to.

favicon.title: What the favicon pack contains
favicon.p1: The pack is not a matter of taste. Every file in it exists because some specific client asks for it: favicon.ico at 16, 32 and 48 is what a browser requests from your site root whether or not anything links to it, and what Windows reads for a pinned shortcut; favicon-96x96.png covers a high-DPI tab; apple-touch-icon.png at 180 is what iOS puts on the home screen; and the 192 and 512 PNGs are the pair an install prompt looks for through the web app manifest.
favicon.p2: The .ico holds PNGs rather than the older headerless bitmap-plus-mask form. Every browser reads PNG-compressed entries, and so has Windows since Vista — while a 48×48 bitmap entry costs nine kilobytes where the PNG costs a few hundred bytes. If you are targeting Windows XP, this is the one thing here that will not work for you.
favicon.p3: The site.webmanifest takes its name and short_name from your filename, because the alternatives were to invent a site name or to add a text box for one. Edit it — it is two fields at the top of the file. The manifest deliberately leaves out theme_color and background_color: this tool does not know your site's colours, and a guessed #ffffff is a wrong answer wearing the clothes of a considered one.
favicon.p4: The manifest icons declare purpose "any", never "maskable". A maskable icon promises that its content stays inside a safe zone the launcher may crop to a circle; these icons are scaled to fill the square, so claiming maskable would cost the edges of your logo on Android and nowhere else. If you want maskable icons, add padding to your source picture first and declare it yourself.
favicon.p5: head.html in the pack holds the same four link tags shown above the queue, and assumes the files sit at your site root. Move them into a subfolder and the href values need the same move.

transparency.title: Transparency, and what happens to it
transparency.p1: PNG, WebP, AVIF and both icon targets carry an alpha channel. JPG does not — it has no way to record it — so the Background control drops its transparent entry the moment you pick JPG, rather than accepting a setting it would then have to ignore.
transparency.p2: Flattening composites the picture over a solid colour: each pixel becomes source × alpha + background × (1 − alpha). It is not the same as deleting the alpha channel. An encoder handed transparent pixels with no instruction keeps whatever colour happened to sit underneath, which is usually black — and a logo that turns into a black rectangle is the single most common surprise in image conversion.
transparency.p3: For an icon, the padding around a non-square picture follows the same setting. Keep transparent and a wide logo sits on nothing, which is what a favicon usually wants; choose a colour and it sits on that colour, edge to edge, with no seam between the picture and its margin.
transparency.p4: A picture with no transparency at all is left alone whatever you choose here, so the setting costs nothing to leave where it is.

icons.title: How a rectangle becomes a square icon
icons.p1: An icon is square and most pictures are not, so something has to give. This tool scales the picture to fit inside the square with its proportions intact and fills what is left with the background — it never stretches. Stretching is immediately visible on a logo, and a logo is what people convert to icons.
icons.p2: Every size is scaled from the source pixels, not from the size above it. Chaining a 512 down to a 256, then a 128, then a 64, then a 16 compounds the resampling error four times over, and a 16×16 icon has no pixels to spare.
icons.p3: Asking for a size larger than the source is allowed, and the row says so. A 512 icon made from a 200-pixel logo is a genuinely enlarged picture and will look soft; the tool would rather tell you than quietly drop the size or refuse the file.

quality.title: Choosing a quality
quality.p1: Quality is not a percentage of anything. It is a knob on the quantiser, and the same number means different things to different encoders — MozJPEG at 80 and libaom at 80 are not the same trade.
quality.p2: 80 is the default here, higher than the compressor's 75, because the jobs differ. Compressing is a request for a smaller file. Converting is a request for a different format, and the picture is expected to survive the trip — including when the source was already lossy and this re-encode compounds with it.
quality.p3: Below about 60 the artefacts stop being subtle: blocking on flat areas in JPG, smearing on fine detail in WebP and AVIF. Above about 92 you are mostly spending bytes on noise. If a specific gradient bands, raise the quality rather than switching format — banding is a quantiser problem, and every encoder here has one.

metadata.title: What the conversion destroys
metadata.p1: Decoding a picture to pixels drops everything that was not pixels. EXIF goes, which includes the camera model, the exposure settings and any GPS coordinates. The embedded colour profile goes too, so a photograph in Display P3 or Adobe RGB comes back as plain sRGB and its most saturated colours will shift.
metadata.p2: The one metadata field that is honoured rather than dropped is orientation. A phone writes the picture in the sensor's own rotation and records which way up it was, so an encoder that drops the tag without applying it turns every portrait photograph sideways. This tool applies it first, then discards it.
metadata.p3: Losing EXIF is often the point — it is the simplest way to strip GPS coordinates out of a picture before publishing it. But if you need the metadata, keep the original: nothing here can put it back.

limits.title: Limits, and why they are where they are
limits.p1: Forty files at a time, twenty-five megabytes each. Both numbers are about memory in one browser tab rather than about bandwidth, because nothing here is uploaded.
limits.p2: There is also a forty-megapixel ceiling, checked after decoding rather than from the file size, because the two are barely related — a two-megabyte PNG can hold a hundred megapixels, and four bytes per pixel is what actually has to fit.
limits.p3: The favicon pack does seven encodes per picture where a raster target does one, so a batch of packs takes appreciably longer than the same batch converted to WebP. The progress count is per file, not per encode, so a pack row sits on one number for a while.

privacy.title: Privacy
privacy.p1: No picture you drop here is uploaded, and no server is involved in the conversion. The codecs are WebAssembly modules fetched once from this site and then run in your tab.
privacy.p2: Nothing is stored either. Close the page and the queue, the previews and every converted file are gone with it — so download what you want before you leave.
privacy.p3: That also means this works offline once the page and the codec for your chosen format have loaded.

faq.title: Questions people actually ask
faq.q1: Is this the same as the Image Compressor?
faq.a1: They share the same four encoders, and they answer different questions. The compressor's job is a smaller file — it will pick a format for you, or encode to all of them and keep the shortest result. This tool's job is a specific format you named, plus the two icon containers the compressor does not write at all. If you want a picture smaller, use the compressor; if you want it as AVIF or as a favicon, use this.
faq.q2: Which favicon files do I actually need?
faq.a2: If you only take one thing, take favicon.ico at your site root — browsers request it by path with no link tag at all. Everything else in the pack buys a specific improvement: the 96 for high-DPI tabs, the 180 for the iOS home screen, and the 192 and 512 with a manifest for the install prompt. Take the pack and delete what you do not want; adding one back later means regenerating it.
faq.q3: Why did my transparent logo come out with a white background?
faq.a3: Either you converted to JPG, which has no alpha channel and therefore has to put the picture on some colour, or the Background control was set to white. Set it to Keep transparent and convert to PNG, WebP or AVIF instead.
faq.q4: Can it convert HEIC, SVG or a RAW file?
faq.a4: No. This tool can read whatever your browser can decode — JPG, PNG, WebP, AVIF, GIF and BMP. HEIC is only decodable in Safari, SVG has no intrinsic pixel size to convert from, and RAW formats need a demosaicer that no browser ships. Convert those to PNG elsewhere first.
faq.q5: What happens to an animated GIF?
faq.a5: You get its first frame. Nothing here writes an animated format, so the other frames have nowhere to go — this is the one case where the conversion loses something the file extension will not warn you about.
faq.q6: Why is AVIF taking so long?
faq.a6: libaom is a slow encoder, and it is running in WebAssembly on one thread. That is the price of AVIF's size. On a large photograph, expect seconds rather than an instant; on a batch, expect to leave the tab open. WebP gets most of the saving for a fraction of the time.
faq.q7: Does converting a JPG to PNG make it better quality?
faq.a7: No, and this is worth being clear about. PNG is lossless, so it will preserve exactly what the JPG contained, artefacts included, usually in a much larger file. Detail lost in the original compression is gone; nothing can reconstruct it. Convert to PNG to stop further loss, not to undo loss already taken.

The grid is fitted to your picture's proportions, and the blur is painted beside it at full size so you can see whether it actually resembles the original. Everything happens in this tab.

whatItIs.title: What a blur placeholder is for
whatItIs.p1: An image that has not loaded yet leaves a hole. Fill it with nothing and the text below jumps when the picture arrives; fill it with a grey box and the page looks broken rather than loading. A blur placeholder fills it with the picture's own colours, in roughly the right places, so the layout is settled before a single byte of the real file has arrived and the load reads as a photograph coming into focus.
whatItIs.p2: BlurHash is one way of writing that down. It is a short string — twenty to thirty characters for the usual settings — that encodes the low frequencies of a picture and nothing else. It is short enough to sit in a database column beside the image's URL, to travel in the same JSON response as the rest of the record, and to be rendered from server-side markup with no extra request.
whatItIs.p3: That last point is the whole trick. A placeholder that needs its own HTTP request is a placeholder that arrives after the thing it was standing in for. A hash inlined in the response has already arrived by the time the browser reads it.
whatItIs.p4: This tool does both directions. Give it a picture and it produces the hash, the base64 blurDataURL that next/image wants, and the snippet to use either one. Give it a hash somebody else made and it paints it back, so you can see what a string in your database actually looks like.

howItWorks.title: How the encoding works
howItWorks.p1: The picture is decoded to pixels, converted from sRGB into linear light, and projected onto a small grid of cosine basis functions — the same transform JPEG uses, stopped early. Each basis function has a coefficient per colour channel: how much of that particular wave the picture contains.
howItWorks.p2: Only the first few coefficients are kept. Four across and three down means twelve of them, and everything finer than that is thrown away — which is exactly the point, because what is left is the blur.
howItWorks.p3: Those coefficients are then quantised hard and written in base83. The alphabet is 83 characters chosen because every one of them survives being written inside a JSON string, an HTML attribute and a URL query with no escaping. That is why a hash can be pasted anywhere without a second thought.
howItWorks.p4: The average colour gets four characters of its own and full precision, because it is the one value the eye will notice being wrong. Every other coefficient gets two characters, expressed as a fraction of a scale that is itself stored in the hash.
howItWorks.p5: Working in linear light rather than in sRGB matters more than it sounds. Averaging gamma-encoded values darkens the result — a blur of a bright picture comes out muddy — so the conversion happens on the way in and again on the way out.

controls.title: Every control on this page
controls.intro: Controls that cannot affect what you are doing are disabled rather than left live and quietly ignored, and the hint underneath each one says why it went grey.
controls.tableCaption: The generator's controls and what each one does
controls.modeDoes: Switches between making a hash from a picture and painting a hash you already have.
controls.modeWhen: Always — it decides which of the two inputs below is shown.
controls.sourceDoes: Decodes a picture in this tab and keeps it, so changing a setting costs a transform rather than a re-read.
controls.sourceWhen: You have the picture and want the string.
controls.hashDoes: Takes a hash and paints it. Waits for you to stop typing before redrawing.
controls.hashWhen: You have a string in a database and want to know what it looks like.
controls.componentXDoes: How many cosine terms are kept left to right, 1 to 9. Each one adds two characters. Fitted to the picture until you set it yourself.
controls.componentXWhen: The fit is not what you want — you are matching an existing hash's shape, or trading detail for a shorter string.
controls.componentYWhen: Same reason, the other way. Keep the pair near the picture's proportions.
controls.ratioDoes: Chooses the proportions the preview is painted at. Live only when decoding.
controls.ratioWhen: You are looking at a bare hash and know what shape the real picture is.
controls.edgeDoes: Sets the longest edge of the PNG inside the data URI, from 16 to 64 pixels.
controls.edgeWhen: The data URI is longer than you want, or the blur looks blocky rather than soft.
controls.punchDoes: Multiplies every coefficient except the average, pulling the colours further apart.
controls.punchWhen: The placeholder looks washed out next to the real picture.
controls.snippetDoes: Switches between the next/image, react-blurhash and plain CSS forms of the same result.
controls.snippetWhen: You know where this is going and want it in the right shape.
controls.disabledNote: Two controls change meaning with the mode. The detail counts are yours to set when encoding and are read out of the hash when decoding, because the first character of every hash records them. The shape is the opposite: the picture you dropped in already has proportions, so the control only opens up when there is no picture to ask.
controls.punchNote: Punch is the one setting that does not touch the hash. It is applied while painting, which means it is also a decision your reader's browser makes rather than one you bake in — react-blurhash takes it as a prop, and the PNG this page writes has it baked in because a PNG has no coefficients left to scale. Change punch and the hash above it stays exactly the same string.

components.title: Choosing how much detail to keep
components.p1: The two detail numbers are the only real quality knob, and the trade is straightforward: each extra component costs two characters and buys one more cosine term in that direction. Drop a picture in and both are chosen for you from its proportions; change either one and the pair stays where you put it.
components.p2: That fit matters more than it sounds, and it is why the old flat default of four by three is not used here. A 16:9 photograph given a four-by-three grid spends a third of its coefficients on vertical detail that is not there and starves the direction that is; the same picture at seven by four resolves three separate rock formations where the smaller grid showed one red band. The pairs are matched on the ratio of the two numbers, so a portrait gets the mirror image of what its landscape rotation would.
components.p3: Nine by nine is the format's ceiling — the size flag is a single base83 character holding both numbers, so a tenth column has nowhere to go — and at 166 characters it is well past the point of usefulness. If you find yourself wanting that much detail, what you want is a real thumbnail, not a hash.
components.p4: Detail beyond about six by six also stops being visible once the placeholder is blurred by the browser scaling it up, which it always is. The picture is 32 pixels on its longest edge and it is being drawn across a card.

aspect.title: A hash has no shape
aspect.p1: This surprises people, and it is worth being explicit about: a BlurHash records coefficients and nothing else. No width, no height, no aspect ratio. The same string is a perfectly good 16:9 banner and a perfectly good square avatar, and it will paint happily at either.
aspect.p2: That is why this page asks you for a shape when you paste a hash, and why it does not when you drop in a picture. It also means the shape is your application's problem at render time: store the real image's dimensions alongside the hash, or the placeholder will be the right colours in the wrong box and the layout will still shift.
aspect.p3: The same freedom is what makes the size control cheap, and it is why the preview here is not the PNG. A hash is a continuous function sampled onto a grid, so painting it at 384 pixels rather than 32 costs nothing but arithmetic — there is no source resolution to run out of. Stretching the 32-pixel PNG across a card instead would show you bilinear interpolation between 32 samples rather than the curve they came from, which hides most of what raising the detail bought you. The PNG stays small because it is inlined into your HTML; the preview does not have to be.

usage.title: Using the result
usage.p1: For next/image, take the blurDataURL. Next's blur placeholder reads a data URI and has no idea what BlurHash is, which is why this tool writes a PNG as well as a string. Store the hash if you want to re-render at other sizes later; ship the data URI if you just want it working.
usage.p2: For react-blurhash, take the hash. It decodes in the reader's browser onto a canvas, so nothing is inlined into your HTML — cheaper markup, slightly later paint, and punch becomes a prop you can change without regenerating anything.
usage.p3: For anything else, the CSS form is a background image and two lines. It works in an email template, a static site generator, a server-rendered template with no JavaScript at all.
usage.p4: Whichever you pick, generate at upload time and store the result, not on every request. The transform is fast but it is not free, and the answer never changes for a given picture.

alternatives.title: BlurHash, ThumbHash and a tiny JPEG
alternatives.p1: The oldest approach is a genuinely small JPEG — twenty pixels wide, quality 20, inlined as a data URI. It is simple, it needs no library, and it costs a few hundred bytes of markup per image. Its weakness is that it is still an image file, with a header and a decoder, and it cannot be stored as a short string in a text column.
alternatives.p2: ThumbHash is the closer relative: the same idea with a better transform, roughly the same length, and it carries the aspect ratio and an alpha channel, both of which BlurHash lacks. If you are starting fresh and nothing in your stack expects BlurHash, it is worth a look.
alternatives.p3: BlurHash's advantage is that it arrived first and is everywhere — Wolt's original, react-blurhash, plus ports in Swift, Kotlin, Python, Rust, PHP and Go. A hash written by this page is read by all of them, which is the reason this implementation is checked against the reference one rather than only against itself.

limits.title: Limits, and why they are where they are
limits.p1: Twenty-five megabytes per file and a forty-megapixel ceiling. Both are about memory in one browser tab rather than bandwidth, because nothing here is uploaded — a decoded picture costs four bytes per pixel whatever the file size.
limits.p2: Before the transform runs, the picture is scaled down so its longest edge is 128 pixels. Encoding costs width × height × components, so a camera original at nine by nine components would be hundreds of millions of operations and a frozen tab. Nothing survives the downscale that could have survived the transform: at most 81 cosine coefficients come out the other end.
limits.p3: The hash also loses everything that was not colour. No EXIF, no colour profile, no transparency — BlurHash has no alpha channel, so a picture with a transparent background is encoded as though the transparent parts were black.

privacy.title: Privacy
privacy.p1: No picture you drop here is uploaded, and no server is involved. The image is decoded by the browser, the transform is arithmetic in this tab, and the PNG behind the data URI is written by a WebAssembly build of OxiPNG fetched once from this site.
privacy.p2: Nothing is stored either. Close the page and the picture, the hash and the data URI are gone with it — so copy what you want before you leave.

faq.title: Questions people actually ask
faq.q1: Does this produce the same hash as blurha.sh?
faq.a1: Yes, character for character. This implementation follows the JavaScript reference implementation exactly, down to which rounding it uses and which order it sums the pixels in, and it is tested against that library across every combination of detail settings. A hash from here is read by react-blurhash, and by the Swift, Kotlin, Python and Rust ports, without qualification.
faq.q2: Why do I get a hash and a data URI rather than just one?
faq.a2: Because the two ecosystems want different things. react-blurhash and the mobile ports want the string and decode it themselves. next/image and plain CSS want a data URI and have never heard of BlurHash. Storing the hash and generating the data URI from it is the flexible answer; storing both is the fast one.
faq.q3: Should I store the hash or the blurDataURL in my database?
faq.a3: The hash, if you can. It is a quarter the length, it does not change when you decide the placeholder should be 48 pixels instead of 32, and you can always produce a data URI from it later. Store the data URI when the thing rendering it cannot run a decoder — a static export, an email, a template with no JavaScript.
faq.q4: Why is my transparent PNG's placeholder black behind the logo?
faq.a4: BlurHash has no alpha channel. Transparent pixels are read as whatever sits underneath them, which in a decoded canvas is black. Flatten the picture onto the background colour you actually use before generating the hash — the Image Converter on this site will do that — or use ThumbHash, which does carry alpha.
faq.q5: How long should the hash be?
faq.a5: Let the fit decide, which lands between forty-four and sixty characters depending on the shape. That is longer than the four-by-three, twenty-eight-character hash a lot of code ships, and it is deliberate: at twenty-eight characters a landscape photograph is a smudge with the right colours in roughly the right places, and the difference is plain when the two sit side by side. If storage genuinely matters, dial the pair down and watch the preview — two by two is a gradient, which is sometimes exactly right for a hero image.
faq.q6: Does the punch setting change what I store?
faq.a6: No. Punch is applied while painting, never while encoding, so the hash is identical at every punch value. What it does change is the PNG this page writes, because a PNG is pixels and has no coefficients left to scale — so if you are shipping the data URI, punch is baked in, and if you are shipping the hash, it is a prop your renderer sets.
faq.q7: Can I generate these on my server instead?
faq.a7: Yes, and for a real application you should — at upload time, once per picture, stored beside the URL. The blurhash package on npm does exactly what this page does, and there are equivalents for most languages. This tool is for the cases where you want to see one, check one, or produce a handful by hand.

what.title: What this answers
what.p1: A domain is several independent systems wearing one name. A registry knows who registered it and when it lapses. Its nameservers know what it resolves to. The network it resolves into belongs to somebody else again. And the machine at the far end presents a certificate, sends headers, and serves a page built out of software with its own licences.
what.p2: Asking each of them separately is four tools and a terminal. This asks all of them at once and puts the answers side by side, which is usually where the interesting part is: an expiry date next to a certificate date, a nameserver next to the CDN it points at, an SPF record next to the MX records it is supposed to cover.
what.p3: Nothing here is privileged information. Every answer comes from a service that publishes it deliberately — the DNS, the registry, the routing registries, and the site's own responses.

panels.title: The seven panels
panels.intro: Each panel answers one question, from one source.
panels.strip: Above them sits a strip of six readings — addresses, network, registrar, domain expiry, certificate expiry and header grade — each tinted by whether it needs attention. It is there so the question "is anything wrong with this domain" can be answered without opening a single panel, and so the panel that does need reading is the one with a coloured rail down its edge.
panels.tableCaption: What each panel shows and where it comes from
panels.overviewShows: The hostname split into subdomain, registrable domain and public suffix, with the Unicode form of an internationalised name.
panels.dnsShows: A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, NS, TXT, SOA, CAA and DS records with their TTLs, plus SPF, DMARC and MTA-STS.
panels.dnsSource: DNS over HTTPS, from the resolver you pick.
panels.registrationShows: Registrar and IANA id, creation, change and expiry dates, EPP status codes, delegated nameservers, DNSSEC, and the abuse contact.
panels.registrationSource: RDAP, the protocol that replaced WHOIS.
panels.hostingShows: For each address: its reverse name, the autonomous system announcing it, the announced prefix, and the registry record for the block.
panels.hostingSource: Reverse DNS, Team Cymru's origin zones, and RDAP.
panels.propagationShows: The same record asked of nine public resolvers, whether they agree, and the answer each returned with its TTL.
panels.propagationSource: DNS over HTTPS against nine independent operators.
panels.certificateShows: Issuer, validity window, days remaining, whether it covers the name you asked for, key type, negotiated cipher, and the issuing chain.
panels.httpShows: The redirect chain, the final URL, the server headers, six security headers, the page title, and any licence the page declares for itself.
panels.httpSource: One GET request for the home page.
panels.technologiesShows: Servers, CDNs, frameworks, content systems, analytics and mail providers, each with its version where one is exposed and the licence it ships under.
panels.technologiesSource: Patterns matched against headers, cookies, markup and delegation.
panels.independence: No panel can fail another. A registered domain that serves nothing shows a full registration panel and four refusals, each naming the lookup that could not be made and why — which is more useful than one blank page.

records.title: The records it asks for
records.intro: Nine types are queried at the apex, and every answer keeps its TTL, so you can see how long an old answer will linger after a change.
records.tableCaption: DNS record types and what each one means
records.srvNote: SRV is deliberately absent. It is only ever published under a _service._proto prefix, so a query at the apex returns nothing — and an empty row would read as “this domain publishes no SRV records” rather than “that is the wrong name to ask”. DMARC and MTA-STS are the exception that proves it: both have fixed prefixes, so they are queried at _dmarc and _mta-sts and folded into the mail chips.

propagation.title: Propagation, and what it can honestly tell you
propagation.p1: After you change a record, the question is not whether the registry accepted it — it is whether the resolvers people actually use have caught up. Every recursive resolver keeps its own cache and does its own resolution, so for as long as the old record’s TTL has left to run, some will answer with the new value and some with the old. That divergence is what a change in flight looks like from outside, and the propagation card is nine independent operators asked the same question at the same moment.
propagation.p2: Nine operators is not nine locations. Every query leaves this server, so an anycast service such as Cloudflare or Google answers from whichever of its nodes is nearest this server, not from the country its pin sits in. The map shows where each operator runs its service, which is a fact about the operator; it is not a claim that the query travelled there. A tool that drew nine flags and implied nine vantage points would be easier to build and would be lying to you.
propagation.p3: Disagreement also has a second, entirely healthy cause. A name can be configured to answer differently depending on where the asker is — GeoDNS steering, which is how many large sites hand visitors a server near them. Ask nine resolvers about github.com on a perfectly ordinary day and you will get several different addresses back. From a single vantage point, that is indistinguishable from a change still spreading, so the card says so rather than colouring it as a fault.
propagation.p4: Read it, then, as a comparison and not a verdict. Every resolver agreeing means the change has reached all nine caches. Some disagreeing means either the change is still spreading or the name steers by region — and the TTL beside each answer is the number that tells you how long the stale ones can still be stale.

controls.title: Every control
controls.intro: Two settings and three buttons. Nothing else changes what is looked up.
controls.tableCaption: Controls, what each does, and when to reach for it
controls.hostDoes: Takes a hostname, a full URL, or an IP address. A URL is reduced to its host: scheme, port, path, query and credentials are dropped.
controls.hostWhen: Always. Paste whatever you happen to have.
controls.resolverDoes: Chooses which public resolver answers the DNS queries — Cloudflare, Google, or DNS.SB.
controls.resolverWhen: You suspect an answer is stale, or one resolver filters what another does not.
controls.probeDoes: Opens a TLS connection and requests the home page. Feeds the certificate, HTTP and technologies panels.
controls.probeWhen: Leave it on, unless you want only the DNS and registry answers, or the host should not see a request.
controls.copyDoes: Puts the short form on the clipboard: addresses, registrar, expiry, network, certificate and stack.
controls.copyWhen: Pasting into a ticket or a chat.
controls.downloadDoes: Saves the whole report, including the panels that failed and the reason each gave.
controls.downloadWhen: Filing a before-and-after record of a migration.
controls.probeCaveat: Turning the site fetch off does not empty the technologies panel: mail and DNS providers are still named from the MX and NS delegation. What goes is everything that needs a connection — the certificate, the response headers, and anything read out of the page.
controls.resolverCaveat: The resolver setting changes the record panel and everything built on it, because the reverse names and ASN lookups ride the same transport. It does not change RDAP or the site fetch, which are ordinary HTTPS requests to the registry and to the host.

licensing.title: Licences, and where they come from
licensing.p1: Every technology this recognises carries the licence it ships under: an SPDX identifier where the project publishes one, and the literal Proprietary where none exists. WordPress is GPL-2.0-or-later, nginx is BSD-2-Clause, Cloudflare is not licensed to anybody. Each identifier links to its own SPDX page.
licensing.p2: That is the licence of the software, not of the words on the page. Where a site declares terms for its own material — a rel="license" link, or the older meta tag — it is shown separately in the HTTP panel, exactly as the publisher wrote it.
licensing.p3: Both are claims worth checking rather than facts to rely on. A version is whatever a header or a filename admitted to, a licence is what that project used at the time this table was written, and neither is legal advice. Read the project's own LICENSE before you build on it.

privacy.title: This one does not run in your browser
privacy.p1: Every other tool here is offline by design. This one cannot be. A web page cannot make a DNS query, cannot speak RDAP, and cannot open a raw TLS connection to read a certificate — all of that happens on our server, on your behalf.
privacy.p2: In practice: the name you type is sent to us, and from there to the resolver you picked, to the registry's RDAP service, and — if the site fetch is on — to the host itself, which sees one request from our address identifying itself as ToolForgeBot. Nothing is written to a database, and the report exists only in the tab in front of you.
privacy.p3: The challenge is there for the same reason. An endpoint that fetches whatever host a stranger names is a scanner and an open proxy if it is left unguarded, and the traffic would arrive at other people's servers carrying this site's name. Addresses on private, loopback, link-local and reserved ranges are refused outright — on every redirect hop, not only the first.

limits.title: What it will not tell you
limits.p1: Where the machine physically is. The country shown is the one the routing registry records for the address block, which is where it was allocated rather than where it is plugged in. City-level geolocation needs a commercial database, and is still a guess.
limits.p2: Whether a site is safe, or whether a header is any good. The header grade counts how many of six were sent; it says nothing about whether a Content-Security-Policy is meaningfully restrictive or an HSTS max-age is long enough. Grading contents is a different tool, and a confident letter on a guess would be worse than no letter at all.
limits.p3: Anything a registry declines to publish. Registrant names and addresses have been redacted from gTLD records since 2018, and some country registries run no RDAP service at all — those say so, and point you at the registry's own WHOIS.

useCases.title: What people use it for
useCases.intro: The lookups that actually get run:
useCases.migration: Checking a DNS change has spread — compare the same name across two resolvers, and read the TTL to see how long the old answer will linger.
useCases.expiry: Catching a domain or a certificate about to lapse, before somebody else notices first.
useCases.mail: Confirming SPF, DMARC and MTA-STS are published, and seeing which provider the MX records actually point at.
useCases.diligence: Working out what a site is built on before quoting for work on it — including whether its stack is something you may legally build on.
useCases.incident: Finding somebody to contact: the abuse address at the registrar, and the organisation holding the network the address sits in.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Is this WHOIS?
faq.a1: It is RDAP, which is what replaced WHOIS. The same data, published as JSON over HTTPS instead of as free text on port 43 — which is why the fields here are read rather than guessed at out of prose. Every gTLD is required to run one; a few country registries still do not, and those are reported as such.
faq.q2: Why is the registration panel empty for my .de domain?
faq.a2: Because that registry publishes no RDAP service, so there is nothing to query. The panel says so instead of showing a blank record, and the registry's own WHOIS page has the answer.
faq.q3: Why is the registrant's name hidden?
faq.a3: Since GDPR came into force in 2018, gTLD registries have redacted personal data from public records. The registrar, the dates, the status codes and an abuse contact stay public; the person does not.
faq.q4: The technologies panel found nothing — is the site hiding?
faq.a4: Possibly, and possibly it is just quiet. A CDN configured to strip identifying headers, a page rendered entirely by script after load, and a stack with no fingerprint of its own all look identical from outside. Absence of evidence is the honest reading.
faq.q5: Can I look up an IP address?
faq.a5: Yes. The name breakdown, hosting, certificate and HTTP panels all work. Forward DNS and domain registration do not apply to an address and say so. Private and reserved addresses are refused.
faq.q6: Does the site I inspect know about it?
faq.a6: If the site fetch is on, yes: it receives one GET request for its home page from our server, identified as ToolForgeBot. Turn the switch off and only the resolver and the registry are contacted.
faq.q7: Why is there a challenge on a read-only lookup?
faq.a7: Because the alternative is a public endpoint that fetches whatever host anyone names, from our address. Without the challenge it would be somebody's free scanner within a day, and the complaints would arrive here.
faq.q8: The propagation card says resolvers disagree. Is my DNS broken?
faq.a8: Not necessarily. Two ordinary things produce that result. The first is a change still spreading: until the previous record’s TTL expires, resolvers that cached it keep serving it, and the TTL shown beside each answer is how long that can last. The second is GeoDNS steering, where the name is configured to return different addresses depending on where the question came from, which is how many large sites route visitors to a nearby server. If you have not changed anything recently, the second is the likely explanation.

meta.title: BSON ↔ JSON ↔ TOON Converter — Every Type Survives the Trip
meta.description: Convert BSON to JSON, JSON to TOON, and every pairing between the three. Canonical Extended JSON returns the exact bytes MongoDB stored — ObjectId, Decimal128, int64 and dates included — while TOON's tabular form cuts a uniform array down for an LLM prompt. Reads hex, base64 and .bson files, and says on your own document what the conversion cost. Runs in your browser; nothing is uploaded.

understanding.title: Three notations, one data model
understanding.p1: BSON, JSON and TOON all describe the same thing: objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans and null. They agree about almost nothing else. BSON is binary, length-prefixed and typed — MongoDB's storage and wire format. JSON is text with exactly six types. TOON is text too, and trades JSON's punctuation for indentation and a CSV-style table so that a document costs fewer tokens in an LLM prompt.
understanding.p2: So this tool never rewrites one notation into another. It reads whichever you paste into one plain value, then writes that value out in whichever you asked for. Both halves meet at the same model, which is why BSON → TOON cannot develop its own opinion about what a date is, and why a fourth format would cost one reader and one writer rather than six new conversions.
understanding.p3: Where the model runs out is BSON's type system. BSON knows an ObjectId from a string and an int32 from a double; JSON knows a number. The bridge is Extended JSON, MongoDB's own way of writing those types down as ordinary JSON objects — and because TOON encodes the JSON data model exactly, Extended JSON travels through TOON unchanged.
understanding.p4: Nothing is uploaded. Reading, writing and export all happen in this tab; close it and nothing is left behind.

extendedJson.title: Canonical and relaxed
extendedJson.intro: Extended JSON has two spellings, and the difference is not cosmetic. Canonical writes every value in a $-prefixed wrapper naming its type, and a document read canonically and written back produces the same bytes it came from — every type, byte for byte. Relaxed writes what plain JSON can hold and wraps only what it cannot, which reads far better and quietly loses the distinctions plain JSON has no room for.
extendedJson.costDouble: A double holding a whole number returns as an int32.
extendedJson.costInt64: Past ±2⁵³ the value itself changes — no JavaScript number holds it.
extendedJson.costDate: Nothing. The ISO string round-trips exactly.
extendedJson.costDecimal: Nothing. Decimal128 has no plain-JSON spelling.
extendedJson.costBinary: Nothing. Binary is wrapped in both modes.
extendedJson.outro1: Rather than warn about this in general, the tool checks it on your document: after a relaxed read it writes the result back to BSON and compares the bytes. If they differ you get a note saying so; if they do not, you get silence. Most documents survive relaxed intact, and a warning that is usually wrong is a warning people stop reading.
extendedJson.outro2: Going the other way there is nothing to choose. Both spellings parse to the same bytes, so the mode control is switched off whenever BSON is the output rather than the input.

toonForms.title: Why TOON is shorter
toonForms.intro: TOON picks a rendering from the shape of the value, and the one that pays is the table. A uniform array of objects declares its field list once in the header and then streams one row per element, which is the whole point of the format.
toonForms.whenInline: An array of primitives, short enough to sit on its own header line.
toonForms.whenTabular: An array of objects that all carry the same fields, with primitive values.
toonForms.whenKeyed: An object whose values are uniform objects — config maps, feature flags, records by id.
toonForms.whenList: Anything else: mixed types, or objects that do not agree on their fields.
toonForms.outro: Which is why TOON is not always smaller. A deeply nested document with no uniform arrays encodes to roughly what minified JSON does, occasionally a little more. The counts under the output say which happened for the document in front of you — characters rather than tokens, because a tokenizer is a megabyte of vocabulary and gives a different answer for every model.

options.title: The controls
options.tableCaption: Every option, and when it earns its place
options.encodingDoes: Whether BSON is read and written as hexadecimal or as base64.
options.encodingWhen: Hex for anything copied out of bsondump or the MongoDB documentation; base64 for a blob from a driver log or an API response.
options.ejsonDoes: Whether BSON's types are written as canonical wrappers or as the nearest plain JSON value.
options.ejsonWhen: Canonical whenever the document has to survive the trip back. Relaxed when a person is going to read it.
options.jsonIndentDoes: Spaces per level in the JSON output, or one unbroken line.
options.jsonIndentWhen: Minified for anything a program will read; two or four spaces for anything a person will.
options.delimiterDoes: Which character separates TOON's table columns.
options.delimiterWhen: A tab or a pipe when no value contains one — the encoder quotes any value that does, which costs more than the comma saved.
options.toonIndentDoes: Spaces per level in TOON, on the way in as well as out.
options.toonIndentWhen: Leave it at two unless the block you are pasting was written with four.
options.strictDoes: Whether a declared array length has to match the number of rows under it.
options.strictWhen: Leave it on. Turn it off only to read a block edited by hand, or truncated by a model that stopped early.
options.outro: Each control is switched off when the current pairing cannot read it, with a line saying why. Nudging the TOON delimiter while the output is BSON changes nothing, and a control that looks live but is not is worse than one that is greyed out.

gotchas.title: Traps worth knowing
gotchas.p1: BSON's root is a document. An array or a bare value has no encoding at the top level, and the driver refuses rather than inventing one — so a JSON document or TOON block whose root is an array cannot be written as BSON. Give it a name first, and the wrapper object is what you convert.
gotchas.p2: A hex dump is not a .bson file. The text output downloads as .txt with the notation in its name; the raw bytes get their own button and the real extension. Naming a transcript .bson produces a file every reader of BSON rejects.
gotchas.p3: JSON has one number type. Going into BSON, a whole number becomes an int32 or an int64 and a fractional one becomes a double — which means 1.0 and 1 are the same input, and both come back as 1. Canonical Extended JSON is the only way to say “a double, holding one”.
gotchas.p4: Relaxed dates are still objects. A relaxed date is written as a string inside a $date wrapper, which anything that reads Extended JSON understands, but a program doing a plain JSON.parse sees an object with one string in it. That is a property of Extended JSON, not of this tool.
gotchas.p5: TOON's indentation is load-bearing. Unlike JSON, whitespace is structure: a block written at four spaces and read at two is a parse error rather than a shrug. That is what the indent control is for on the input side, and why it stays available when TOON is what you are pasting.

useCases.title: What people use this for
useCases.p1: Reading a BSON blob out of a log, an oplog entry or a driver trace and seeing what is actually in it, with the types intact rather than flattened into JSON's six.
useCases.p2: Turning a JSON fixture into TOON to cut the token cost of a prompt. Most of the saving comes from uniform arrays of records, which is exactly the shape fixtures and API responses tend to have.
useCases.p3: Building a BSON document by hand from Extended JSON to feed a test, and getting the exact bytes rather than whatever a driver decided the numbers ought to be.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Does this upload my document anywhere?
faq.a1: No. Every conversion runs in this tab and the page has no server behind it. That includes the file you open and the file you download.
faq.q2: What is the difference between canonical and relaxed Extended JSON?
faq.a2: Canonical writes every value in a wrapper naming its BSON type, so the document returns as the exact bytes it came from. Relaxed writes plain values wherever plain JSON can hold them, which reads better but loses the distinction between a double and an integer, and loses precision past ±2⁵³. After a relaxed read this tool checks your own document and tells you which of the two happened.
faq.q3: Is TOON always smaller than JSON?
faq.a3: No. It wins on uniform arrays of objects, where the field list is written once instead of on every row — often by half against indented JSON. On a deeply nested document with no repetition it lands near minified JSON and sometimes slightly above it. The counts under the output tell you which, for the document in front of you.
faq.q4: Can I convert a .bson file from mongodump?
faq.a4: One document at a time. mongodump writes a stream of documents back to back and this tool reads a single document, so opening such a file loads its bytes but the conversion stops at the length check once the first document ends.
faq.q5: Why does my ObjectId come out as a $oid object?
faq.a5: Because JSON has no ObjectId. That wrapper is Extended JSON, which is what mongosh prints, what mongoexport writes and what mongoimport reads — so it is not a lossy fallback, it is the interchange format. Feed it back in and the ObjectId returns.
faq.q6: Which version of TOON does this write?
faq.a6: TOON 4.1, through the format's own reference implementation rather than a re-reading of the specification — so what comes out of here is what every other TOON reader expects to see.
faq.q7: Why does the tool count characters instead of tokens?
faq.a7: Because a token count is a property of a model, not of a document. Two tokenizers disagree, and shipping one would mean shipping a megabyte of vocabulary to answer for a single model. Characters are exact, and the ratio between two formats holds directionally whichever tokenizer reads them.

meta.title: Online Port Checker — Open, Closed or Filtered, Told Apart
meta.description: Check whether a TCP port is open on any public host or on your own address. A real connect scan reports three states, not two: open, closed, and filtered — a timeout is something dropping your packets, which is a different fact from a refusal. Nmap's most-scanned ports, plus web, mail, database and remote-access presets. Scans run from our servers, are rate limited, and never touch private or reserved ranges.
