understanding.title: What a connect scan actually tells you
understanding.p1: A TCP port is not a door that is open or shut. It is a number a program may have asked the operating system to listen on, and the only way to find out from outside is to try to start a conversation and see what comes back. This tool opens a real TCP connection to each port, watches the three-way handshake, and closes it again without writing or reading a single byte.
understanding.p2: Three things can happen, and the difference between the last two is the part most hosted port checkers throw away. The handshake completes, and something is listening — open. The host answers with a reset, meaning it is reachable and has nothing on that port — closed. Or nothing comes back at all before the deadline, which means a packet filter dropped it silently, or the host is not there — filtered.
understanding.p3: Reporting a timeout as "closed" is the common shortcut and it is a false statement about the network. Closed proves a live host declined; filtered proves nothing about the port and quite a lot about the firewall in front of it. If every port on a scan comes back filtered, the useful conclusion is that nothing answered — not that the host is secure.
understanding.p4: What this deliberately does not do is a SYN scan, which never completes the handshake and exists mainly to be harder to log; read the banner a service announces on connect; or guess a software version. The service column is a static table of what each port is registered for, so a web server running on port 22 will be labelled SSH and the label will be wrong. That is the honest cost of not fingerprinting.

states.title: The three states
states.intro: Each row is one TCP connection attempt and what came back from it. The response time is the round trip to the handshake or the reset — it is a rough distance measurement, not a health check.
states.tableCaption: What each state means and what it proves
states.provesOpen: A program is listening and accepted a connection from our address. It may still refuse yours.
states.provesClosed: The host is up and reachable. Nothing is bound to that port, and no firewall is hiding it.
states.provesFiltered: Nothing. A filter dropped the packet, the host is down, or the network in between lost it.

presets.title: The port lists
presets.intro: The default is the set Nmap reports as the most scanned on the internet — the ports that carry the services almost every host runs, and therefore the ones worth checking first.
presets.outro: There is deliberately no "known attack ports" preset, although several hosted scanners ship one. Checking your own host for a backdoor port is a legitimate thing to want, and typing the numbers into the custom field does it. Offering it as a one-click preset against any address somebody types is a tool for finding other people's compromised machines, which is a different product.

limits.title: The limits, and why each one exists
limits.intro: None of these are tuning knobs. A hosted port scanner is an abuse surface before it is a feature, and these are most of what keeps it from being one.
limits.portsWhy: A few hundred half-open connections is rude; several thousand is a denial of service with a progress bar.
limits.timeoutWhy: Comfortably past an intercontinental round trip, which tops out near 400 ms. Longer, and a fully-dropped scan just sits there.
limits.concurrencyWhy: All of them at once looks like a SYN flood from the far end, which is how a server's address gets blocked by the networks it most needs to reach.
limits.quotaWhy: Counted per visitor in a database rather than in memory, because a counter that a cold start resets is not a limit.
limits.rangesWhy: Private, loopback, link-local, carrier-grade NAT, cloud metadata and reserved ranges are refused — including an IPv4 address hidden inside an IPv6 literal.

legal.title: Before you scan somebody else's host
legal.p1: Port scanning a host you do not own is, in many jurisdictions, at best a grey area and at worst a criminal offence — the UK's Computer Misuse Act, the US Computer Fraud and Abuse Act and their equivalents elsewhere are written broadly enough to cover unauthorised probing. Whether a given scan is lawful depends on where you are, where the host is, and what you agreed to. This is not legal advice, and nothing here should be read as permission.
legal.p2: There is a practical point on top of the legal one. The scan runs on our servers, so the entry it leaves in the target's log carries our address, not yours. An operator who notices it blocks us, and every other visitor loses the tool. That is why there is an hourly limit, why the port count is capped, and why we would rather you pointed it at your own address.
legal.p3: Nothing about a scan is stored — not the host, not the ports, not the result. The one thing kept is a salted hash of your address with a count against it, so the hourly limit can be enforced without the table knowing who you are.

useCases.title: What people use this for
useCases.p1: Checking what your own connection exposes: whether the router is forwarding 3389 to a desktop, whether a home server's SSH is reachable from outside, whether a port you opened for one evening is still open.
useCases.p2: Confirming a firewall rule did what you meant. A port that reads filtered from outside and works from inside is the rule behaving; one that reads closed is the rule missing.
useCases.p3: Checking that a service you just deployed is actually reachable — the difference between "the process is running" and "the internet can get to it" is a security group nobody edited.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Does the host I scan see my IP address?
faq.a1: No, it sees ours. A page in a browser cannot open a raw TCP socket, so the scan has to run on a server, and the connection comes from this site's address. That is a property of every hosted port checker, not just this one — and it is why the tool is rate limited and why the copy asks you to scan hosts you are authorised to test.
faq.q2: Why is a port reported as filtered rather than closed?
faq.a2: Because nothing came back. Closed means the host actively refused — it sent a TCP reset, which took a reachable machine to send. Filtered means the probe vanished: a firewall dropped it without replying, or the host is not there at all. They are different facts, and folding them together is a lie a lot of port checkers tell.
faq.q3: Can I scan an internal address like 192.168.1.1?
faq.a3: No. Private, loopback, link-local, carrier-grade NAT, cloud metadata and reserved ranges are all refused, including an IPv4 address disguised inside an IPv6 literal. The scan would run from our network rather than yours, so it would tell you nothing about your LAN and would turn this tool into a way through our own firewall. For an internal scan, run nmap on a machine inside that network.
faq.q4: Why only a few scans an hour?
faq.a4: Because the scan carries our address, an unmetered scanner is an anonymous scanning service, and the first thing that happens to one of those is that the networks worth scanning stop accepting traffic from it. The count is kept against a salted hash of your address in a database rather than in memory, because a limit that resets when a serverless instance recycles is not a limit.
faq.q5: Why does the service column say SSH when I am running something else there?
faq.a5: Because it is a static table of what each port is registered for, not a reading of what answered. Nothing here reads the banner a service announces or probes for a version — that is fingerprinting, it doubles the time per open port, and it is a meaningful step from "is this reachable" toward reconnaissance. The column tells you what the port is conventionally for; the state tells you what is true.
faq.q6: Can it scan UDP?
faq.a6: No, TCP only. UDP has no handshake, so there is nothing to observe: an open UDP port and a filtered one both usually answer with silence, and telling them apart means sending protocol-specific payloads and waiting far longer per port. A UDP scan that reported anything useful here would be guessing.
faq.q7: Is it legal to scan a host I do not own?
faq.a7: It depends where you are, where the host is, and what you agreed to — and in several jurisdictions the answer is no. Unauthorised probing falls under computer misuse law in the UK, the US and elsewhere. Scan your own hosts, or ones you have written permission to test. This is not legal advice.

meta.title: Visual Mock Server Studio — Build Mock APIs Without Writing JSON
meta.description: Build mock REST APIs by dragging nodes onto a canvas instead of hand-writing JSON. Workspaces need no account: a secret in your browser proves ownership and a recovery key moves it to another machine. Mock endpoints answer from our servers, so they keep working after you close the tab.

hero.title: Mock Server Studio
hero.subtitle: Design an API before it exists. Build each endpoint as a graph, give it the shape of the response you want back, and point your app at a real URL that answers exactly that.
hero.disclosureTitle: This part does not run in your browser
hero.disclosureBody: Every other tool on ToolForge works entirely on your machine. This one cannot: a mock endpoint has to answer requests from your app, so your workspaces, endpoints and their responses are stored on our servers and served from them. Anyone who has the address of a mock endpoint can call it — treat what you put in a response as public, and never put a real credential in one.

flow.title: From nothing to a live endpoint
flow.intro: Seven steps, and only the first two are about the studio itself. Everything after that is you describing the API you wish existed.
flow.workspaceBody: A workspace is the container for everything else — your mock servers, their routes, their variables and their request log. There is no email and no password: a secret written into an HttpOnly cookie is what proves this browser owns it.
flow.recoveryKeyBody: It is shown once, on the screen straight after creation, and only a one-way digest of it is stored — so nobody, us included, can show it to you again. It is how you reach the same workspace from another machine, and the only way back after you clear this browser's cookies.
flow.serverBody: A server owns a group of routes and answers on its own address. The key is the part callers type; leave it blank and one is drawn from the name. The address starts answering the moment the server has a route.
flow.routeBody: Pick a method and a path. A segment written as :name becomes a parameter, a trailing star matches everything below a prefix, and the query string is not part of the path — a route on /game answers /game?id=7 as well.
flow.responseBody: The response is built as a tree of fields rather than typed as JSON. Each field says where its value comes from: a fixed literal, something out of the request, a variable, or generated data such as a name, an email address, or a fresh UUID on every call.
flow.logicTitle: Put logic in front of it, if you need any
flow.logicBody: A route with no flow simply returns its body. Open the flow editor to add authentication, conditions, delays, weighted branches, variables and logging between the request arriving and the reply going out.
flow.callTitle: Point your app at the address
flow.callBody: Copy the address, call it from your code or from curl, and the calls appear in the workspace's request log. It answers whether or not this page is open, so a deployed front end can reach it too.
flow.outro: Nothing here is private. Anybody holding the address of a mock endpoint can call it, so treat everything in a response as public and never put a real credential in one.

ownership.title: Ownership without an account
ownership.p1: There is no account here. Creating a workspace writes a random secret into an HttpOnly cookie on this browser and stores only a digest of it, so owning the workspace means holding that secret. Nothing about you is recorded and nothing has to be verified by email.
ownership.p2: The recovery key is the portable half. It is shown once, on the screen that follows creation, and it is stored the same one-way way — so if it is lost, no support request can bring it back. Importing a workspace with its key adds the new browser alongside the ones that already have access rather than replacing them; nothing is signed out.
ownership.p3: Forget here and Delete permanently are different actions, and the difference matters. Forgetting removes the workspace from this browser only — its endpoints keep answering, other browsers keep their access, and the recovery key brings it back. Deleting destroys every server, endpoint, variable and log under it, for everyone, and no key recovers it.
ownership.p4: Creating and importing both sit behind a Cloudflare Turnstile challenge, and creation is metered per address per hour on top of that. The per-browser count is an affordance rather than a wall — the cookie belongs to you and clearing it buys more — so the limit that actually holds is the per-address one.

routes.title: Routes: methods, paths and how one is chosen
routes.intro: A route is a method and a path. The path is matched against whatever follows the server key in the address, and the query string is not part of it — a route on /game answers /game?id=7 too, and you read id in the response through From the request, then Query.
routes.tableCaption: Path patterns and what each one matches
routes.staticMeaning: That exact path and nothing else. A static segment is the most specific thing a path can hold.
routes.paramMeaning: Captures one segment. The value arrives in the response builder under the name you gave it, as From the request, then Path parameter.
routes.wildcardMeaning: Every path below the prefix, however many segments follow. This is the catch-all to put underneath more specific routes.
routes.p1: When more than one route could match, the most specific wins: a static segment beats a parameter and a parameter beats a wildcard, read left to right. That ranking is computed when the route is saved, so which route answers never depends on the order rows come back from the database.
routes.p2: A request matching no path gets 404. A request whose path exists under a different method gets 405 with an Allow header naming the methods that do exist — a different fact from the path being wrong, and the one that tells you it is your verb rather than your URL. HEAD falls through to GET with the body stripped, and an OPTIONS you have not defined is answered from what the path supports, because it is a preflight.
routes.p3: Two switches turn things off without deleting them. A disabled route answers 404 as though it had never been created. A paused server answers 503 on every route under it, and tells the caller the server exists but is not answering — which is what you want while you are half-way through changing something.

responses.title: Building the body
responses.intro: The body is built as a tree rather than typed as JSON, because most of what makes a mock useful has no JSON spelling — there is no literal that means a different name on every call. Every field picks a value type, and these are the ones on offer.
responses.tableCaption: Value types and what each one puts in the response
responses.colGives: What it puts in the response
responses.givesStatic: Exactly what you type: text, a number, true, false or null.
responses.givesRequest: Something out of the incoming call — a body field, a header, a cookie, a query parameter or a path parameter, addressed by name.
responses.givesVar: The value of a variable set on this workspace or server, or one written earlier in the flow by a Set variable node.
responses.givesEnv: The value in the environment this call is running under, so one route can answer differently for a staging set and a production set.
responses.givesFaker: Generated data of a named kind — a full name, an email address, a company, a city, a price. A different one on every call.
responses.givesUuid: A fresh v4 UUID each time the route is called.
responses.givesNow: The time of the call, in the format you pick.
responses.givesTemplate: Text with other values interpolated into it, for the cases where a string has to be assembled rather than chosen.
responses.givesObject: A nested object. Its fields are values of these same types, so the tree goes as deep as the response needs.
responses.givesArray: A list built from one item template, repeated a fixed number of times or a random count between two numbers.
responses.givesOneOf: One of several options, drawn per call. This is how you model a field that is sometimes present and sometimes null, or one of a small set of statuses.
responses.p1: There is a JSON tab beside the builder, and it is honest about when it can be an editor. A response made only of fixed values has an exact JSON spelling, so there the tab is an editor and pasting into it replaces the tree. A response holding generated values has no such spelling, so the tab becomes a viewer and says so — applying JSON there would silently freeze every generated field into one sample of itself.
responses.p2: The content type comes from an allowlist: JSON, plain text, XML and CSV. A value outside it is served as plain text rather than refused. That is not fussiness — mock endpoints answer on this site's own origin, so a response able to declare itself HTML would be a page anybody could publish under our name. Every response also carries nosniff and a sandbox policy.
responses.p3: Request bodies are read too, and not only JSON. Form-encoded and multipart posts become fields you address the same way, and an uploaded file arrives as a value carrying its filename, contentType and size — enough for a condition to branch on the type or refuse anything over a size. The file itself is never stored.

logic.title: The flow editor
logic.intro: Every route has a flow, even when it is only two nodes: the request arrives, the response goes out. The flow editor is where anything in between goes. Nodes run left to right along the connections you draw, and the path taken decides which response node is reached — which is how one route answers 200 to one caller and 401 to another.
logic.tableCaption: The node palette and what each node does
logic.doesAuth: Checks for a credential of a given shape — API key, bearer token, basic or JWT — and sends the call down its Pass or Fail output. It checks shape, never validity: there is no identity provider behind a mock, so a JWT signature is not verified.
logic.doesCondition: Compares two values and branches True or False. Either side can be a fixed value or something out of the request, and the tests include equals, contains, starts with, greater than, is present, is missing and matches pattern.
logic.doesSwitch: The same idea with more than two outcomes: one value, a list of cases, and a Default for everything unmatched.
logic.doesDelay: Waits before continuing, so you can see what your loading states actually look like.
logic.doesRandomBranch: Sends calls down one of several outputs by weight — the way to make a route fail one time in twenty rather than never or always.
logic.doesSetVariable: Writes a value that later nodes and the response can read, under a name you choose.
logic.doesLog: Writes a line into this call's trace in the request log. It never reaches the server's own logs.
logic.doesHttpRequest: Calls a real service and continues with its reply on OK or its failure on Error. Addresses are checked before every hop and redirects are followed one guarded step at a time, so a mock cannot be pointed at a private network.
logic.doesTransform: Reshapes a value between two nodes. It can be placed and wired, and a request that reaches it answers 500 rather than pretending it worked.
logic.doesResponse: Ends the flow and sends a reply. A flow can hold several, and each one owns its own status, content type and body.
logic.p1: The canvas has the shortcuts you would expect: drag from a node's right edge to connect it, double-click a connection to remove it, ⌘Z and ⇧⌘Z to undo and redo, ⌘C, ⌘V and ⌘D to copy, paste and duplicate, and the bracket keys to fold the panels either side. Tidy up re-lays a graph that has grown tangled.
logic.p2: A route whose flow branches has more than one response, so the single response box on the route screen stops being the whole answer and says which one it is showing. That is deliberate: one box could only ever show one branch, and quietly showing the first would be worse than pointing at the editor.

variables.title: Variables and environments
variables.p1: Variables are values your routes read instead of hard-coding them — a base URL, a fixture id, a token your own tests expect. Set one on the workspace and every server in it sees the value; set the same name on a server and that server's value wins.
variables.p2: Environments are separate sets of the same names. Overriding happens inside one environment, never across two, so a staging set and a production set cannot leak into each other.
variables.p3: A variable marked as a secret is never sent back to the browser — the list shows dots, and saving over it replaces the value rather than revealing it. It is still stored on our servers and still readable by anything your mock returns it in, so secret here means hidden from the screen, not safe to publish.

portability.title: Bringing an API in, and taking it away
portability.p1: You do not have to build from nothing. Import OpenAPI takes a Swagger or OpenAPI document, in JSON or YAML, and turns every operation in it into a working route with a response shaped from its schema — paths, methods, status codes, and any example the document supplied. Internal pointers are resolved; remote ones are left alone rather than fetched.
portability.p2: Export this server gives you a JSON bundle holding everything the studio knows: every route, its response and the flow behind it. That is the one to commit next to your code or keep as a backup, and it is the format that comes back in whole.
portability.p3: There is an OpenAPI export as well, for describing the API to other tools. It cannot carry generated data — a field that returns a different name on every call goes out as one example of a name — so treat it as a description rather than as a backup.

limits.title: Limits, logs and what is public
limits.intro: Every ceiling here is either about stopping one workspace from making the service unusable for everybody else, or about a mock staying a mock. These are the numbers the server actually enforces.
limits.tableCaption: Limits, their values and the reason for each
limits.whyWorkspaces: An affordance rather than a wall — the cookie is yours and clearing it buys more. Creation is metered per address instead.
limits.whyServers: Enough to split a project by service, few enough that one workspace stays navigable.
limits.whyRoutes: Comfortably above what an imported OpenAPI document brings across.
limits.whyDelay: An uncapped delay is a denial of service anybody could configure in two clicks.
limits.whyRuntime: Whatever is unfinished at this point reports an error instead of hanging.
limits.whyResponse: A mock is a fixture. Anything larger is a file host.
limits.whyOpenapi: Larger than any specification anyone has pasted in, small enough to parse without pinning a server.
limits.whyLogs: Newest first; the oldest are trimmed after each write.
limits.whyRetention: Anything older is dropped, and a large body is truncated and marked rather than kept whole.
limits.outro: Credentials are stripped before a log row is written rather than filtered when it is read, so an Authorization header your code sent by accident was never on disk here. Everything else about the call is: path, query, headers, both bodies, and the nodes that ran.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Do I need an account to use the Mock Server Studio?
faq.a1: No. Creating a workspace writes a secret into this browser and hands you a recovery key; between them, those are the whole of ownership. There is no email, no password and nothing to verify.
faq.q2: Does a mock endpoint keep answering after I close the tab?
faq.a2: Yes. Endpoints are served from our servers rather than from your browser, so a deployed front end or a colleague's machine can call them whether or not this page is open.
faq.q3: Can anybody else call my mock endpoints?
faq.a3: Anybody holding the address can. There is no password on a mock endpoint, so treat everything in a response as public and never put a real credential, key or customer record in one.
faq.q4: What happens if I lose my recovery key?
faq.a4: Any browser that already owns the workspace keeps working, so the fastest fix is to open it on one of those. If none is left, the workspace cannot be recovered — only a one-way digest of the key is stored, so nobody can look it up or reissue it.
faq.q5: Can a response return different data on every call?
faq.a5: Yes, and that is most of the point. Fake data, UUIDs, the current time and One of fields all resolve per call, and a random branch can vary which response is reached at all.
faq.q6: How do I make a route fail, or be slow?
faq.a6: Add a Response node carrying the status you want and route to it — through a Condition to fail for particular input, or through a Random branch to fail a set share of calls. A Delay node in front of it models a slow service.
faq.q7: Can I take my work somewhere else?
faq.a7: Yes. Export this server gives a JSON bundle carrying every route, its response and its flow, and there is an OpenAPI export for describing the API to other tools. The bundle is the one that round-trips; the OpenAPI cannot carry generated values.

endpoints.empty: No routes yet. Add one above.
endpoints.noSelection: Pick a route to edit its response.
endpoints.enabledHint: A disabled route answers 404 without being deleted.
endpoints.bodyHint: Build the shape you want back. Every field picks where its value comes from — a fixed value, something out of the request, or generated data.
endpoints.uploadsHint: Form posts are read too. JSON, form-encoded and multipart bodies all become fields you can address by name — and an uploaded file becomes a value carrying filename, contentType and size, so a condition can branch on its type or its size in bytes. The file itself is never stored.
endpoints.bodyBranchedHint: This route answers differently depending on the request, so it has more than one response.
endpoints.bodyBranched: This flow branches into {count, plural, one {# response} other {# responses}}. Each one is edited on its own node in the flow editor — a single box here could only ever show you one of them.

endpoints.pathHelp: Use :name for a parameter and a trailing * for everything below a prefix — /users/:id, /files/*. Leave the query out: /game answers /game?id=7 too, and you read id in the response with “From the request” → “Query”.
endpoints.flowHint: The body above is what this route sends back. Open the flow editor to put logic in front of it — authentication, conditions, delays, variables and branches.

serverErrors.storage_unavailable: This deployment has no database configured.
serverErrors.not_owner: This browser does not have access to that workspace.
serverErrors.invalid_name: Give it a name of 60 characters or fewer.
serverErrors.invalid_key: A key is 3 to 32 characters of lowercase letters, digits and single hyphens, not starting or ending with one.
serverErrors.key_taken: That key is already in use. Try another.
serverErrors.key_reserved: That key is reserved. Try another.
serverErrors.server_limit_reached: This workspace is holding the maximum number of servers.
serverErrors.endpoint_limit_reached: This server is holding the maximum number of routes.
serverErrors.invalid_path: That is not a usable path. Use :name for a parameter, and a * only as the last segment.
serverErrors.path_has_query: A route is the path only — drop the ? and everything after it. /game?id=:game_id becomes the route /game, which answers whatever the query says. Read the value in the response with “From the request” → “Query” → id.
serverErrors.path_has_fragment: A route cannot contain a #. Browsers strip the fragment before the request is sent, so the server never sees it.
serverErrors.route_taken: This server already has that method on that path.
serverErrors.invalid_status: A status code is a whole number between 100 and 599.
serverErrors.invalid_body: The response body is not valid JSON.
serverErrors.graph_entry: A flow needs exactly one Request node — the point every call starts from.
serverErrors.graph_no_response: This flow has no Response node, so there is nothing for it to send back.
serverErrors.graph_dead_end: One branch of this flow ends without a Response node. Every path has to finish at one, including the ones a condition or a switch rarely takes.
serverErrors.graph_unreachable: A node in this flow is not connected to anything the Request can reach. Wire it up or delete it.
serverErrors.graph_cycle: This flow loops back on itself, so a request could run forever. Remove the connection that closes the loop.
serverErrors.graph_unsupported_node: This flow uses a node this version cannot run yet.
serverErrors.graph_unreadable: This flow could not be read. Reload the route and try again.

meta.title: Hosted JSON Server — A Real REST API From One db.json
meta.description: Paste a db.json and get a public REST API with full CRUD, filtering, sorting, pagination and relations — the json-server you know, without leaving a laptop running. No account: a secret in your browser proves ownership and a recovery key brings the server back anywhere.

hero.title: JSON Server, hosted
hero.subtitle: Write or upload a db.json and every route is built for you — list, read, create, replace, update and delete, with the same filtering, sorting, pagination and relations json-server has. The difference is that this one keeps answering after you close the laptop, so a front end you deploy somewhere can actually reach it.
hero.disclosureTitle: This one does not run in your browser
hero.disclosureBody: Almost everything on ToolForge works entirely in your tab. This cannot: a page has no way to answer somebody else's HTTP request, so your document is stored on our servers and served from there. That means we hold your data, anyone who has the address can read and change it, and there is no password on it — treat a JSON server as a public fixture for prototyping, never as somewhere to put anything real.

flow.title: From a db.json to a live API
flow.intro: Six steps, and only one of them differs from running json-server on your laptop — this one keeps answering after you close it.
flow.documentBody: The box on this page already holds json-server's own example document, so you can press Create and have something to call straight away. Replace it with your own whenever you like — every top-level key becomes a resource.
flow.createBody: Give it a name, and an address if you want to choose one; leave the address blank and one is generated. The address is the part that appears in the URL your client calls.
flow.recoveryKeyBody: It is shown once, right after the server is created, and only a hash of it is stored — so it cannot be shown again or looked up. It is how you reach this server from a browser that does not already own it, including this one after you clear cookies.
flow.routesBody: The Routes tab lists every path the document publishes, derived from the document rather than authored. If a route is on that list it answers; if a key publishes nothing, the tab names it and says why.
flow.callTitle: Point a client at the address
flow.callBody: Copy the base address and call it from fetch, curl, an HTTP client, or a front end you have deployed. Nothing has to be running on your machine.
flow.watchBody: The Requests tab shows the most recent calls the server answered. The Data tab is the live document — editing it there replaces everything at once, which is the same thing a client does one record at a time — and Download db.json takes it away.
flow.outro: There is no password on a JSON server. Anybody with the address can read and change the document, so it is a public fixture for prototyping and never somewhere to put anything real.

document.title: What a db.json has to look like
document.p1: A db.json is an object at the top level, with one key per resource. What each key holds decides what that key publishes.
document.p2: An array of objects is a collection and gets the full six routes — list, create, read, replace, update and delete. A lone object is a singular resource and gets three, because there is nothing to create a second of and nothing to delete by id.
document.p3: Anything else — a bare number, a string, an array of strings — publishes no routes. That is not an error: the value is still stored and still comes back from the document root, and the Routes tab names the keys it could not publish so nothing reads as having vanished.
document.p4: A resource name has to survive being a path segment, so it starts with a letter or a digit and continues with letters, digits, underscores and hyphens. posts and blog_posts are resources; a key holding a slash or a question mark is stored but not published, because its own routes would be unusable.
document.p5: Every record in a collection has to be an object with an id that is unique within that collection. A duplicate id is refused rather than accepted, because one of the two records could never be reached by any URL.

routes.title: The routes you get
routes.intro: The route table is derived from the document by the same function the server matches against, so a route printed in the studio is a route that answers. These are the paths a collection named posts and a singular resource named profile publish.
routes.tableCaption: Derived routes and what each one does
routes.doesList: Every record in the collection, filtered, sorted and paged by the query string.
routes.doesCreate: Adds a record. An id is generated when the body does not carry one.
routes.doesReplace: Replaces that record entirely with the body.
routes.doesMerge: Merges the body into the record, leaving unmentioned fields alone.
routes.doesRemove: Removes the record, and nulls foreign keys in other collections that pointed at it.
routes.doesSingular: The whole object. There is no id, so there is no record route and nothing to delete.
routes.doesSingularWrite: PATCH merges into the object; PUT replaces it.
routes.doesRoot: The whole document, including keys that publish no routes of their own.
routes.p1: Paths are the resource names exactly as written in the document, so renaming a key renames its routes. The Routes tab is the list to trust: it is generated from the same code the matcher uses, rather than being a second description that could drift from it.
routes.p2: A paused server answers 503 on every route until you resume it. Nothing is deleted and the document is untouched.

query.title: Filtering, sorting, paging and relations
query.intro: A filter is written as field, colon, operator, equals, value. Leaving the operator out means eq, so ?views=100 and ?views:eq=100 are the same query, and a dotted field descends into nested objects — ?author.name:eq=typicode.
query.operatorCaption: Filter operators and what each one matches
query.meansEq: The field equals the value. This is the default, so the operator can be left out.
query.meansNe: The field is anything other than the value.
query.meansLt: The field is less than the value.
query.meansLte: The field is less than or equal to the value.
query.meansGt: The field is greater than the value.
query.meansGte: The field is greater than or equal to the value.
query.meansIn: The field is one of a comma-separated list.
query.meansContains: The field's text contains the value, ignoring case.
query.meansStartsWith: The field's text starts with the value, ignoring case.
query.meansEndsWith: The field's text ends with the value, ignoring case.
query.keysIntro: Six query keys are read by the engine itself. Everything else in the query string is treated as a field condition.
query.keyCaption: Reserved query keys and what each one does
query.doesSort: Sorts by one or more fields, comma separated, each optionally prefixed with a hyphen for descending.
query.doesPage: Turns the reply into a paginated envelope carrying first, prev, next, last, pages, items and data.
query.doesPerPage: How many records a page holds. It only has an effect alongside _page.
query.doesEmbed: Embeds a related resource. A plural target brings in the children pointing at this record; a singular target brings in the parent this record points at.
query.doesWhere: A JSON expression for conditions the flat syntax cannot express, including and and or groups.
query.doesDependent: On a DELETE, also removes records in the named collection whose foreign key pointed at the deleted row.
query.p1: Sorting compares text the way a person reads it rather than by character code, so a title sorts before Tenth instead of after every capital letter. Ascending order also puts empty and missing values last — except zero, which sorts as the number it is.
query.p2: A query value is read by its own shape, not by the type of the field it is compared against. true, false and null become those values and anything reading as a number becomes one, which has a consequence worth knowing in advance: ?code=007 asks for the number 7 and will not match a field holding the text 007. That is json-server's behaviour, and matching it is the point — a fixture that behaved differently once hosted would be the one defect this tool cannot have.
query.p3: _per_page on its own is not pagination; without _page you get a plain array. When a page is asked for and no size is given, a page holds {value, number} records, and asking for a size of zero gives you one rather than the default.
query.p4: _embed runs before filtering and sorting, which is what lets you sort on an embedded field — embedding post and then sorting on post.title works, and would not if the order were reversed.

writing.title: Creating, replacing, updating and deleting
writing.p1: POST adds a record to a collection. PUT replaces one entirely, so fields left out of the body are gone. PATCH merges, leaving unmentioned fields alone. All three answer with the record as it now stands.
writing.p2: DELETE removes a record and then nulls any foreign key in other collections that pointed at it, so nothing is left referring to something that no longer exists. Add _dependent to remove those orphaned children rather than leaving them.
writing.p3: The Data tab in the studio edits the same document those routes write to. Saving there replaces the whole thing at once, which is worth knowing if a client is writing at the same time — the last save wins.
writing.p4: Reset to the original puts back the document the server was created with, and Download db.json gives you the current one as a file. It is an ordinary db.json, so json-server runs against it unchanged.

storage.title: Storage, the warning, and the lock
storage.intro: There are two size numbers and the gap between them is deliberate: what may be uploaded is smaller than where writes stop, so a server created at its own ceiling is not full before its first POST.
storage.tableCaption: Limits, their values and the reason for each
storage.whyServers: An affordance rather than a wall — the cookie is yours and clearing it buys more. Creation is metered per address instead.
storage.whyUpload: What may be pasted, uploaded or written back from the editor. Below the stored ceiling on purpose.
storage.whyDocument: Where growing writes stop. Reads and deletes carry on.
storage.whyWarn: Where the usage bar changes tone and the copy starts naming the bytes left.
storage.whyCollections: Top-level keys. More than this is a database rather than a fixture.
storage.whyRecords: A bound on work rather than on size: every write rewrites the collection it touches.
storage.whyDepth: Deep enough for any realistic fixture, shallow enough to report a refusal instead of crashing on one.
storage.whyPerPage: Above this, one request could serialise the whole document many times over.
storage.whyLogs: Newest first; the oldest are trimmed after each write.
storage.p1: At the ceiling, POST, PUT and PATCH answer 507 while GET, DELETE and OPTIONS carry on. That is what makes the lock recoverable: a full server can still be read, and deleting records you no longer need is the way out. A limit that also refused DELETE would be a trap whose only escape was discarding everything.
storage.p2: The usage bar changes tone well before that point and names how many bytes are left, so the lock is something you saw coming rather than something that happened to you.

differences.title: Where this differs from a local json-server
differences.p1: The routes, the query language and the shapes are json-server v1's, and they were checked by running both engines over the same document rather than by reading the documentation — which found seven behaviours a hand-written implementation had got wrong. A well-formed query behaves here exactly as it does locally.
differences.p2: What differs is where it runs. There is no process on your machine to keep alive, so a preview deployment, a phone on another network or a colleague can all reach the same fixture. There is also no localhost to hide behind: anybody with the address has full read and write access.
differences.p3: Malformed input is refused rather than ignored. A _where that is not valid JSON and an unknown operator both answer 400 here, where the reference silently drops the filter and returns the whole collection. A filter that is quietly ignored looks exactly like one that matched everything, which is the worse failure.
differences.p4: One _where clause is honoured here that the reference matches nothing for, and that is strictly additive. None of these three differences can change what a correct client sees.
differences.p5: Where the reference has a defect, it is matched rather than fixed — a nested _where clause against a field that is not an object passes there and passes here. Imposing a judgement about which behaviour is nicer is exactly what would make a hosted fixture disagree with a local one.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Do I need an account?
faq.a1: No. Creating a server writes a secret into this browser and hands you a recovery key; between them, those are the whole of ownership. Nothing to verify and no password to choose.
faq.q2: How is this different from running json-server locally?
faq.a2: The behaviour is the same — same routes, same query language, same shapes. The difference is that this one keeps answering after you close the laptop, so a deployed front end, a phone on another network or a teammate can reach the same fixture.
faq.q3: Is my data private?
faq.a3: No. There is no password on a JSON server, and anybody with the address can read and change the document. Use it for prototyping fixtures and never for anything real.
faq.q4: What happens when the document fills up?
faq.a4: POST, PUT and PATCH answer 507 while GET, DELETE and OPTIONS keep working, so deleting records you no longer need is the way back. The usage bar warns you well before that point.
faq.q5: Can I still use my db.json locally?
faq.a5: Yes. Download db.json gives you the current document as a file, and it is an ordinary db.json — run json-server against it and you get the same API on your own machine.
faq.q6: Why did my filter return nothing, or everything?
faq.a6: A local json-server drops a filter it cannot parse and returns the whole collection; here that answers 400 instead, so a typo is visible rather than silent. If a well-formed filter returns nothing, check the value's type: a numeric-looking value is compared as a number, so ?code=007 will not match the text 007.
faq.q7: What happens to related records when I delete one?
faq.a7: Foreign keys in other collections that pointed at the deleted record are set to null, whether or not you asked. Add _dependent with the collection name to remove those children instead of leaving them orphaned.

article.introBody: You give it a JSON document; it gives you a GraphQL endpoint. Every top-level key holding an array of objects becomes a type with a list field, a by-id field, a page envelope and four mutations. Every lone object becomes a type you can read and replace. Every foreign key becomes a relation you can follow from either end. Nothing is configured and nothing is generated into a file — the schema is derived from the document on every request, so it is never out of step with the data.
article.introSibling: The JSON Server Studio serves the same document as REST. The two run side by side on the same file, and a document sorted through one comes back in the same order through the other.
article.schemaBody: A collection's fields come from reading every record, not a sample — a type inferred from the first fifty records that record four thousand contradicts is a schema its own data fails to validate against. A whole number inside GraphQL's 32-bit Int is Int; anything larger is Float, because serialising a bigger value through Int is an error at response time rather than a rounding. A field that is a string in one record and a number in another is JSON, not the wider of the two. A field absent or null anywhere is nullable. A nested object is JSON rather than a generated nested type, because a name invented from a field key would collide across collections and multiply the schema by the document's depth.
article.namesBody: posts becomes the type Post, the fields posts and post, and the mutations createPost, updatePost, patchPost and deletePost. The inflector carries the irregulars — people becomes Person, categories becomes Category, series stays series — because a wrong guess here is a published type name that ends up in whatever your codegen wrote. It is not complete, and no inflector is, so the studio prints the derived name beside every key: a guess it got wrong is visible before anything depends on it. GraphQL has no hyphen in its name grammar, so blog-posts is published as blogPosts, and a key starting with a digit gains one underscore. Both are reported rather than done quietly.
article.relationsBody: A field named like the singular of a collection followed by Id — postId against a posts collection — publishes Comment.post and Post.comments in one go. That convention is json-server's, so a document that works there works here. Three rules keep it honest: the foreign key has to actually be present on the child, a relation never shadows a field the document already has, and a self-reference is skipped. Both sides take page arguments, and the many side is the reason to reach for GraphQL over the REST studio — you get both ends in one round trip and pick the fields on each.
article.queryBody: Every list field takes where, orderBy, order, page and perPage. The filters are typed inputs rather than a convention, so an IDE completes them and a codegen types them: views: '{' gt: 100 '}', title: '{' contains: "draft" '}', id: '{' in: ["1", "2"] '}'. Clauses on different fields AND together, and AND, OR and NOT nest. Fields of type JSON and list fields have no filter, because there is no comparison over an arbitrary nested value that means anything and one that quietly matched nothing would be worse than none. perPage defaults to ten — a list field with no ceiling would make the cost estimate below impossible.
article.mutationBody: create returns the record including the id it was given, which is the only way you learn what to ask for next. update replaces every field; patch merges. A record's id is absent from the update input rather than accepted and ignored, so you find out at validation instead of discovering your write went somewhere else. Mutations are refused over GET: the specification reserves GET for safe requests, and honouring that is what stops a link — in an email, in a crawler's queue, in a chat client's preview fetcher — from writing to your fixture. The input types hold the fields the collection already has, so adding a new field means editing the document rather than inventing one through the API.
article.limitsBody: GraphQL moves the cost of a request from the server's route table to your query, which is the whole security difference from a REST fixture. A single document can ask for every collection, joined to itself, many times over, in two hundred bytes — and the derived relations are cyclic by construction, since a post has comments and every comment has a post. So three bounds run before any resolver: depth stops the cycle, an estimated node count stops breadth, and a root-field count stops aliasing one field two hundred times. Every response carries x-graphql-cost and x-graphql-depth so you can watch the estimate climb as you nest, rather than discovering the ceiling as a mysterious 400. Introspection is exempt from all of it, because its cost is bounded by the schema and an endpoint no IDE can read is most of the point gone.
article.storageTitle: Size, and the way back from full
article.storageBody: A document may be up to {upload} when it is pasted in, and may grow to {stored} before writes stop. The gap is deliberate: a server created at its own ceiling would be full before its first mutation. Past {warn, number}% the usage bar changes tone and names the bytes left, so the lock is something you saw coming. When it does lock, queries and delete mutations keep working — deleting a record is the way out, and a ceiling that refused every write would be a trap whose only escape is discarding the whole document.
article.privacyTitle: What is stored, and what is not
article.privacyBody: The document is stored, because serving it is the point. The last {logs, number} operations are logged as a name, a type, a status, a duration and a cost — the query text is not kept, because a query is mostly your own field names against your own data and a second copy of that is more than this service should hold. A browser's claim on a server is a random secret in an HttpOnly cookie; the server stores only its hash. The recovery key is shown once and stored only as a hash, so it cannot be looked up or shown again. Deleting a server removes its document, its logs and every browser's access.
article.argWhere: Filters the collection with typed comparisons.
article.argWhereWhen: You want a subset. It is the one argument an IDE can complete for you, because it is a real input type rather than a convention.
article.argOrderBy: Names the field to sort on, as an enum of that type's own fields.
article.argOrderByWhen: Order matters. JSON and list fields are absent from the enum — there is no sort over an arbitrary nested value.
article.argOrder: ASC or DESC. Defaults to ASC.
article.argOrderWhen: You passed orderBy. On its own it does nothing.
article.argPageWhen: You are walking a collection. A page past the end is empty rather than an error, so a loop ends cleanly.
article.argPerPage: How many records per page. Defaults to {default, number}, capped at {max, number}.
article.argPerPageWhen: Always worth thinking about — this is the number the cost estimate multiplies down your query tree.
article.argsCaveat: Two things a table cannot hold. orderBy disappears entirely from a type with no sortable field, so a schema that has it is telling you something. And perPage having a default is what makes the cost bound possible at all: without one, every list would have to be assumed at its maximum and ordinary two-level queries would be refused.

faq.q1: Is the endpoint public?
faq.a1: Yes. Anyone with the address can query it and can run its mutations. There is no key and no authentication — that is what makes it useful for a front end on localhost and what makes it wrong for anything private. Pause the server from its settings tab when you are not using it; it then answers 503 rather than serving.
faq.q2: Can I use it with Apollo, urql or graphql-codegen?
faq.a2: Yes. Introspection is on, the SDL is a normal GraphQL schema using the standard scalars plus one JSON scalar, and the studio offers both schema.graphql and the introspection JSON as downloads. Point apollo client:download-schema or graphql-codegen at the endpoint and it works like any other server.
faq.q3: Why did my query come back as too costly?
faq.a3: The estimate multiplies each list field's page size down the query tree, so nesting three ten-item lists is a thousand nodes before any field is read. Narrow it with a smaller perPage, a where filter, or fewer nested relations. Every response carries x-graphql-cost, so you can see what a query costs before it becomes a problem.
faq.q4: Why is my Post type called Postt, or my people collection called Peopl?
faq.a4: The inflector guessed wrong. It carries the common irregulars but it is not a dictionary, and the studio prints the derived name beside every key so a wrong guess is visible. Rename the key in your document to something it reads correctly — the schema follows the document, always.
faq.q5: Can I add a field through a mutation?
faq.a5: No. The input types hold the fields the collection already has, so a value of the wrong shape is refused at validation rather than stored and discovered later. To add a field, edit the document in the Document tab and save — the schema rebuilds from it immediately.
faq.q6: Does it support subscriptions?
faq.a6: No. A subscription needs a transport that stays open and a source of events, and a stored fixture has neither. A schema that advertised subscriptions and never fired one would be worse than saying so.
faq.q7: What happens if I stop using it?
faq.a7: Nothing is deleted automatically today, but this is a free fixture service and dormant servers may be swept in future. Anything you would mind losing belongs somewhere else — and the document is one download away in the Document tab.
faq.q8: Can the same document be served as REST and GraphQL at once?
faq.a8: Not from one server, but the two studios read the same db.json, so you can paste one document into both and compare. They deliberately agree on the things that could otherwise differ: how records sort, how ids are generated and coerced, what counts as a collection, and where the size ceiling is.
